[The statement of Hon. Angelo D. Roncallo follows:] STATEMENT OF HON. ANGELO D. RONCALLO 

DEFENDING THE RIGHT TO LIFE OF THE UNBORN 

Mr. Chairman, I very much appreciate the opportunity to testify before the 

Subcommittee today in support of Senator Helms' Constitutional Amendment to protect the rights of our unborn children. It is identical to the Amendment which was introduced originally in the House by Congressman Hogan and to which I have given my unqualified support. It is the proposal which I feel has generated the most interest in the House and which has the best chance of success in a floor vote. For this reason, I have signed the discharge petition sacred. In jeopardy is not only that right which we in this country have consideration of the same language on the Senate Floor will reduce the controversy and focus the debate squarely on the issue involved. 

The Supreme Court decision which over a year ago upheld the legality of abortion has placed us in the untenable position of weighing one life against another, when for two hundred years we have acknowledge that all life is sacred. In jeopardy is not only that right which we in this country have considered one of our most fundamental and cherished rights-the right to life. 

But also at risk in such a situation is a deadening of our moral sensibilities and responsibilities and an erosion of our respect for life. Respect for life should be nothing less than the most precious of our values; it should not be treated lightly. For when it is decided that one stage of human life is of no real value, when its continued existence is considered an inconvenience to others and may be terminated without scruple, then our reverence for life at any and every other stage is compromised. Our regard for the absolute right of each individual to his own life can only be diminished in such circumstances. 

Congressional intervention is imperative, for human lives, hundreds of thousands of human lives are at stake. Let there be no mistake; abortion destroys human life. It has become increasingly common for medical authorities to agree that life begins at the moment of conception. To those who assert that human life begins only at birth we can only reply rhetorically: What then is the entity which develops within the mother's womb if not actually a human being? 

When a child is born prematurely and survives-as he is likely to do given continuing medical advances-is that being more human than one which was forcibly aborted at the same age?

There exists no rational basis for an assertion that the unborn child is a mere appendage to the mother; for medical science has shown as that genetically mother and child are separate individuals from conception. Nor can the developing child's dependency upon the mother provide reason for regarding it as something less than human life. We are all dependent upon others in various degrees at one point or another in our daily lives. Dependence per se, therefore, cannot be judged a valid criterion for determining the humanity of a developing child. 

The Constitutional amendment which I have supported would reestablish the birthright of every unborn child. It would do so simply by applying existing principles of due process of law and the equal protection of the laws to all human beings, including the child in the womb. We cannot subscribe to the Supreme Court's view that the unborn child is not a person or does not possess meaningful life. Our reverence for the sanctity of life must allow no exception; it can be nothing short of absolute. The American constitutional guarantee of the equal protection of the law is rooted in such reverence as well as in the ultimate dignity of the individual and the invioability of innocent human life.

Legalized abortion, on the other hand, presents a disturbing reversal of our law's steady progress toward recognition of the dignity, value, and essential equality of human life. It is, as David Louisell and John Noonan in the Morality of Abortion have pointed out, a negation of the constitutional guarantee of equal protection of the law. It is a loveless act offensive to the conscience of our common law tradition. Attempts to justify it on the ground that the fetus is not fully human want for logic. To pick any moment other than that of concepion as the starting point of human life is artificial and arbitrary. All human life, whether fetal, infant, adolescent, mature, or aged, is in the process of becoming. Abortion can be justified only if society has the right to prescribe the conditions of continuing life and to authorize the weighing of the right to life against other values.

Mr. Chairman, I would like to conclude my remarks with an observation by 

Mr. Noonan, who has penetrated to the core of the matter at issue here today in very simple and eloquent terms. simple coexistence with other humans demands that the lives of some not be open to sacrifice for the welfare and convenience of others. If man can be recognized at all in the multiple forms of humanity, the notion of man necessitates respect for the human person's right to live. One person's freedom to obtain an abortion is the denial of another person's right to live. 

It is for this reason, Mr. Chairman, that I support the Constitutional Amendment which Senator Helms has introduced into your chamber. We in Congress must not renege on our responsibility and obligation to protect and defend the inalienable rights of all individuals in this Nation. We must diligently hasten to restore the full protection of the law for human life at every stage of development..

Senator BAYH. We will recess pending the calling of the Chair. 

I understand that the next hearings are going to be April 23. [Whereupon, at 1:05 p.m., the hearing was recessed subject to the call of the Chair.]

STATEMENT OF THE HONORABLE GEORGE M. O'BRIEN, A REPRESENTATIVE FROM ILLINOIS. 

Mr. Chairman, we are here today to, hopefully, commence serious Congressional consideration of amendments to the Constitution which are urgently needed to nullify the January 22, 1973 U.S. Supreme Court abortion decisions in Roe v. Wade, 410 U.S. 113 and Doe v. Bolton, 410 U.S. 179. I have stated on prior occasions, and repeat here, that these decisions, which strip the states of the power to prohibit abortions in approximately the first six months of pregnancy, are bad law. The decisions have been variously denounced by legal scholars as "unfortunate",¹ replete with error and fraught with dangerous implications", lacking "constitutional foundation", and lacking "colorable support in the constitutional text, history, or any other appropriate source of constitutional doctrine." On reading the decisions, one is struck by the Court's reliance on decisions concerning the right to receive contraceptives as justification for sustaining an absortion right, the fundamental distinction being the difference between prevention of conception and the destruction of human life; by the Court's utter disregard for numerous lower court decisions clearly establishing the legal personhood of the unborn in various areas of the law; by the Court's disinclination to factually determine when human life begins, yet its willingness to read the unborn out of the protection afforded by the Fourteenth Amendment, without so much as a reference to the intent of the Framers; and by the Court's arbitrary selection of fetal viability as the time in pregnancy at and after which states may conditionally prohibit abortions. 

1 Loewy, Abortive Reasons and Obscene Standards: A Comment on the Abortion and 

Obscenity Cases, 52 N.C.L. Rev. 223 (1973). 

2 Byrn. An American Tragedy: The Supreme Court on Abortion, 41 Fordham L. Rev. 807, 

809 (1973). 

3 Supreme Court Review 1973-Abortion, 64 Jour. Crim. L. and Criminology, 393, 399 (1973).

Ely, The Wages of Crying Wolf: A Comment on Roe v. Wade, 82 Yale L. J. 920, 943 

(1973).

As a result of such faulty legal analysis, the seven majority justices in Wade and Bolton have visited on 210 million Americans a legal system that permits hundreds of thousands of legal abortions a year. That the Law, in all its Majesty, stoops to permit such behavior wounds me as a lawyer and as a human being. 

The Congress must take the lead in ensuring that human life, at all stages of development, receives the protection of the laws of this country. While it is true that Wade and Bolton allow the states certain regulatory authority over abortions, both decisions make clear that such regulation must not unduly inhibit the exercise of the abortion right. Simply put, the states are now helpless to stem the pro-abortion tide. Clearly, Congress must assume the leadership role. It is to this end, hopefully, that we are gathered here today. 

A Constitutional amendment is needed to restore the right to life to the unborn. This conclusion is compelled from the fact that, as a result of the Wade decision, the Fourteenth Amendment to the Constitution must now be read to (1) insulate the abortion decision with a right of privacy that precludes the prohibition of abortions in the early months of pregency and (2) deny to the unborn the protections of that Amendment.

This Committee has before it two proposed Constitutional amendments, S.J. 

Res. 119, the so-called "Buckley Amendment" and S.J. Res. 130, introduced by

Senator Helms, either of which would correct the immoral and legally illogical Wade and Bolton decisions and ensure constitutional protection for the unborn. 

I personally favor S.J. Res. 130 which is identical to H.J. Res. 631, a proposed 

Constitutional Amendment which I have introduced in the House. S.J. Res. 119, unfortunately, embodies an exception to the general prohibition on abortion; an exception which I fear may be subsequently interpreted in the courts in such a manner as to render the general prohibition meaningless. I urge this Committee however to give its prompt attention to weighing the virtues and vices of both measures so that action may be completed at the earliest possible date. 

Before closing, I would assert that it is possible that Congress would be reluctant to vote for a Constitutional amendment which would effect a nationwide abortion ban. In addition to proposed amendments such as S.J. Res. 119 and 

S.J. Res. 130, which would have such an effect, I therefore urge alternative consideration of an amendment which would, at least, return to the states the plenary power to regulate or limit abortion practices. I have co-sponsored such a measure, H.J. Res. 537, in the House. The substantive language of this amendment reads:

Nothing in this Constitution shall bar any State, or the Congress with regard to any area over which it is granted the power to exercise exclusive legislation from enacting laws respecting the life of an unborn child from the time of conception.

Rather than prohibit abortions in every state, an amendment such as H.J. Res. 

537 would enpower each state to regulate abortion as it saw fit. Such an amendment would restore that notion of Federalism which was destroyed in Wade. 

As Mr. Justice White noted in dissent, the result of Wade is that "the people and the legislatures of the 50 states are constitutionally disentitled" to decide the abortion question. White continued:

As an exercise of raw judicial power, the Court perhaps has the authority to do what it does today; but in my view its judgement is an improvident and extravagant exercise of the power of judicial review that the Constitution extends to this Court. [The abortion] issue, for the most part, should be left with the people and to the political processes the people have devised to govern their affairs. 

Indeed, given the opportunity to offer direct expression on the question of abortion, voters in two referenda, one in North Dakota and one in Michigan, on 

November 7, 1972, resoundly defeated efforts to liberalize the availability of abortions in those states. However, the Supreme Court-or rather seven Justices has decreed that states may no longer decide for themselves; that abortions must be available in all the states. This usurpation of a traditional state power is another shocking result of the Wade decision. The Court of Appeals for Kentucky, the highest appellate court in that state, recently invalidated the Kentucky abortion statute, under the constitutional compulsion of the principles enunciated in Wade. Mr. Justice Osborne of that court, in concurring in the decision, remarked on the usurpation of state power effected by Wade:

I concur in the actions of the court in this matter simply because I feel I have no alternative. By doing so I do not want it to be interpreted that I agree to any part of the United States Supreme Court's decision in Roe v. 

Wade. . . . I believe that court, in this instance and in many others, has and is usurping the rights of the several states in this Union to determine for themselves what constitutes a crime and to enforce their own criminal laws. This inference has now reached the point of the ridiculous. The citizens of the several states are forced, more and more, to look to the seat of our National Government for guidance, regulation and control and when they look they are perceiving more and more of nothing but confusion and incompetence.

The federalist government which our ancestors established in this land has, at this time and point, been obliterated. This has been accomplished by all three branches of our Federal Government with no reason or purpose but to seize for themselves power. Now that they have seized the power, it daily becomes apparent that they totally lack the qualifications to properly exercise it.

If the court's decision in Roe v. Wade is a barometer of what is about to befall we should all turn our heads to heaven for mercy for there is nothing left. 

To conclude, Mr. Chairman, this Committee must act immediately on measures to ensure the right to life to the unborn. Congress must present to the states such a measure at the earliest possible occasion. At the very minimum, we must permit the individual states to decide the abortion question for themselves. And we must never lose sight of our purpose-to preserve the sanctity of human life. 

My personal views, and I would hope the views of most people here today, find expression in the eloquence of the distinguished French philosopher, Francois 

Mauriac, when he wrote:

I believe as I did as a child, that life has meaning, a direction, a value; that no suffering is lost, that every tear counts, and each drop of blood, and the secret of living in today's troubled world is found in the simple phrase of St. John, "Deus caritas est."

STATEMENT BY SENATOR FLOYD K. HASKELL 

Mr. Chairman: I appreciate the opportunity afforded me to present my views on a proposed Amendment to the Constitution of the United States. 

The proposed amendment, offered jointly by my colleague from New York, Mr. Buckley, and my colleague from North Carolina, Mr. Helms, would prohibit abortions from being performed in this nation for any reason other than ". emergency when a reasonable medical certainty exists that continuation of the pregnancy will cause the death of the mother." an I can well understand the serious religious and moral objections to legalized abortion. Indeed, all of us must recognize what a momentous and difficult decision it must be for anyone to make regardless of the particular situation. 

Nonetheless, feel it is too personal and too private a matter to be determined by federal legislation or to be prohibited by adoption of an Amendment to the Constitution.

The decision of the Supreme Court of the United States in Roe v. Wade, 410 U.S. 13 (1973), sets forth both the legal and moral arguments for and against statutes restricting a woman's right to seek an abortion. 

Mr. Justice Blankmun acknowledged the Court's sensitivity to the controversy when he delivered the Court's opinion:

We forthwith acknowledge our awareness of the sensitive and emotional nature of the abortion controversy, of the vigorous opposing views, even among physicians, and of the deep and seemingly absolute convictions that the subject inspires. One's philosophy, one's experiences, one's exposure to the raw edges of human existence, one's religious training, one's attitudes toward life and family and their values, and the moral standards one establishes and seeks to observe, are all likely to influence and to color one's thinking and conclusions about abortion.

In addition, population growth, pollution, poverty, and racial overtones tend to complicate and not to simplify the problem. 

The Court concluded in part that: the Court has recognized that a right of personal privacy, or a guarantee of certain areas or zones of privacy, does exist under the Consti-

tution. In varying contexts the Court or individual Justices have indeed found at least the roots of that right in the First Amendment; in the Fourth and Fifth Amendments; in the penumbras of the Bill of Rights; in the 

Ninth Amendment; or in the concept of liberty guaranteed by the First 

Section of the Fourteenth Amendment. These decisions make it clear that only personal rights that can be deemed "fundamental" or "implicit in the concept of ordered liberty,". They also make it clear that the right has some extension to activities relating to marriage, procreation, contraception, family relationships, and child rearing and education. 

This right of privacy, whether it be founded in the Fourteenth Amendment's concept of personal liberty and restrictions upon state action, as we feel it is, or, as the District Court determined, in the Ninth Amendment's reservation of rights to the people, is broad enough to encompass a woman's decision whether or not to terminate her pregnancy. The detriment that the 

State would impose upon the pregnant woman by denying this choice altogether is apparent.¹ 

Mr. Justice Blackmun concluded:

We therefore conclude that the right of personal privacy includes the abortion decision, but that this right is not unqualified and must be considered against important state interests in regulation. 

We note that those federal and state courts that have recently considered abortion law challenges have reached the same conclusion. 

Mr. Chairman, I do not believe that we here in Congress should set in motion an action which would be contrary to the rights otherwise guaranteed by the Constitution.

The Court has clearly recognized the need for some degree of flexibility to be preserved to the individual States. The States are given the authority to determine whether or not abortions are to be available for "the stage subsequent to approximately the end of the first trimester". The States are also empowered to determine the procedures under which abortions shall be available during the first trimester of the pregnancy-who is to perform them, for example, and whether or not they must take place in accredited hospitals. 

I cannot, in good conscience, support Federal action which would be aimed toward limiting rights currently protected by the Constitution of the United States and reaffirmed by the Supreme Court of the United States. 

STATEMENT OF THE HONORABLE JAMES A. BURKE RIGHT TO LIFE 

Mr. Chairman, I want to thank you and the other distinguished Members of the Subcommittee for permitting me to submit testimony on what I believe to be the most important issue facing Congress and the nation today, the safeguarding 1 The appropriate citations have been eliminated for the sake of brevity. of the individual sacred right to life. It is a tragic reflection upon our society that a Member of Congress should even need to rise to the defense of this most basic right.

Yet, we have suddenly found ourselves in a society where abortion is a common, everyday experience, and where physicians and intellectuals freely discuss taking the lives of those whom they judge to be of no use to society. No principle is more deeply rooted in the history of our moral and legal development than the principle of preserving and protecting human life. Once life has begun it may not be ended at another's will. "Thou Shalt Not Kill" is more basic to human society than any other law. To assume that a mother has total discretion over whether a child lives or dies is to grant her power and authority unprecedented in morality or law. Once having given paramount authority, that of determining life or death, to the mother, how then could we justify the continued maintenance of laws dealing with child abuse, or laws requiring the support and education of the child? If we allow the physician to take the lives of the handicapped and the infirm, then why seek means to prevent and cure disease? Indeed, if these human rights are so trivial, if the individual means so little, then why have a represent". tive form of government?

The fact is, these rights do exist, and they must be preserved and protected. 

The unborn have long been held to have legal rights under the law. They have property rights. They may inherit property, family names, and in some societies, family titles. Their rights to property have long been affirmed by the courts of this country. If a child should die prior to birth, a death certificate is required certifying that an individual in legal existence has ceased to live. An unborn child has legal standing under tort law. The courts of this land have affirmed that the unborn have the right to sue for injury caused before birth. To argue that such principles of law are irrelevant where the child is not born alive is absurd. Obviously, there can be no rights claimed at birth if the person was not in legal existence at the time the injury or the property right first arose. 

The very existence of these rights is predicated upon the recognition that the unborn, at whatever stage of development, are in legal existence. As such, they deserve to be safeguarded, just as an adult is protected under existing laws governing homicide. 

There is, of course, the moral question which arises when the mother's life is severely endangered by the continuation of the pregnancy. In this case, it is clear that abortion may be permissible. This adheres to self-defense principles long established within our body of laws. But, we must remember that abortion statutes were designed to protect the unborn child-not to serve the whims of one or both parents. The responsibility of saving the child should be equal to the responsibility of saving the mother in those cases where abortion is necessary.

This requirement is not arbitrary or vague in nature, rather it serves a totally clear and well established motive which is the protection of the civil rights of the unborn. The question most often raised by proponents of abortion is that the mother's civil rights should take precedence over the unborn child's, even to the point of killing the child. It is argued that each woman should have the final and only say with regard to her reproductive life. In Corkey v. Edwards the court ruled that a great deal more was involved than the simple question of a woman's right not to bear children:

The basic distinction between a decision whether to bear children which is made before conception and one which is made after conception is that the first contemplates the creation of a new human organism, but the latter contemplates the destruction of such an organism already created. 

The unborn have rights which must be protected, and I believe that my bill offers the best possible way of insuring that those rights are recognized and safeguarded under the Constitution of the United States. The following is the text of my resolution, H.J.Res. 769:

Resolved by the Senate and House of Representatives of the United States of America in Congress assembled, (two-thirds of each House concurring therein), that the following article is proposed as an amendment to the Constitution of the United States, which shall be valid to all intents and purposes as part of the Constitution when ratified by the legislatures of three-fourths of the several States within seven years from the date of its submission by the Congress:

Section 1. With respect to the right of life, the word "person," as used in this article and in the fifth and fourteenth articles of amendment to the

Constitution of the United States, applies to all human beings, including their unborn offspring at every stage of their biological development, irrespective of age, health, function, or condition of dependency. 

Section 2. No abortion shall be performed by any person except under and in conformance with law permitting an abortion to be performed only in an emergency when a reasonable medical certainty exists that continuation of pregnancy will cause the death of the mother and requiring that person to make every reasonable effort, in keeping with good medical practice, to preserve the life of her unborn offspring.

Section 3. Congress and the several States shall have power to enforce this article by appropriate legislation within their respective jurisdictions. 

It is my belief that this resolution sufficiently covers the subject so that there can be no question as to the individual's right to life. 

As you will note under Section 1, the right to life is guaranteed to "all human beings, including their unborn offspring at every stage of their biological development, irrespective of age, health, function, or condition of dependency." 

This means, very simply, that there is no time during which a person in the general sense, is not a person in the legal sense, and in short, there is no time during which he or she may be deprived of life. 

Section 2 of my resolution not only clearly stipulates the one condition under which an abortion is permissible, but it also clearly provides that it is the physician's responsibility to save the child wherever possible as well as the mother. This, I think is a crucial consideration, and I respectfully urge the 

Members of the Subcommittee to include such a provision in whichever right to life resolution you might report out.

The bill which I have introduced, and which I have presented here today, is the result of many long months of careful study during which I held detailed and lengthy meetings with some of the finest constitutional lawyers in the country. Every care was taken to insure that the wording was precise, explicit, and not open to varying interpretations. The National Right to Life Committee, Inc., and several right to life organizations throughout the nation have expressed full support for the terminology of my resolution. I hope that the Members of the Subcommittee will join me in working for prompt and favorable action on enacting effective legislation to safeguard the individual's right to life. 

It is important to remember that the passage of the legislation does not impose any Congressional mandate upon the individual, but rather that it allows all of the people, through their state representatives, to make their own decision as to the future direction of our national policy in this vital area. 

STATEMENT SUBMITTED BY HON. JOHN N. ERLENBORN, A U.S. REPRESENTATIVE FROM THE STATE OF ILLINOIS PROPOSALS FOR CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENTS RELATIVE TO ABORTION 

Mr. Chairman, I am grateful for the opportunity to address your subcommittee on the subject of abortion. I believe you are to be commended for considering the Constitutional amendments in this regard. I am the originator of one proposed amendment which has been introduced on the other side of the Capitol; and I wish the members of this distinguished subcommittee could see the outpouring of letters from all parts of our country. 

They are heartfelt letters of encouragement. 

Mr. Chairman, on January 21, 1973, there were 50 State laws regarding abortion. Some of them were permissive and some restrictive. Some had been passed in recent years, some had been on the statute books for many decades. Some were antiquated and some were ultra-modern. 

All that changed on January 22, 1973; for that is when the United States 

Supreme Court decided the case of Roe v. Wade. That decision not only made all 50 State abortion laws unconstitutional, but also outlined the kind of statute which would measure up to the Court's standard. 

The varying State laws which were in effect on January 21 reflected the diverse beliefs of the 50 State jurisdictions. They were legal declarations of the moral and ethical sensibilities of the American people. I want to return to this thought in a moment.

In 1971 and 1972, I served on the Presidential Commission on Population Growth and the American Future, the Chairman of which was John D. Rockefeller, III. The majority recommended abortion on request, and I was one of four who offered a dissenting opinion. Because the four dissenters were Catholics our point of view was promptly dismissed as a religious quirk.

In the wake of Roe v. Wade, organizations have been formed to give expression to other points of view. These, too, have been dismissed as representing only the dogma of a few old-fashioned zealots. 

Now let me come back to the thoughts about the sensibilities which I expressed a moment ago.

My opposition to the Supreme Court's decision is based on moral and ethical values, and I cannot believe that the Catholic Church has a monopoly on concern about these matters. 

I am sure of this much: That many of the State laws in effect up to January 

22, 1973, were based upon these considerations, and few State legislatures have ever been dominated by members of the Catholic Church. Rather, the legislatures have been chosen by members of Protestant, Catholic, Jewish and other churches-and by about 60 million persons who profess to no church creed. 

Ethics and morality are common to all people. 

Now, let me turn to some of the less emotional arguments. 

I asked my colleagues on the Commission on Population Growth and the American Future this question: How do we distinguish between abortion and infanticide? Nobody tried very hard to make that distinction until Mr. Justice 

Blackmun addressed the problem in the Supreme Court's decision. 

It is almost infanticide, the Court ruled, if an abortion takes place in the seventh, eighth or ninth month of pregnancy. It is less like infanticide if the fetus is aborted in the fourth, fifth or sixth month. And it isn't infanticide at all in the first, second or third month.

At what point in its development does a fetus become worthy of the protection of society? Mr. Justice Blackmun, in the Court's opinion, points out that we can get no firm answer if we look to medicine, to philosophy or to theology. There simply is no consensus. 

The effect which the Court hoped for was that, in the absence of a medical, theological or philosophical consensus, its decision would create the legal fiction that there is a legal consensus. Legal fiction, like literary fiction, may retain our allegiance for a long time if it reflects truth as human beings know it. Otherwise, fiction, or whatever kind, is soon forgotten. It loses force.

I believe we were closer to truth before January 22, 1973, than we have been since. We were closer to truth when the people of our 50 States, through their duly constituted legislative, executive and judicial authorities, gave their varying answers to the question, "When does life begin?"

This is a crucial question because the State is bound to be interested in every living thing. The Supreme Court, in discussing it, pointed out that there were divergent opinions among the courts of the 50 States. Then it came to this conclusion: "Although the results are divided, most of these courts have agreed that the right of privacy, however based, is broad enough to cover the abortion decision; that the right, nonetheless, is not absolute and is subject to some limitations; and that at some point the State interest as to protection of health, medical standards and prenatal life become dominant."

From there, the Court went on to ignore the moral issue and to rule that a woman's right to privacy overrrides her child's right to life for three months and, with some restrictions, for six months. If she is married, she need not even consult her husband.

Proponents of abortion on demand point out that the decision does not compel anybody to have an abortion who doesn't believe in abortion. Mr. Justice White, in his dissent, however, points out that the decision means "that the people and the legislatures of the 50 States are constitutionally disentitled to weigh the relative importance of the continued existence and development of the fetus, on the one hand against a spectrum of possible impacts on the mother, on the other hand."

Perhaps the Supreme Court decision does not compel any woman to have an abortion, but it does compel any child which may be growing in her to accept without question or recourse her decision to abort or not to abort.

I believe that a fetus has a right to life unless there is a moral, ethical and legal reason for cutting short that life.

In my view, human life begins at conception. Millions of Americans share this conviction. Our deeply-rooted belief is that, if we are to concern ourselves about the quality and enhancement of life, then we must value life itself above such considerations as privacy and convenience. Without such a standard, the enrichment of life must become wholly materialistic.

Mr. Chairman, without a firm base in fact, in law, or in our Constitution, the 

Supreme Court, in its Roe v. Wade opinion, has brought us perilously close to a legal justification of infanticide and perilously near justifying killing of the aged, the ailing and the incapacitated. Without unequivocal support in fact, in law, or in our Constitution, the Court has arbitrarily decided when life begins. 

We believe these judgments must be returned to the people. We believe the adoption of a Constitutional Amendment is the right way to make this return. 

We ask that your subcommittee start this process.

STATEMENT BY REPRESENTATIVE EDWARD I. KOCH 

Mr. Chairman, I thank you for this opportunity to submit a statement concerning the proposed Human Life Amendments to the Constitution. 

It has been a little over a year since the Supreme Court decision on abortion in effect established a constitutional right of privacy allowing a woman in the first six months of pregnancy to decide whether she wishes to have an abortion. The 

State of New York was one of the first States in advance of the Supreme Court decision to give women this right. I supported early efforts in the State of New 

York to change the law so as to protect that right by legislation. I applauded the Supreme Court decision in that it removed the matter from legislative debate by finding that this is a right protected by the Constitution and one that cannot be negated by simple legislation. Furthermore, it extends the protection uniformly in the 50 states.

There are now efforts underway to change the Constitution and limit or prohibit entirely abortion, in effect erasing last year's Supreme Court decision. 

Because the question of abortion is a religious and philosophical one and therefore involves fundamental questions which can only be answered by each individual, I believe that these efforts, if successful, would abridge a woman's First Amendment right of religious freedom. It was to protect our freedom of religion and the holding of various religious beliefs that the Founding Fathers included in the Constitution the first amendment. To deny a woman the right to have an abortion would be to encroach upon the religious and philosophical freedom guaranteed by that amendment.

There are those who because of their own religious and philosophical convictions believe abortions are wrong. I respect their right to hold this view, as does the Constitution. It must be remembered that no one is compelled to undergo an absortion unless she desires to do so. Nor can anyone be compelled to perform or assist in an abortion if it is against his or her religious or philosophical convictions and I am in accord with that protection. It is, however, equally important that no one be denied the opportunity to make the moral and constitutionally protected decision of whether or not she wishes to terminate her pregnancy. 

Our country permits and encourages those who believe the laws to be unjust to change them legislatively and constitutionally. I do not concur with the position of those who would rescind the Supreme Court's decision by amending the Constitution. And I will resist their efforts to do so while acknowledging their right to try.

On a number of occasions I have met with those who would seek to change my point of view on this matter and who seek to persuade me that their sense of morality is greater than mine on this subject. My response to them is that 

I respect their sense of morality and hope they will find it in their hearts to respect mine. On a matter of morality, a legislator should not simply decide where the votes are and count the mail-on these issues in particular, a legislator must follow his or her conscience, and I will. 

STATEMENT OF REPRESENTATIVE GEORGE BROWN 

Mr. Chairman, I wish to thank you and the distinguished Members of this

Subcommittee for the opportunity to address myself to this most important issue. 

Mr. Chairman, I have been following with interest and concern the hearings before the Subcommittee on Constitutional Amendments to deny women the option of legal abortions. Emotions on both sides of the issue run high-both opponents and supporters of the amendments believe their position to be both morally and legally correct.

The testimony before the Subcommittee has led me to believe that the proposed 

Constitutional Amendments should be opposed.

The first point is that unedr the Supreme Court rulings the decision to have an abortion is entirely a voluntary one. Those whose moral convictions forbid abortions, whether to regulate the size of a family or to save the life of the woman,

need not have them. My own moral convictions find compulsory abortion, or compulsory sterilization abhorrent. However, the prospect of a woman endangering her life because she is forced to carry a pregnancy full term or of a child beginning life unwanted or abandoned is equally abhorrent. 

The Constitutional Amendments would deny women their constitutional freedom of choice.

Another point that has become apparent during the hearings so far is that the experts do not agree on major areas that we as legislators will have to define in a constitutional amendment. There is no single, authoritative answer to such questions as: -When does life begin? -What is the mechanism of action of IUD's and morning-after pills? -When does fetus became viable?

These critical issues are themselves the subject of intense debate within the medical and religious communities. 

The resolution of these basic questions is moral and religious, and, ultimately, personal. Legislation should not attempt to answer these questions. The experience of this country prior to the Supreme Court decisions when a million women per year obtained illegal abortions demonstrates that legislation cannot prevent the practice of abortion.

A major concern that arises is whether the constitutional principles of individual freedoms are seriously threatened by the amendments before the Subcommittee. The means which would be needed to enforce the Constitutional Amendments would restrict these fundamental principles. 

If the Subcommittee defined the fetus as a person, then women who have miscarriages (spontaneous abortions) may be subject to investigations for criminal negligence or deliberate intent to abort. What kind of guidelines would have to be established? Would the woman who took a strenuous forty-mile hike and miscarried be held criminally responsible? What about the woman who walked to the local supermarket and miscarried? 

Doctors would be under intense pressures as well. Would they begin to hestitate to prescribe certain drug treatments or postpone needed surgery because of the possibility of inducing a miscarriage? 

These questions illustrate that the amendments are not only inconsistent with our constitutional freedoms, but at the same time are unwieldly and unenforceable in practice.

All the distinguished Subcommittee Members are familiar with the law. A re-definition of the word fetus to mean person would require changes in tort, inheritance, tax, property, and criminal law. It is my understanding that the Subcommittee will be hearing from legal experts, and I am certain that the testimony will raise more questions on the problems of implementation than it will answer. 

Mr. Chairman, I support the Supreme Court decisions; I believe it would be a mistake to attempt to overthrow them with restrictive legislation. Abortion should remain medically safe, and, at the same time, legal. 

TESTIMONY AGAINST THE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT PROPOSED BY SENATOR JAMES BUCKLEY OF NEW YORK 

Submitted by the Reverend E. Spencer Parsons, Associate Professor in the field of Ethics and Society, The Divinity School, and Dean of the Rockefeller 

Memorial Chapel, The University of Chicago. 

PERSONAL CREDENTIALS-CURRENTLY 

A member of the Executive Committee of the General Board of the American 

Baptist Churches, U.S.A.

A member of the Committee on Christian Unity of the General Board of the 

American Baptist Churches, U.S.A.

Member of the Commission on Communications, The Church Federation of 

Greater Chicago.

Member of the Committee on Human Sexuality, Pritzker School of Medicine, University of Chicago.

Member of the Board of the Drexel Clinic and the Community Reproductive 

Health Center, University of Chicago.

Founder and Chairman of the Illinois Clergy Consultation Service on Problem 

Pregnancies.

The amendment submitted by Senator James Buckley of the State of New York in my judgment poses a serious threat to the freedom of conscience so long championed by my own denomination and protected by the Constitution of the 

United States.

I concur with most of the arguments which have been presented to your committee against the wisdom of trying to nullify the Supreme Court's January 

1973 ruling on abortion.

My statement will confine itself to the interlatedness of birth control, contraception, and pharmaceutical, mechanical, and surgical abortion.

The birth control methods presently available may be divided into two fundamental types: pre-conception and post-conception. The pre-conception birth controls include, of course, all sexual activity which does not, indeed cannot in some instances, result in conception. All auto-sexual activity, all homo-sexual activity, and non-coital orgasmic activities obviously do not result in conception. For the male, the condem is a mechanical barrier in coitus to conception, thus making the condom a true contraceptive. Likewise, for the woman, a diaphragm with spermicidal jelly and foam, still widely used, are preconceptual chemical means of birth control. A vasectomy for the male and a tubal ligation for the female are obviously preconceptual methods of controlling reproduction. At the present time they must be regarded as irreversible, a factor which means that the patients must be fully advised as to the implications of these procedures. 

Now we come to the PILL. There are two types in widespread use. The first is the sequential pill which is intended to function as a simple straightforward method of preventing ovulation. The second type, the so called combination pill, has three modes of action. It is designed first to suppress ovulation, second to maintain the cervical mucus in a state which makes sperm penetration through the cervical canal more difficult, and third, and important for this discussion, the combination pill throws the endometrium out of phase so that it is not ready to receive a fertilized egg, if conception occurs.

While the combination pill is primarily a true contraceptive, its abortifacient characteristics cannot be ignored. It is the abortifacient aspect of the combination pill that makes it an unacceptable form of birth control to all those who take the absolutist position, namely, that a human person exists at the moment of conception.

The second most effective birth control device is the Intrauterine Device (IUD). While marketed as a "contraceptive," it is in fact a post-conception method of birth control. There is little evidence that the IUD actually prevents the impregnation of the female ovum; rather it prevents any already fertilized egg from implanting itself in the wall of the uterus. It is in largest measure, if not totally then, a post-conception birth control measure, mechanical to be sure, in contrast to the pharmaceutical characteristics of the pill, but like the combination pill also an abortifacient. 

If one can come to terms morally and psychically with the combination pill and the IUD then in principle one has prepared oneself to accept other clearly post-conception methods of birth control such as stilbestrol, provera, and prostaglandins. These, of course, are chemical abortifacients, not really contraceptives. 

The U.S. Senate Sub-Committee on Constitutional Amendments has before it a constitutional amendment submitted by Senator Buckley of New York. He and his co-sponsors believe that they are engaged in an effort to prohibit abortions which they regard as morally offensive acts. The amendments is carefully drawn so as to prohibit all birth control measures which function wholly or in part as abortifacients. It is incomprehensible that anyone in 1974 would attempt to outlaw the combination pill, the IUD, the use of diethylstilbestrol, provera or the increasing use of prostaglandins. Yet that is precisely what the Buckley amendment is prepared to do.

Since at the present time, the most effective birth control measures are either wholly or in part abortifacients, what we are really left with is the question as to whether, and to what degree, the manual removal of the products of conception by a live physician, particularly during the first trimester of pregnancy, is morally and legally different from achieving the same results pharmaceutically with the combination pill, stilbestrol, provera, prostaglandins, or mechanically with the IUD. That is the moral and legal question which must be decided. 

The Court has already declared that there are areas of privacy and intimacy into which the government cannot intrude without doing violence to those per- 1 43-245-75- -37

sonal freedoms guaranteed by the Constitution. Ever since the decision in 1966 involving Griswold and the State of Connecticut, that privacy has presumed to include the sexual and reproductive activities of men and women. 

Just as we acknowledge the interrelatedness of humanness, human sexuality, and human reproduction, we must recognize that we cannot discuss birth control and family planning without being honest about abortion.

This presentation is based upon the assumption that the popular understanding of the difference between birth control and abortion is no longer tenable. Whereas once we saw contraception and abortion as mutally exclusive aspects of birth control we can no longer do so.

Abortion, spontaneous and induced, is a part of the biological and cultural scene in the last half century. Abortions late in the second trimester should be avoided if at all possible because they constitute serious medical and psychological risks to the patients. Furthermore, by virtue of the extensive development of the fetus, important philosophical and moral issues are raised by the later terminations. However much we regret the circumstances that impel a woman to seek an abortion in the latter weeks of the second trimester, we must acknowledge that not all of our moral preferences should be translated into criminal law. It is this distinction which the U.S. Supreme Court wisely recognized in its 

1973 decision.

I would hope that your Committee is sensitive to the plight of many women in the second trimester. My experience with over 700 women would indicate that this group (which constitutes only about 15% of the total number of women seeking abortion) includes many 11-13 year old children who, out of fear, ignorance, or fantasy that the problem would go away, have failed to seek help or even recognize early pregnancy. The other large group are those women bordering on menopause whose irregular periods make it difficult for them to know whether or not they are pregnant. It is imperative in a free society that as a matter of public policy we be prepared to make available to the poor as well as the rich, the single as well as the married, those birth control methods and medications, including surgical abortion, if necessary, which are consistent with the health and sensitivities of the people for whom we seek to provide responsible medical care.

Most of the Protestant denominations in the United States have gone on public record approving birth control as a moral imperative. Almost every one has given either conditional or full support to early surgical abortions under some or all circumstances. Likewise, Reform and Conservative Judaism have through their various organizations and rabbinic leadership accepted the moral appropriateness of both chemical and mechanical birth control and surgical abortions, whenever the latter procedure is deemed necessary and desirable by the pregnant woman, particularly in the early weeks of pregnancy. 

May I respectfully suggest that questions of morality related to human sexual activity and reproduction are not matters appropriate for majority regulation and prescription, rather they are personal matters to be decided in accordance with the consciences of the individuals involved. 

The attached resolution of my own denomination speaks, I believe, persuasively to the problem of morality, law, and coersion in a pluralistic society such as ours, and I trust the members of your Committee will see the practical wisdom of not being party to the national effort to nullify the Supreme Court's January, 1973 decision on abortion.

RESOLUTION ADOPTED BY THE GENERAL BOARD OF THE AMERICAN BAPTIST CHURCHES, U.S.A., FEBRUARY 24, 1974 

The General Board of American Baptist Churches in the USA feels it imperative to address itself to the current efforts of the U.S. Conference of Catholic 

Bishops to seek a Constitutional Amendment through the Congress and the States to nullify the January, 1973 decision of the United States Supreme Court on abortion. 

1. Encouraged by the growing areas of mutual understanding and cooperation toward which Roman Catholics and Protestants have been moving during the past decade, we are nevertheless impelled to express a divergent view regarding the Constitutional Amendment before the Senate Sub-committee on Constitutional 

Amednments on March 7, 1974. 

2. We acknowledge the legal right of all individuals and groups, both religious and secular, to seek the enactment of laws which reflect the values they hold to be necessary to the exercise of their freedom and on behalf of the common wel-

12 fare. However, we believe that the present national effort of the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops to coerce the conscience and personal freedom of our citizens through the power of public law in matters of human reproduction constitutes a serious threat to that moral and religious liberty so highly prized by Baptists and so long protected for all people under the nation's policy of the separation of church and state. 

3. We recognize the moral ambiguities involved for many people, including 

American Baptists, in the birth control and abortion issues. We are nevertheless saddened when such crusades seek the passage of laws which violate the theological and moral sensitivities, and hence the freedom, of other church bodies. 

All must be given their constitutional rights in a free society to guide and assist their constituencies in formulating a responsible life style in matters of sexual expression and family planning. 

4. We affirm freedom of conscience for all but object to an appeal to the State which could coerce all citizens to accept a moral judgment affirmed by one member of the body of Christ. We urge a continuation of dialogue with our Roman 

Catholic brothers and sisters on this and other matters. Let us seek a common understanding of the mind of Christ, and let us listen to each other in love. 

We therefore request our General Secretary to communicate this concern to the appropriate Roman Catholic leadership in the hope that the progress and strides which have been made in the area of Christian unity may continue. 

STATEMENT OF GEORGE H. MUEDEKING 

Mr. Chairman and members of the Committee: My name is George H. Muedeking, of Minneapolis, Minnesota. I am the editor of The Lutheran Standard, the official publication of the American Lutheran Church, a denomination of 2½ million members. The Lutheran Standard reaches into more than 325,000 homes twice a month, on a paid subscription basis. The testimony being offered today before the Committee is that of the editor alone; it does not purport to be the official view of the American Lutheran Church. Official positions on issues are taken by the American Lutheran Church by and at its biennial conventions. 

In considering amendments to the Constitution which would define personhood, the charge is often made that it is a religious bias or loyalty, particularly Roman Catholic, which prompts concern for the unborn. It is therefore important to be aware of Lutheran viewpoints. Officially, all three of the large Lutheran denominations in the U.S., totaling some 10 million members, have taken serious and considered stands against indiscriminate abortions. My own church in 1952 stated, "Abortions must be regarded as the destruction of a living being, and except as a medical measure to save the mother's life, will not be used by a 

Christian to avoid an unwanted birth (Planning for Parenthood, 8.1). In 1966 the American Lutheran Church allowed only that, "there are times and circumstances when interruption to a pregnancy may be necessary for therapeutic reasons" (The Church & Human Sexuality, 8). 

An effort by the Commission on Research and Social Action of the American Lutheran Church to widen the church's acceptance of abortion for other reasons, by proposing a new statement, was turned back, unpassed, to the Commission at the 1970 convention of the church. 

The second major Lutheran group, the Lutheran Church in America, adopted a statement at its 5th Biennial Convention saying that the termination of the development of a fetus is always a serious matter, but that a quantitative distinction must be made between the claims of an unborn child and the rights of a responsible person who is in a living relationship with God and with other human beings. Considerations to be made include the life and total health of the mother, the stage and development of the fetus, the stability of the home, the laws of the land and the consequence for society as a whole. 

Third, the Lutheran Church-Missouri Synod adopted a statement at its 1971 convention which regards "willful abortion as contrary to the will of God." 

Its president, J.A.O. Preus, is a director of the Missouri Citizens for Life, a non-sectarian agency to oppose ilberal abortion legislation. 

A clear test of Lutheran, particularly American Lutheran Church (ALC), sentiment on the abortion issue has been made. In that state where the ALC is numerically the largest church-North Dakota-a 78% vote was made against a referendum last November 11, which would have liberalized the abortion statutes which allow termination of pregnancy only when the mother's life is endangered. The state's church population is 47.8% Lutheran (all three bodies),

and the Roman Catholic Church is about one-fourth of the state's population. 

Evidently, concern for the unborn is not a "Catholic prejudice," but is strongly and politically supported in the ALC. 

It may not be extraneous to recall also that the Hon. Albert Quie, the sponsor of the House resolution (HF Res. 603) on Human Life, which parallels the 

Buckley-Hatfield resolution (SJ 119) to say that the word "person" as used in the 5th and 14th Amendments applies to all human beings at every stage of biological development, irrespective of age, health, function, or condition of dependence, is a highly respected and leading member of the American Lutheran Church. Mr. Justice Rehnquist, one of those who wrote in a dissenting opinion "that the 'right' to an abortion is not so universally accepted as the appellants would have us believe" in the Roe et al vs. Wade case on the findings for which the Supreme Court overthrew state abortion laws last January 22, is likewise an active Lutheran layman (LCA). Senator Buckley points out that seven of the nine Senate sponsors of his Human Life Amendment are Protestant. It is clear that pro-life sentiment for the unborn child is not a sectarian religious viewpoint sponsored and abetted by Roman Catholics. 

It is not even a "religious" viewpoint as such. As Senator Buckley stated it to a Philadelphia banquet sponsored by Pennsylvanians for Human Life, "The disastrous Supreme Court decisions nullified the abortion laws of all fifty states, and the ethical heritage of more than twenty centuries of Western enlightment." 

Concern for life instead of for death has marked Western ethics and philosophy from the days of Hippocrates. His Hippocratic oath for "life," as the eminent 

Margaret Mead notes, was one of the turning points of human history, because it separated the power to kill from the power to heal, heretofore resident in the same sorcerer functionary.

On such foundations of respect for life, Western philosophy and law were built, aided and reinforced by the concern "to love thy neighbor as thyself" that came from the Judeo-Christian impulse. In consequence, in the words of 

Attorney Irving Hinderaker, a recent member of the Church Council, the governing body of the American Lutheran Church, there arose "the principle of law that the law ought to be most interested in those who are least able to take care of themselves-in this case, the unborn child. When abortion is extended, the person who most needs defense-the unborn child-is not being consulted." 

The abortion controversy points directly to "the obligation of a civilized society to restrain or prevent barbarous and violent acts," according to another commentator. The law cannot expect to remain neutral under the guise of protecting the privacy of the women who in this first year of the abolition of the abortion statutes have achieved their personal desires at the expense of their 700,000 destroyed unborn children (U.S. News and World Report estimate, March 4, p. 43).

The law has the duty to control abortion. The religious citizen can remind the state of this duty. So to remind it is in no sense to be guilty of trying to impose its own value system on society as a whole. It is Western society which has made the protection of the unprotected, the advocacy of the weak and friendless, into the significant purpose of law. 

Law defines the limits of its own protection and concern. If it refuses to do so, it must, and regularly has been, corrected. It could say, for example, that blacks imported from Africa were outside its concern-they were not persons entitled to protection. Or Hitler could say that Jews were non-persons. But society would not abide that feigned neutrality, for in every case, neutrality toward the weak is support of the powerful. 

It was Justice Blackmun himself who in his majority opinion called upon theology; so it cannot be amiss to refer to theology in this testimony. He used the historic disagreements on the "ensoulment" of a fetus as conclusive evidence that consensus could not be obtained on when a person becomes a person-at conception, at 40-80 days (Aristotle, and his pupil St. Thomas), at quickening, at birth, or later still. It should not be out of order therefore to examine this appeal to theological history more circumspectly. 

In the abortion issue then, we must argue that even if all the theologians, philosophers or scientists on earth could not agree upon the moment that this helpless being merited the protection of personhood, the law still would have the duty to define that moment. Not to define and thereby protect by its limitation, is to take the side of the exploiter and the powerful. 

Actually, the early Christian Church, to return to Justice Blackmun, was conspicuously united upon the meaning and repudiation of abortion, though its

theologians could not agree upon the supporting rationale. In itself this virtual unanimity is striking, since the church grew up in a Roman and Greek society which not only tolerated abortion, but had no qualms about infanticide. Onward from the earliest catechism of the church, the Didache (c. 125 A.D.), willful termination of pregnancy is called murder. Disagreement later centered in whether aborting the "unquickened" fetus also merited excommunication for murder, as a sin that could never be forgiven in this earthly lifetime. The counter view was that the abortion of the unquick demanded only a penitential period of say, ten or more years. That is to say, theological arguments on when ensoulment occurred were not promoted as Justice Blackmun was led to believe, by disagreements on when the conceived embryo became a person. They were joined over the pastoral problem of how serious this guilty act was-was it always like idolatry and fornication, that is, unforgiveable in this life; or was the absence of quickening an extenuating circumstance that allowed the penance to be worked out for this guilt and sin. 

The whole discussion among theologians becomes empty and meaningless as soon as biological research made the history of the conception and growth of a child available. As has been said frequently, nothing at all except time and nutrition are introduced between conception and birth. The organism is human from the beginning; at least no other factor to make it suddenly and thereafter human has ever appeared.

The argument from the ignorance of the theologians and ancient philosophers can be understood. But that it should become the basis by the Supreme Court for the deprivation of life for 700,000 tiny humans in a single year, as has occurred, is almost incomprehensible. The action does not make Cardinal Krol's observation too expansive, "The Supreme Court opened the doors to the greatest slaughter of innocent life in the history of mankind."

The use of wrangling theologians to excuse the Court from accepting the responsibility to grant the protection of law is incomprehensible even on logical grounds. Allegations were made on March 1 of this year, for example, that at the University of Minnesota hospital two fetuses were aborted live, and left to die. They would be considered "premature babies," since their respective gram weights of 598 and 698 put them in this eligible-for-survival classification. If left to die, however, the attending physicians should be counted as murderers. But if they had been pickup up and cared for and had either died or survived, they would have been suddenly human, worthy of the mighty protection of the 

Supreme Court!

Obviously, the difference of attending to or neglecting those organisms dare not be the defining of their personhood. If it is left to die it is a thing; if it is kept to live, it is a person. According to New York City Health Department officials, about 70 fetuses out of 400,000 aborted in two years "showed signs of life."

If they had lived, would the Supreme Court majority have said they were "human"? Because they died, they weren't? Even logically, wiping out the abortion laws because biologists, psychologists, and theologians cannot gain their own consensus, becomes an appalling spectacle of rationalizing instead of reasoning. 

No, the fetus is not a potential human being; he is a human being with potential.

As silly as to argue that because we use only 5% of our brains, our brains are therefore only potentially brains, so is it silly to say that because the embryo does not exercise all its potential human history, is it therefore only potentially human.

On the other hand, if it is not silly to argue so, then the exact moment of realized potential, whereat the unborn can receive the protection of personhood, must still be stated explicitly by the Court or the laws of the land. It simply will not do to run away from the question and to rest in uncertainty merely because a consensus cannot be reported concerning when a distinctively "human" character, istic confers person-ness upon the fetus. 

According to the Holy Book, the Judeo-Christian tradition has been seismically sensitive to the implications of our social commitments also. The prophets named what alliances with Egypt would lead to; Jesus wept over a Jerusalem that did not know the things that belonged to her peace. It has not only been, therefore, that the religious people of the U.S. have been appalled at the reckless destruction of those in the womb who are helpless to protect themselves. But they have sensed that the disregard and disrespect for life that allowed the abortion laws to be liberalized and then overthrown would never stop there. After all, it took only

from 1969, when the constitutional challenge first began, to 1972, when the laws were totally overthrown, which embodied the ethical heritage of twenty centuries. The same powerful minority who captured the media would not be expected to stop with this victory.

The hatred toward life, which has become so dominant a theme in secular society in this half of the century has other life systems that it can move against also. Not distant is the legislation, already proposed in Florida, for example, to destroy the mongoloids and retarded. Not distant is the euphemistic "right," and then imposed insistence, "to die with dignity." Cost-benefit schedules, as they have been applied to abortion to solve welfare case loads, will not be long lacking for other sectors of the weak and the helpless. 

It is possible, however, that the entire process can be turned around. Passage of the Human Life Amendment would indicate that this nation, at least, wants to sign up for service, not in the war against the unborn, but for service in the celebration of life.

Paul Ramsey of Princeton speaks of "the pedagogical effect of law." The law itself teaches what it describes. Thus in Hook's study of Swedish girls who were refused abortions, 86% did not go elsewhere to attempt to secure an abortion anyway. They carried their babies to term. 

Reverence for life is the starting place for the renewal of spirit. For spirit arises out of life, not out of death. Jesus said, "I came that they might have life, and have it more abundantly." His words can be our nation's rally call also. [From the Lutheran Standard, Mar. 20, 1973]

LET'S TALK IT OVER 

ABORTION DECISION 

Calling it a "day of disaster for our nation," Roman Catholic bishops of northern California condemned the Supreme Court ruling on abortion. The court "rejected the right to life for the unborn and legalized another form of genocide," they said. They quoted Vatican II, "From its conception, life must be guarded with the greatest care, while abortion and infanticide are unspeakable crimes." 

Dr. Sergio Cotto of Rome University, authority in jurisprudence, commented on the decision, "Abortion is neither more nor less than the killing of a living human being, who, in addition, is innocent. The lawfulness of abortion is affirmed [by the U.S. Supreme Court] by maintaining that although the fetus is a human individual-which is now impossible to deny it is not yet a person." 

The Committee for Pro-Life Affairs of the National Council of Catholic Bishops called the Supreme Court's decision, "a flagrant rejection of the unborn child's right to life," and charged that the court failed to justify its opinion on theological, historical, or scientific grounds. "Although as a result of the court's decision abortion may be legally permissible, it is still morally wrong and no court opinion can change the law of God, prohibiting the taking of innocent human life . . . and we urge people not to follow its reasonings or conclusions." 

They pledged the resources of the church for a program to "present the case for sanctity of the child's life from conception to birth." 

Cardinal Boyle of Washington, D.C., said, "Defenseless children whose only crime is to be unwanted by their parents, are condemned to death before birth. and our government seems no longer to consider the right to life as 'unalienable.' 

Now we are told that unborn children, whose hearts are already beating (from four weeks of gestation), whose minds are functioning (measurable brain activity at 12 weeks), who might even be doing such normal acts for a baby as sucking their thumbs, can be slaughtered at whim."

He said that everyone should keep clear the distinction between what is legal and what is moral. "The Supreme Court has decreed that abortion is legal. That does not make it morally permissible."

He also likened the ruling to the Dred Scott Decision by the same Supreme Court more than a century ago. In that case the court held that black Americans were not legally persons, and thus could be treated as property to be bought and sold. 

THE CHRISTIAN PATH AHEAD 

Christians have their future blocked out for them. This is not the first time they have been called on to stand for life and for personhood against a cruel and heartless culture: women, children, and slaves became persons entitled to the life God gave them, under the moral persuasion of Christians.

Vice-president of the Rabbinical Council of America, Rabbi Fabian Schonfeld, said at a meeting of his group, "As religious leaders we must continue to teach the moral imperatives and religious dictates which frown upon taking the life of the fetus even during this early period." He indicated that "over 600,000 abortions were performed last year and the expected figure for the coming year will be closer to 1.5 million. Obviously, such astronomical figures are bound to have a tremendous impact upon the entire structure of our society. They may affect the very fabric of our society." 

A Lutheran pastor, the Rev. Lester Messerschmidt, of Dix Hills, N.Y., head of the state's Right to Life Committee, told newsmen that the "biggest fallacy” in the abortion struggle is that it is a "Catholic issue." He cited the overwhelming defeat of liberalized abortion referenda last fall in states like North Dakota and Michigan, where Catholics are not in a majority, as indicators of the nonsectarian nature of the question. He stated that a campaign for a constitutional amendment to protect the unborn would begin immediately. 

Rep. Lawrence Hogan of Maryland has proposed an amendment which reads in part: "Neither the United States or any state shall deprive any human being, from the moment of conception, of life without due process of law." 

We can only hope that more of our church leaders will be as courageous as those we have cited in affirming the right of the tiniest human to live. God give us compassion again, so that we may shed the diabolical disrespect of human life which has gripped our souls-where we can see six million Jews destroyed, millions of Russian kulaks liquidated, two million Vietnamese wiped out, oldsters invited by legislative permissions to self-chosen suicide, and now the tiny innocents wiped out, because they are inconvenient to the mother who bears themall with legal rationale to justify our hardness of heart. 

STATEMENT BY MS. PATRICIA R. BRUNER, FOR THE NATIONAL ASSOCIATION OF LAITY 

Members of this subcommittee, and staff, we appreciate this opportunity to submit testimony on this important proposed legislation, and trust that our testimony will be of value to you.

The National Association of Laity is an organization of Catholic men and women, comprising both affiliate groups and single memberships, from throughout the United States. Organized in 1968 to implement the decrees of Vatican 

Council II and work for greater lay participation in the ministries of the church, it has endeavored to promote better communications between members of the Church, and particularly to arouse greater concern and efforts within the Church toward the goals of social justice. 

During the past seven years, NAL has achieved unanimity on such positions as supporting the peace movement, opposition to the war in Vietnam, equal rights for women, ordination of women and married persons to the priesthood, the United Farm Workers, their lettuce and grape boycotts, public housing in suburban areas, busing to achieve racial integration, conscientious objector status and amnesty for Vietnam War resisters, popular election of Bishops, opposition to state aid for parochial schools, and reparation and episcopal representation for Black and Spanish speaking Catholics. There has been no such unanimity on the issue of abortion, per se.

As president of the Washington affiliate, and thereby a member of the National Board of Directors of NAL for three years, and as NAL representative to the Joint Committee of Organizations Concerned With the Status of Women in the Church, I have been intimately involved in the more than four and one-half years of intensive debate on the subject of abortion. 

Three resolutions and a study paper entitled, "Statement on Human Life," were the focus of most of these debates and discussions. Resolutions on the subject of abortion were adopted by the NAL annual assembly of delegates in 1971 and 1973, and the 15-page legally-oriented "Statement on Human Life," was accepted as a position and study paper by the Board of Directors in July 1972. A third resolution was presented in 1972 but was later withdrawn, after two and one-half days of hearings, because no agreement could be reached on the wording of the document. Copies of these Resolutions and the statement are herewith submitted as a part of this testimony, along with a brief summary of the 15page document written by Attorney Leo Jordan who was chairperson of the committee which prepared the statement, and testimony from Dr. Joseph Skeehan, President of NAL. 

The predominance of opinion in NAL is that the unborn child is, in fact, a human person entitled to human rights as a person, from conception, or a point

so near to conception as to be indistinguishable. Whereas the 1971 resolution referred to the "life or potential human life of the fetus" and, quoting Daniel Callahan, stated that "the bias implied by the principle of the sanctity of human life should be accorded even to potential or doubtful life," the 1973 resolution states simply that "... NAL affirms the sanctity of human life in all stages of biological development." The Statement on Human Life is more precise: "Based upon the available evidence, religious, legal and scientific, it is contrary to reason for us to conclude that an unborn person is not a human life. 

If consensus is at all available among our brothers and sisters within NAL, it is that the 'moment' of conception or some state of development very close to the 'moment' is the point at which distinctively human life begins. We have agreed therefore, that there are fundamental rights of an unborn child which must be recognized and respected. An unborn child is a person and is entitled to basic, fundamental rights enjoyed by other persons. Included among these rights are: (a) The right to attain the end of prenatal development; (b) the right to become a free and responsible adult, a contributing member of the human community; and (c) the fundamental rights guaranteed by the United States Constitution; including the right to due process of law."

However, although the wording of both the 1972 statement and the resolution of 1973 closely approximate the wording of both these proposed amendments, this testimony should not be construed to be an endorsement of this legislation, it is in fact neither endorsement nor opposition. Just as the Supreme Court decision totally ignored the humanity and rights of the unborn child, so does this legislation totally ignore the humanity and rights of the mother and her right to self-defense.

This right of a women to defend herself is basically the same right to defense that is the basis of our criminal laws, our right to protect our homes from intrusion, our wages and property from confiscation without due process and our right to wage wars to protect a way of life or property, as well as the right to protect one's person from physical attack. While it is doubtful that self-defense is a 

Christian principle, it is unquestionably a basic natural right recognized universally. Moreover, the right to life has not been held by law to be absolute, and morally speaking, in Christian terms, the value of human life has been held to be relative to the attainment of salvation, and in attaining the capacity to love God, oneself and one's neighbors, parental love is remarkably important.

If the public is grossly uneducated regarding the humanity of the unborn child, it is even more ignorant or unaware of how the enormity of the pressures that come to bear on a pregnant woman or mother constitute a definite and serious threat to her life, and that pregnancy and parenthood are also stages of biological development. We underestimate the power of a child to destroy the life of the mother, a power not possessed by the child itself, but a power that men and society (which includes women) use to destroy a woman's life solely because she can or does become a mother. It is the force of these pressures that have created a situation of primarily equal and directly conflicting rights between mother and child, a conflict that has been created by our society as a whole.

It is this conflict which constitutes an immoral situation, and presents the legal problems of a serious social dilemma. It cannot be resolved with a decision one way or the other. This is, after all, not just an academic or theoretical question, but a situation involving real-life problems and people. 

It is the consensus of the National Association of Laity that the only equitable solution to this conflict lies in "recognizing the rights of the child-bearing mother, as well as the life .. of the fetus," (to quote the premise of the 1971 Resolution on Abortion). Any legislation that proposes to resolve the question of abortion will have to look for solutions that will benefit both the mother and the child, and while it seems that abortion has a more serious and irrevocable effect on the child than non-abortion has on the mother, it is also true that the welfare of the child both during pregnancy and after birth depends on the well-being of the mother.

NAL has recommended that public education and personal counseling in the use of contraceptives could do much to avoid the conflicts sometimes caused by pregnancy, and that both contraception and voluntary NAL also recommends conscientious deliberation) are preferrable to abortionerilization (presuming an intensive program of public education regarding the fetal period of personal development, not as a part of sex education, but in the very earliest primary
