grades, as a part of health education and appreciation for their own development as a person. It is entirely possible that if more people were aware of the human capabilities of the unborn child, there would be greater personal efforts to avoid a choice of abortion..

The NAL Statement on Human Life goes into considerable detail in defining the limits of the variously conflicting rights of the unborn child, the mother, the father and society, and of defining those areas where rights are superior. Although this legislation (S.J.R. 119) defines the mother's rights as superior only in the event her life is endangered, it is our belief that the mother's rights are also superior when the pregnancy results from an unlawful act such as rape, and certain cases of incest such as those involving a minor, as well as certain cases where the mother is herself a child or approaching old age, and/or where severe and permanent psychological or physical impairment would result from continuation of the pregnancy. It is obvious, however, that neither excellent legal arbitration between the rights of the mother and the rights of the child, as described in the Statement on Human Life, and proposed in Senate Joint Resolution 130, nor contraception and sterilization will sufficiently protect the rights of the mother, or of the child who is dependent upon her. This legislation will not change the baby's diaper, or feed it, or provide clothing or housing or the 168 hours per week care that a child requires; nor will it make it any easier for the mother to care for the child. Either this legislation or companion legislation must address itself to removing the threat to the life of the mother, by relieving those pressures that cause conflict between the mother and child, if any permanent solution is to be realized in this serious situation. For that reason, I would like to describe what some of these pressures and attitudes are. 

It is almost impossible to describe these attitudes and social pressures that create alienation between mother and child without using generalizations that may seem unfair. Many men and women are not consciously aware that they subscribe to attitudes and behavior that pressure towards abortion and against the child and its mother. Some of these attitudes are, ironically, held most avidly by people who are most violently opposed to abortion. Many men and women, on the other hand, prove by their own behavior that they do not personally subscribe to these attitudes. However, the fact remains that these are generalized and prevalent attitudes to which everyone subscribes in more or lesser degree, since they are promoted by our laws and ethics and the general workings of society. 

Society has, as a whole, literally dumped the entire responsibility for conception and care of children on women, and then systematically limited and denied them use of their own capabilities and access to community resources in fulfilling these responsibilities. The means by which this is accomplished are so pervasive, so all-encompassing and so overwhelming as to almost defy description or identification, particularly for the pregnant woman, giving her the justifiably hopeless impression that the whole world is against her, not just because she is a woman, but precisely because she is, or can be, a mother. 

Some of these attitudes began centuries ago, during the patriarchal period of our development, when a child was not considered a person until she or he reached 12 years of age. Until that age the father was considered to have absolute rights over the child, including the right to take the child's life if he so desired. We have long since abandoned this barbaric attitude, yet chauvinistic obeisance to male whims and caprices still exist in our society today, so that the value and worth of any child, born or unborn, is often judged not on the basis of its personal worth as a member of society, but on the basis of whether or not the father values it.

Whether or not the mother claims and wants her child is not ever the question; it is assumed that she does and will want the child. On the other hand it is assumed that the father has no natural attachment to his child, and accepted that a father is only as responsible for sexual behavior and paternity as he chooses to be, or can be forced or persuaded to be, and that he has no responsibility as a father, per se. If the father does not claim his child (which at this time means marrying its mother) the child is considered to be illegitimate and having no claim on the protection or support of its father. If the father deserts his child during pregnancy or afterwards, society considers the child and its mother as undesirable.

No where is this attitude more evident than in the attitude towards "the welfare rolls" which government officials are so proud of reducing. More than half of our welfare recipients are children who have been abandoned by their fathers, and half the remainder (25% of the total) are their mothers. Mothers

who cannot both work outside the home and care for their children, who cannot always find adequate child care services, whose salaries will not support the family and outside child care, and who cannot really choose between working outside the home and taking care of their children 24 hours a day. All of these children have fathers, some fathers may not know they have children, others are unwilling or unable to support them. Many of these children (probably or more) are entitled to child support awarded by the court, but society considers that it has no responsibility to compel or persuade a father to take care of his child. Instead it deems it the mother's responsibility to persuade or force the father to claim and support his child. Even when the mother takes the time, effort and expense to secure a court order for child support, law enforcement people make little or no effort to contact the father and collect this financial support for the child. Although the amount of money needed to support the needs of a child runs into far more than one or two hundred dollars, desertion by a father is usually considered a misdemeanor. And although the courts and the law assist the mother, the government never does so on its own, in behalf of the child, nor does it force a father to both financially support and personally care for his child, as this legislation forces the mother, nor does it consider that desertion by the father in any way is contrary to the good of society, even though the costs of "welfare" run into the millions. 

Basic to the attitude that men are not directly responsible for and to their children is the idea that men really do not have children, only women have children, and therefore men are not as responsible for their sexual behavior as women. Even though we know, even as children, that both men and women are necessary for the procreation of children, and that men are taught that it is manly to be aggressive and forceful in sexual matters, and therefore physically more responsible, we tend to forget this. Although we know that a child is created not months after intercourse, but within a few hours, and that during pregnancy the mother merely shelters and feeds the vulnerable child that is thus created, we tend to forget it. We act as though pregnancy rather than sexual intercourse creates children, and use pregnancy rather than sexual intercourse as the basis for establishing responsibility. It is this attitude that is most directly responsible for abortion, and the most valid argument for abortion. 

Whereas the child during pregnancy has a right to claim support from its father even more because of its mother's incapacity. 

We also tend to set women up as the absolute authority in sexual matters.. the one who says, "yes" or "no", so that if pregnancy does occur, it is all her own fault. We ignore the facts that women have the same sexual and emotional needs as men, and that both are rational beings with the same capacity for control and the same weaknesses. In the words of the NAL Statement: "Our basic premise here is that a human being is responsible. His or her actions have consequences and a person is responsible for the foreseeable consequences of what that person freely does. Men and women are moral beings. They cannot abdicate responsibility for a new life by saying simply that they did not intend that there be conception." As a society of rational beings, we must also be responsible for the foreseeable consequences of our own nature and being. As a bi-sexual society we are going to have sexual needs and we are going to have children, and we need to provide realistically for satisfying our sexual needs, and providing care for the children of our society. 

I do not want to dwell on this too long but I think it is impossible to over emphasize it. We do teach our young men and women that men really do not have children, that women have superior capabilities, rights and responsibilities with regard to children, that the parent-child relationship is not important to men personally as it is to women, that the father-child relationship is not important to the child, and that fathers can be excluded from intimate involvement in the first three and most formative years of the child's life without damage to anyone. We not only permit, but encourage and reward the father economically for deserting the care and education of their children. It is not possible to exaggerate the effect these attitudes (and the general anti-parent propaganda that I will explore later) have on the pregnant woman, or even to approach realizing their impact toward abortion; whether she is married, single, young or old, healthy or ill, rich or poor, a high-school drop-out or holding a master's degree, they affect a woman's attitude towards her pregnancy, her child, herself and her position as a mother in society.

Another sex-related attitude that creates conflict between a mother and her child is our tendency to regard pregnancy more as evidence of sexual behavior, than as evidence of a growing child. While of course the two cannot be entirely separated, it should be obvious that we cannot undo what we may consider "undesirable" sexual behavior by rejecting the child or making life difficult for the mother when she is essentially trying to care for the child. If we are to approach the subject of abortion with reasonable intelligence, we must distinguish between moral and legal forces necessary to promote "desirable" sexual behavior, and those necessary to promote responsible respect for the life of a child. (Or perhaps we need to talk about social and educational forces toward responsible sexual behavior.) Society has no right on the one hand to demand that parents assume responsibility for the care of a child regardless of their attitude toward the sexual union that created the child, and then conversely, say that society has no responsibility for the child because we disapprove of the sexual union that created the child. In a society where more than half our marriages end in divorce (and vice-versa), where premarital sex is commonplace, and where promiscuity is widely tolerated, we have no majority of people who have a right to legally judge against people who have problems working out their personal relationships within a "proper" framework of marriage, with "proper" affluence. To pass legislation or maintain legislation forbidding abortion while maintaining socially crippling attitudes toward the child and discriminating against the mother who must care for it, because of these so-called "moral" attitudes, smacks of rank hypocrisy, and yet, the pregnant woman is excluded from schools, from employment, from medical insurance benefits, from credit resources, from the care and support of her immediate family and community, and often from the company of her friends and even the father of the child himself, simply because society sees her pregnancy as evidence of undesirable sexual behavior, for which she is primarily responsible, rather than as a mother caring for her child. 

A woman's sexual behavior may be considered undesirable because she is "unwed," "underage" or poor, however, these are not personal attributes exclusively under her personal control. Being "unwed," "underage" or poor are relative situations. Poverty is a relative situation, created by our economic system. What is poor in one society could be untold wealth in another time or place. 

Likewise, being unwed or underage are legal definitions . . judgments of our society as defined by our laws and customs, rather than accurate descriptions of reality. A man and woman must be wedded to one another in a biological sense in order to conceive a child, and they also must be physically mature. Many young people who are willing and capable of assuming responsibility for their sexual behavior, have been prevented from doing so by our laws and customs. Centuries ago a young man was considered an adult at 12 years, and a woman never achieved adulthood, except in a limited sense, as a mother; now it takes 18, 21 or even 24 or 25 years before a young man is accepted into society as an adult, capable of assuming responsibility for himself and others, while a young woman is expected to assume the responsibilities of adulthood as early as 12 or 13, or as soon as it is possible for them to become pregnant. Young men are prevented from assuming the responsibilities of parenthood and sexual behavior until they are 18 or 21, young women on the other hand are "permitted" to assume these responsibilities legally, without their parents protection, when they are 18, 16 and in some states even younger. Up to these "legal ages" young people must have their parents "permission" to marry legally, and to make contracts for housing, household goods, etc. Although young women can and do become pregnant whether or not they are legally married or of age, and therefore must assume the responsibility, the age requirement does prevent young men from assuming responsibilities they might be quite willing and able to assume, and puts more than a fair share of responsibility on the young woman. 

Young people are denied opportunities for employment simply because of their age, or because they lack educational degrees or accomplishments that may have nothing to do with the work to be done, and are paid lower wages although they may have needs for income to establish a new home, pay family expenses and further their education that are equal to or exceeding those of any other age. 

Many parents also predicate paying college expenses for their children on a promise they will not marry until after graduation and/or establishing themselves in a business or vocation. By all these means, we make it very difficult for young people to assume responsibility for their sexual behavior and/or as parents, dur-

ing those years when when sexual impulses are most difficult to cope with, being associated as they are with establishing one's personal and social identity and maturity, and during those years when people are most inclined by nature to make life-long commitments and establish new homes and families. 

While the reasons behind these laws were no doubt well-intentioned efforts to prevent too-young marriages that all too often result in divorce, we must reexamine these efforts, and consider whether or not they are instead merely encouraging irresponsibility and chaos, and whether or not these young marriages fail because they are essentially a rebellion against their classification as children or minors and a denial of their rights as human beings, to be accepted into our social and economic systems as persons according to their abilities, rather than some arbitrary age.

Both social and economic maturity come through assimilation into society and accepting responsibility for our actions. We can assimilate people into society from infancy on, allowing them to assume responsibility for their behavior gradually, rather than excluding them from participation until some arbitrary age or accomplishment, that has nothing to do with ability, and then assuming they can and must become assimilated and be able to hnadle responsibility all at once. Assimilation into the larger society cannot be accomplished by parents alone, acting outside the society, and it is senseless to charge parents with the responsibility for developing social maturity when it is something that the entire society must participate in. We must recognize, by law, that there is a distinct difference between a 10 year old child and a young woman or young man of 17 years who is physically mature and possesses an academic knowledge far beyond that of 17-year-olds of even a generation ago, but whose knowledge and physical maturity have no practical relevancy to the workings of society. 

I cannot help but compare the assimilation of people into the larger society, with the assimilation of children into the family: take for example simple tasks such as washing dishes or doing household repairs. You do not wait until a child has achieved some abitrary age or unrelated accomplishment before you demand that the child be competent and responsible for doing these tasks. First the child will observe the father or the mother doing household carpentry or washing the dishes and asks to help, wants to try it, or the parent may suggest doing it to the child as a divertissement, knowing that the child will not be able to do it well. Either in the trying or in playing, the child learns how different materials behave and how to control the use of tools, etc. by using them, the water, the soap, the dishcloth, the faucets, the drain rack, the hammer, the nails, the wood, a screw, the screwdriver. The parent offers suggestions, criticizes, encourages and supervises so that the child learns more quickly how to accomplish and what the goals are. This is repeated over a period of time until the child gains enough expertise that he or she can be expected to be able to assume total responsibility for doing these tasks. Parents assume it is their responsibility to teach their children how to do things that need to be done so they can assume responsibility, they do not assume that a child has no responsibility in the home except as a kind of favor to the child, or expect it to assume a responsibility without any prior experience or learning.

Yet there is an increasing tendency to view caring for children not as caring for people until they are able to care for themselves, but rather as a specialized work of raising adults. Someone recently referred to the family as the "factory where people are made." Under this kind of philosophy, the child is considered as having no value except as a potential adult. "What are you going to be when you grow up?" This not only puts a lot of pressure on young adults and their attitudes towards parental responsibility when they have been excluded from learning what they can do economically by observation and doing, but makes pregnancy seem like a twenty-year sentence with a tremendous burden at the end, rather than a responsibility of diminishing proportions gradually, as the child assumes responsibility. This tremendous increasing of the burdens of parenthood, and the attending attitude that children are sort of a luxury product rather than an ordinary part of life, puts a great pressure on the mother par ticularly to produce an acceptable "finished product" at the same time that parenthood is less and less regarded as important or worthwhile to society or children.

With child care considered a personal interest rather than a worthwhile need of society, the maintenance of a home and caring for one's own children are considered of so little importance that they are not worthy of any compensation, consideration or support by society. Mothers on welfare, for example, were re-

cently told by the provisions of proposed welfare legislation that matter how menial or low-paying, was of more value to society thy work, no work of caring for their own children at home. Mothers are expected to take any job such as cleaning public restrooms or picking up papers in the park at far less than minimum wages, while their children are cared for in a day care center that is paid more for one week of 8-hour days than the mother receives to care for her child for a month. Income tax provisions consider predominately male-run business enterprises so important that wall-to-wall carpeting, air conditioning, and steak lunches for their salesmen are deductible items of expenses, while mothers trying to run an adequate home for the care of children, cannot even deduct rent, peanut butter sandwiches, diapers, a crib or medical expenses, much less the books, art supplies, musical instruments, recreation and physical exercise accommodations that are necessary to good education and development of children. Studies have shown that the importance of the home environment in the education and outlook of children, particularly during the first five years, is of over-riding significance to all other education, yet we have made no provisions for encouraging or evaluating its importance in economic terms or social goals. 

The care of children requires intelligence, great physical strength and efforts, emotional stability, social awareness and psychological acuity, and is necessary to society, and yet, the woman who becomes a mother is treated economically as though she had acquired an instant degree in idiocy, and treated to that same deference society shows to the feeble-minded and senile aged. The more time she spends at this occupation, the more a woman will be considered not suitable for "real" employment. It will be assumed that a mother will be compensated for her work by the mere pleasure of doing it, although this is not assumed for any other occupation, no matter how personally rewarding, altruistic, or socially necessary the work. It is assumed that the mother is suited by nature to be a good mother, however, there is nothing instinctive about the work of caring for children, it is a learned ability, and many young women from today's smaller families have had no opportunity to learn how to care for and educate children. At the same time psychologists and doctors, educators and social scientists are telling parents how seriously they can handicap their children mentally, physically, emotionally, socially and economically unless they know what to do and how to do it; hacking away at parental self-confidence and personal interest in the child-parent relationship, the two most important ingredients for successful parenthood. 

Thus many women, and men, doubt seriously their own abilities to be good parents, to do the work required 24 hours a day, 168 hours per week, for 18 or 20 years, and their mental and emotional capabilities to stand the isolation, lonliness and responsibilities now imposed on those who care for children. Although we spend billions of dollars on highways and transportation facilities to get people to and from work, we cannot find the money for child care centers that would permit both parents to work and provide other relief from the pressures of parenthood. We require many things from employers regarding conditions of work, hours, etc., but we cannot seem to find the power to require employers to provide child care centers at places of work. We spend billions and billions of dollars for defense of our "way of life," a way of life that we are effectively destroying ourselves if we do not involve the next generation in its workings. There has been found no substitute for parental care that anywhere nearly approaches the effectiveness of parents in guiding the development of children despite the possibilities of abuse or failure, unless it is a larger parental groups such as the larger family or a community substitute which includes the parents. Certainly there is no substitute for parental love. Unless we are ready to commit ourselves to a society without children, we must recognize the importance of child care in the home and make arrangements to support and encourage parents. We cannot have it both ways; so important that we insist mothers must assume the responsibility, and so unimportant that we will do everything to discourage effective means of discharging that responsibility. 

The proposed legislation will not make fathers more responsible for their children, it will not diaper a baby, give it its 2 a.m. bottle, or see that it does its homework, bandage up a scraped knee, or make it possible for a mother to work and take care of her children at the same time. It will not eliminate employer discrimination against a woman who has children, or who is likely to have children, or open the doors to higher paying jobs, jobs that have been traditionally reserved for men, that would enable her to adequately support herself, her children and/or pay for child care while she is working, as the salaries of men have traditionally done whether they are supporting anyone selse or not. It will

not eliminate discrimination in housing that makes it difficult to rent a house if you have children, are a single woman, or if you have a low salary. I cannot emphasize too much the importance of housing, and the lack of reasonably priced available housing: more than two-thirds of the children who are wards of the court in Washington, for example, are there because their parents could not find adequate housing. The proposed legislation will not make credit resources available for emergency needs, housing, household furnishings, clothing, or medical bills; it will not make creditors recognize the salaries and paying records of married women or the child support and alimony payments to divorced mothers as valid income sources. It will not make schools more responsive to the educational needs of children, rather than to the need to judge children as they now do. It will not establish day care centers, pay medical bills for childbirth, or provide housing, nutrition, or income for pre-natal and post-natal care associated with child birth. It will not restore the tenure, the job seniority, the educational, professional or occupational momentum a woman loses through pregnancy, childbirth and child care. Without some attention to these needs and some attempt to restore a modicum of respect and support for the necessary social goods of mothering and fathering, this legislation comes across to many women only as hypocritical oppression, an attempt to lay on women heavy burdens that we have not lifted one finger towards removing or relieving. 

It should be obvious that one primary element of pressure is time. Children require round-the-clock care; it is a 24-hour a day job. This 168-hour work week is more than four times that of the "average" 40 hour work week, and yet courts have no difficulty equating this 168 hour week with financial support from less than 40 hours of work. In divorce and child-support settlements, the court always considers that it must give a father some of his income to live on, to continue a full life; yet it thinks nothing of giving a woman no time to live on. The most criminal activity going on in this conutry today is the virtual imprisonment of millions of young mothers, who are "doing time" for no greater crime than the perfectly natural human activity of having a child. Men do not have to choose between being a parent and being a member of society, and neither should women have to make this choice. This incredibly unjust isolation of the mothers of young children makes women virtually slaves to the needs of their children, as determined by society. 

This testimony is, of course, an inadequate attempt to fully describe the pressures toward abortion. Many of the more important aspects have only been touched upon, and many lesser ones not mentioned at all. Attached are some newspaper clippings and reports which define and clarify some of the issues mentioned here. However, the Committee has at its disposal much more detailed discussion and exposition of these pressures in the form of hearings that have been held on legislation for welfare, housing, daycare centers, family life, equal opportunity in employment, and equal rights for women, as well as numerous publications by various administration offices. When studied in the context of this proposed legislation it will be easy to see that almost all the pressures mentioned in this testimony can be quite readily approached from a legislative standpoint.

It must be stressed that this testimony is not given in support of liberalized abortion laws, but to stress that abortion or the rights of the unborn child cannot be considered as an isolated subject, but must be considered in the total context of the society in which pregnancy and the demand for abortion occur. 

We urge this Committee to recommend setting up a legislative task force to study problems associated with pregnancy, childbirth and child care from the viewpoint of drafting legislation that will protect the rights of the mother and the child. While passage of the Equal Rights Amendment will obviously do much in this direction it will not completely solve the problems involved. It is time to divert some substantial portion of the national income, both in the form of positive programs and in tax rebates or exclusions, to solving some of these problems.

With regard to the proposed legislation itself, we would suggest that the Subcommittee seek testimony from scientists engaged in research on the fetal and embryonic infant. fetologists, for a firm foundation regarding the humanity and personhood of the unborn infant, seeking national public media cooperation in exposing the results of this testimony. We also propose that the legislation be amended to secure the right of the child, born or unborn, to knowledge, support and care from its father; and, in relation to its incapacity, to claim from the community, support and education to self-sufficiency and capability to support dependents.

Although we have mentioned some specific areas where legislation can directly, and quickly have an effect on the problems of pregnancy and abortion, we do not want to give the impression that this is a simple problem that can be solved with a few appropriate laws. This is an extremely complex and serious set of problems that are symptomatic of larger pressures in our society which do not readily lend themselves to immediate resolution. For example, there is on sociological aspect of current life which should be kept in mind when considering this subject although it does not lend itself to legislative action, because it bears more importantly than any other on the conflicts involved in pregnancy and childbirth.

We have built up an attitude of importance towards work outside the home that is completely out of proportion to its real value to human life. It has become the center of social activity, and of personal identity, the center of governmental concern, and the focus of family life. Much, if not all, of this importance depends on its being separate from ordinary life, and exclusive of children. Yet there is no real reason why children must be excluded from the workings of business, government or industry, and confined to homes, playgrounds and schools, out of the way of these "important" activities. Truly important and dignified human activities cannot be diminished by the mere presence of children, they are in fact enhanced.

The manufacturing of billions of tons of refrigerators, dishes, airplanes, automobiles, transistor radios, etc., is not more important than the homes and human lives for which these things are supposedly manufactured. Wars are not more important than these homes and human lives they are supposedly fought to defend. There is actually no occupation or enterprise in the world today that did not originate in the home and the family, homes where women not only developed and participated in these occupations, but in many cases originated and invented the processes and products. Weaving, clothing manufacturing, pottery and dish making, agriculture, buying and selling, home building and even wars themselves, are a few of these activities. Since these activities have been taken out of the home through industrialization and incorporation, women, children, the elderly and partially disabled are being told they can no longer participate even though they still possess the same capabilities. 

This change in the economic status of the home, brought about through industrialization and incoporation, have created alienation between the home and the source of income, between husband and wife, children and parents, between neighbors, between the "dependent" home as consumers and the individual wage earner as income source.

The supposition that an employer has absolute and complete rights over a person for a certain and major part of a day, 9 to 5 or whatever, is no less than slavery, however partial, and is as severe a pressure than that of women to the care of the some and children. We must re-evaluate the workings of our society, particularly economically, with regard to developing goals for human life, rather than goals of production, Gross National Product, keeping the economy moving, etc. that only serve to compound the problems.

RESOLUTION OF ABORTION-1971 NAL CONFERENCE AT FORDHAM UNIVERSITY, NEW YORK 

The National Association of the Laity, recognizing the lack of realistic leadership on the part of the heirarchial Church on the critical issue of abortion, believes that it is the responsibility of the laity to assert themselves on the principles which are fundamental to the dignity of the individual and all human lfe, whether real or potential, and to the total well-being of society as a whole. 

Therefore consistent with our previous position on racism, poverty, and our concern for human dignity within the structural Church, we reaffirm our respect for human life, in recognizing the rights of the child-bearing mother, as well as the life or potential human life of the fetus. 

NAL as a statement of policy encourages: 

1. More positive programs of social and economic impact which would lessen the need for abortion (i.e. housing, maternal care child support, and day care centers, to mention a few). 

2. Extensive counseling at all levels, not only to the married couple, but to single people. Such counselling would include adequate education on birth control alternatives as a deterrent to abortion. 

3. A program of public education on birth control which discourages abortion and emphasizes the value of all human life.

We believe that the traditional Catholic position which forbids abortion under any circumstances is much too narrow and totally ignores the rights of the mother and father and of the family in general. 

Further, the "abortion on demand" position is equally as narrow as the traditional position, proclaiming the superior and absolute rights of the mother to determine the fate of the unborn fetus. The determinants in the question of abortion are serious moral, ethical and medical ones. "Morally speaking, abortion is an act of killing, the violent, direct destruction of potential human life, already in the process of development. The fact should not be disguised or overlooked by circumlocution. It is not the destruction of a human person, which implies one who has developed a capacity for reasoning, willing, desiring and relating to others-but it is the destruction of an important and valuable form of human life. Its value and its potentiality are not dependent upon the attitude of the woman toward it; it grows by its own biological dynamism and has a genetic and morphological potential distinct from that of the woman. It has its own distinctive and individual future. If contraception and abortion are both seen as forms of birth limitation, they are distinctly different acts; the former precludes the possibility of a conceptus being formed, while the latter stops a conceptus already in existence from developing. The bias implied by the principle of the sanctity of human life is the protection of the right of life. That right should be accorded even to doubtful life; its existence should not be wholly dependent upon the personal self-interest of the woman."¹ We 

1 Abortion: Law, Choice, and Morality, Callahan, pp. 497-98. affirm that the abortion is a serious moral, ethical and medical question. 

Whereas the NAL affirms the sanctity of life in all stages of biological development; 

Be it resolved that we the Church Community take positive steps to support a woman (both during her pregnancy and afterwards) in a decision not to abort; 

And be it further resolved that we affirm the rights of individuals to hold opposing views and we reject any attempt to force a moral judgment on others. 

NATIONAL ASSOCIATION OF LAITY-STATEMENT ON HUMAN LIFE LEO J. JORDAN, CHAIRMAN, COMMITTEE ON HUMAN LIFE 

On September 22, 1971, the NAL committee on Human Life issued a preliminary statement on the crucially important subject of human life. This committee recognized that considerable controversy and confusion has developed over the increasing demand for induced abortions. The polaric positions of those who voice inflexible opposition to induced abortion on the one hand with those who demand an inherent right of abortion on demand have created serious personal, moral and legal conflicts among the parties concerned: woman, father, unborn child, as well as among the entire community. 

It is a difficult undertaking to attempt to reconcile these vastly separated positions, but we in NAL recognize an obligation to make this effort. Our research has convinced us that there is a public demand for more liberal abortion privileges through the nation.¹ The sensitive issues involved have created great public pressures from those who insist that the direct killing of an unborn child is always immoral,2 and from those who proffer that every woman has the right to abort a child she does not want. We have recognized an alarming divisiveness among the legislative communities on this issue and we are hopeful that our approach can assist those who have been chosen to make the political decision. 

Moreover, we, in NAL, feel it is imperative to set forth a common position to arrest those movements which have gone beyond what we believe to be a reasonable approach to this problem.

Our basic premise here is that a human being is responsible. His or her action have consequences and a person is responsible for the foreseeable consequences of what the person freely does. Men and women are moral beings. They cannot abdicate responsibility for a new life by saying simply that they did not intend that there be conception. 

1 Report to President and Congress by the U.S. Commission on Population Growth and the Amrican Future. 

2 Woywod-Smith, A Practical Commentary on the Code of Canon Law, 1952, canon 938. 

3 Hon. Bella Abzug, Intro message to H.B. 14715, Congressional Record, May 2, 1972.

Moreover, we are assuming a Christian dimension. As followers of Jesus Christ we affirm a belief in the immortality of the human soul (although it seems that we do not know when the soul enters the body) *, the possibility of salvation for the soul, and the basic rule that I must love my neighbor as myself. 

Accordingly, we recognize that human life--in any stage of its growth—is a thing of great value, and it is not to be lightly terminated. 

NAL supports the position that induced abortions are a matter of moral concern; that the decision whether or not to abort an unborn child must be made only following mature, conscientious deliberation. Nevertheless, any decision concerning the continuation of life of the unborn child must be made only after careful consideration of all of the interests affected; for surely the personal conscience does not exist in isolation from the conscience of the community. 

Foremost among these interests is the life of the unborn child, followed immediately by the inherent right of a woman to freedom of conscience and decision in a free society. Moreover, the rights of a responsible father must also merit absolute consideration.

This paper begins with an evaluation of the concerns and rights of an unborn child and continues with an examination of the important roles of the woman, father, and the entire community. In some instances we may find the interests of one or more of these persons competing with rights of another. It is our hope that if these interests are carefully defined, some of the moral, economic, and sociological considerations may be examined and, following mature deliberation, decisions made by the concerned parties. While this paper is prepared primarly for the purpose of providing guidance to those seeking to make conscientious, personal decisions concerning abortions, we are hopeful that the principles contained herein will provide guidance to political leaders who deem it necessary to enact legislation setting out community standards for abortion. 

It is imperative to recognize that all of the affected parties have rights and it is the function of the legislative community to define those rights. Let us first examine the interests of:

THE UNBORN CHILD 

The imperative issue is whether an embryo or fetus is a human being from the time of conception. Philosophic, religious and scientific experts have been unable to agree and, for the moment, we must conclude that the dilemma is beyond precise solution. Nevertheless, while full agreement among experts is wanting, there are those who have concluded that human life begins at conception. Their credentials are so impressive that they demand fullest consideration. For an important example, we observe that in October of 1967 the First 

International Conference on Abortion carefully considered the question of, "When does human life begin?" The near unanimous conclusion of this representative group was as follows: The majority of our group could find no point in time between the union of the sperm and egg and the birth of the infant at which point we could say that this was not a human life. 

They continued:

The changes occuring between implantation, a six weeks embryo, a six month fetus, a one week old child, or a mature adult are merely stages of development and maturation.

Moreover, within the United States and elsewhere, legal doctrine has concluded in a number of important areas, that an unborn child is indeed a person and as such is entitled to specific legal protection. The development of the law of negligence has determined that an unborn child is a "person" entitled to rights of recovery for prenatal injuries from the moment of conception. For

centuries the law of property has recognized that an unborn child is a person from the moment of conception." Recognition of the rights of the unborn person has also been formulated and recognized in the field of criminal law. 

Based upon the available evidence, religious, legal and scientific, it is contrary to reason for us to conclude that an unborn person is not a human life. 

If consensus is at all available among our brothers and sisters within NAL, it is that the "moment" of conception or some stage of development very close to the "moment" is the point at which distinctively human life begins.10 

We have agreed, therefore, that there are fundamental rights of an unborn child which must be recognized and respected. 

1. An unborn child is a person and is entitled to basic, fundamental rights enjoyed by other persons. Included among these rights are: (a) The right to attain the end of prenatal development;" (b) The right to become a free and responsible adult, a contributing member of the human community; and (c) The fundamental rights guaranteed by the United States Constitution; including the right to due proces of law.¹2 

THE WOMAN 

We recognize the identity of a woman as an individual person. Moreover, we recognize that her relationships within her family are so vital that they should be ranked as fundamental and guarded against unreasoned interference. 

We believe that a woman has a fundamental right of possession and control over her own person. This right is now recognized (in law) as the right of privacy and includes the right of an individual woman to marry; to enjoy intimacy in the marriage; to conscientiously decide not to have children and to direct the education of children free from all restraint of interference of others; without lawful justification." 13 We believe that women have a basic right, once the life of the unborn has begun, to claim from the community food and care in sufficient quantities to sustain her and the unborn child during her period of pregnancy, and afterwards. 

A woman has the right to spiritual and temporal counseling from the community, in order to provide her with the necessary information concerning whether or not to seek an abortion. She has a right to this counseling from someone who has taken training in and has achieved some insight into her situation. She has the right to assume that her good faith will not be questioned. 

A woman has the right to complete her childhood before bearing a child; the right to refuse to continue a pregnancy which results from a criminal act such as rape or incest; the right to continue to refuse a pregnancy which poses a definite threat to her own life or health. 

THE FATHER 

The forms which the responsibility of a parent toward a child takes are generally determined by the society in which the individual lives. In American society, the father generally is considered responsible for the support and upkeep of the mother and children and is required to provide whatever other services and goods the children need for their well-being, including love, companionship and personal care.

It would seem then that any rights that a father has with regard to the decision of whether an abortion should be performed will be related to the responsibility that he, the father, is willing to undertake. It makes no difference whether the parents are married or unmarried really. If the father will take absolutely no responsibility for the support and upbringing of the children and the care of the mother during pregnancy, delivery and afterwards, then it would seem that the father would have no rights whatever to participate in a decision regarding an abortion. at 9.

20 However, if the father is willing to take fully the responsibility of a father, then it would seem that he should have an influential voice in determining whether an abortion should be performed. Consequently, therefore, no abortion should be performed then without, attempting to procure the acquiescence of the responsible father; unless, of course, the abortion is necessary to preserve the life of the woman.

THE COMMUNITY 

No discussion on abortion can be complete without serious deliberation concerning the role of the community. A community represents the sum of its entire inhabitants and the culmination of the activities of its members. The principal responsibility of the community is to operate in the public interest and for the public welfare.

The community, through its political representatives, has a vital role to play in determining under what circumstances an unborn child must sacrifice his or her life. The members of the community have the right to know the facts about abortion and the effect an abortion law may have had upon other cultures and societies. The near-community must exert its persuasive influence to foreclose the legislative-community from enacting irresponsible abortion legislation, and to ensure that legislative deliberations are carried out in the absence of divisive political pressures. Society must provide for criminal and civil penalties against those who attempt abortions outside those circumstances provided for by the legislative community.

The community must ensure that once life has begun, it will not be terminated because the prospective mother did not have adequate food or care, or because her social or economic condition created excessive physical or psychological exertion. It must recognize that the fetus, once formed, is a member of the human family and that mere inconvenience cannot justify its destruction.¹4 

The community must provide professional medical advice and services to women seeking abortion. It must ensure that those without sufficient economic resources have direct access to competent medical advice and services. In the event a woman, following mature deliberation, decided against aborting a fetus, the community must recognize a responsibility to make some continuing provision for adequate care and support of the woman and child. We cannot speak of a fundamental right of a person and yet withhold from them the financial means to exercise that right.

But, most importantly, the community must direct its resources to the end of which problems of abortion will not arise. It must make provisions for (1) adequate educational facilities, (2) day care facilities to enable a woman to pursue her right to reasonable employment (3) research into more adequate and safer means of birth control, and (4) the development of an environment whereby unlawful conduct which may result in involuntary pregnancies would be precluded. #Right to life

THE COMPETING INTEREST 

We have concluded that an unborn child is a human being from, at least, very near the moment of conception. As a human being such person is entitled to the fundamental right to survive. Moreover, we also recognize the basic rights of a woman, foremost among which are the right to life, health, and the right of privacy and all that this right involves. At the same time, however, we must recognize that the rights of the inherent party, while subjectively fundamental, are not absolute. It is necessary, at times, that even basic, personal rights must be subordinated to superior rights of others. We acknowledge the role of the legislative community to define the basic rights of its members and to establish priorities of certain rights. We believe, therefore, that the interest of the community is served when the legislative community enacts reasonable abortion laws and procedures, recognizing, of course, that the legislative community may circumscribe the rights of others only under the most compelling circumstances.¹ 15 When pregnancy endangers the woman's life, the fundamental rights of a woman and an unborn child to survive are brought into immediate conflict. Who has the superior right to life? The constitutional protection of due process does 

14 United States v. Vuitch, 91 S. Ct. 1294, (1971). 

15 Supra, note 13.

not guarantee life, only that life may not be taken without due process of law. 

The legislative community must carefully consider the importance of these basic human rights,and decide who has the ultimate right to life. 

Consequently, as the legislative community attempts to weigh the equity of the priorities, they may conclude that there are compelling reasons why the life of the mother may be preferred. The reasons associated with this conclusion should include these following considerations."

First, the woman usually has established familial responsibilities, which would be seriously interrupted by her untimely death. Second, to prefer the life of the unborn child could jeopardize the life of the woman relying upon the possibility that the unborn child would be born and survive. Third, the very nature of the relationship between the woman and the unborn child suggests a preference for the woman. The child is yet dependent upon the woman and this would seem to suggest a somewhat ancillary nature of the life of the unborn child. 

For these reasons then, it would appear appropriate that the application of due process procedure would ensure that the woman be granted an abortion in those situations where there is substantial risk that continuation of pregnancy would endanger her life. We, in NAL, are in accord with this concept. 

Health of woman

Although we have recognized the fundamental right to life of the unborn child, albeit not an absolute right, we urge that any further encroachment on that right must be in the light of the gravest consideration. 

With this premise in mind, we undertake an evaluation of the issue whether an abortion to preserve the health of a woman is a sufficient reason to infringe upon the unborn child's right to survive. Can the life of an unborn child be terminated, under any circumstances, short of the woman's endangered life? 

Or put another way, is the right of the unborn child to life preferred over the right of the woman to soundness of mind and body? 

We believe it is axiomatic that a woman is entitled to, at least, reasonably sound physical and mental health. Nevertheless, when the health of a woman is seriously impaired because of her pregnancy, her right to continued good health may conflict with the unborn child's right to survive. The legislative community has an obligation to enact laws to protect the welfare of its members which, of course, includes the pregnant woman and the unborn child. Does the legislative community have such an overwhelming interest in protecting the health of the woman so as to justify aborting the life of an unborn child, because the continuation of the pregnancy might impair the health of the mother? Because of the fundamental nature of the child's right to life, due process would require an overwhelming or compelling community interest to terminate the life of the child.

It is our considered view that under well defined circumstances, due process would allow termination of the life of the unborn child, if the continued pregnancy would gravely and permanently impair the physical or mental health of the mother." The right of a woman to the control over her body is an imperative right. It would include, as an essential ingredient thereof, reasonably good physi cal or mental health. These objects are an essential part of the community's obligation to recognize the inherent worth of the prospective mother's health, or that of her husband and children whose living standards and opportunities may be seriously jeopardized by the additional pregnancy. 

While great strides in medicine have been obtained, the concerns mentioned above are genuine and deserve understanding. A pregnancy which seriously interferes with the mental or physical health of a woman may have catastrophic results upon the woman, her family, and even upon the future of the unborn child.

While we accept the decision of the legislative community to act to terminate the life of the unborn in order to preserve the mental and physical health of the mother, we are fully aware of the consequences of our recommendation. 

By no means do we intend that the mere declaration of a woman that her health is impaired would be sufficient cause to abort in the absence of further inquiry. 

We should permit normal inquiry into the reasons, but not so far as to impugn the strengths of her beliefs; great weight must be given to the decision of an 

16 Supra, note 6 at 1005. カット 

​17 D. Granfield, The Abortion Decision, Doubleday, at 71; citing The Abortion Act 

(England).

fts 1! individual conscience. In this way we will continue to uphold the identity, reputation and privacy of a woman. Our ultimate program must develop a standard of conduct for those who act with a mature consicence. 

But even with these cautions in mind, the infringement upon the right of the unborn child's right to survive can not be lightly considered. Our recommendation to allow an abortion for reasons of health must be carefully conditioned and allowed only under circumstances authorized by the community. Our specific recommendation is that an abortion be permitted if a continued pregnancy would gravely and permanently impair the mental or physical health of the mother; provided, however, that fear of such risk is genuine and confirmed by the most competent medical opinion.

The argument is made that the issue of abortion should not be the concern of the legislative community, but rather, this important determintaion should be made by the woman in consultation with her physician. This concept is consistant with the woman's right to privacy, including the right to have control over her body. However, because we have recognized the right of person of the unborn child, this inherent right to survive must be decided by someone other than one who has a direct relationship in the outcome. Because the right of the woman and child to survive are essentially equal, it can not be said with certainty that the woman, or her physician, would make this decision with object determination.

Nevertheless, while the woman's declaration of her mental or physical health is an important deliberative factor, there is a decisive role for her physician in the final decision. We believe that the physician must decide, initially, whether the continued pregnancy would impair the health of the woman, in a manner consistant with the intent of the legislative community." 

In the event the physician concluded that impairment of the woman's health was imminent, this decision would be presented to a medical panel convened to receive evidence. The panel would act as a lawful agency of the community and would be charged with establishing precise procedures for both the hearing and the resulting abortion, if permitted. Its decision would be administratively final, subject to reversal by a judicial hearing only in the event it acted in an arbitrary or capricious manner.

We recommend also that in the event the woman's physician decided that the continued pregnancy would not result in an impairment of physical or mental health, the woman could still, if she chose, request a hearing from the medical panel.

While we do not intend in this paper to set out our entire view on the operational procedures of the medical panel, we do offer these suggestions. In order to ensure that due process was afforded the unborn child, a guardian ad litem should be appointed by the community and his or her sole function would be to represent the interest of the unborn child. It is likely that the guardian, if not satisfied that due process was given the unborn child, would undertake a judicial appeal of the decision of the medical panel. 

Testimony from the father would also be received during the medical panel hearing. This testimony would receive subtsantial validity by the medical panel. 

Moreover, the father would be likewise entitled to appeal the decision of the medical panel.

Finally, it is our present opinion that the legislative community must place some time limit upon the procurement of an abortion. Medical experts would seem to agree that an abortion after the 26th week, except as necessary to save the life of the mother, should not be permitted. 

RAPE-INCEST-EUGENICS 

Over the past years, a number of abortion reform laws have allowed the survival right of the unborn child to be divested upon justification of rape, incest and also by what has been termed eugenic considerations. Because of the fundamental nature of the right to survive, due process guarantees would require an overwhelming or compelling interest of the legislative community to overcome this basic right. Does the community have such an overwhelming interest to justify aborting the life of an unborn child because conception had occurred in an uncustomary manner, or because the unborn child may be born with serious mental or physical defects? 

18 D. Granfield, The Abortion Decision, Doubleday, at 97.

It may be argued that the legislative community has a compelling interest in terminating illicit pregnancies or, more precisely, those caused by forcible rape which are indeed an offense against a person's will. Not only is the initial act a violation against the person but the crime is perpetuated during the term of the pregnancy. Moreover, the trauma connected with the initial assault may have a serious psychological effect upon the offended person. The legislative community, therefore, may, for the welfare of its members, assert a compelling interest in permitting abortions where the pregnancy resulted from an actual, forced rape. 19 While we conclude that an abortion should be permitted if requested by the assaulted person, we must recognize that the unborn child will have his or her life terminated. The unborn child is the unintended victim of this assault and the community should encourage the prospective mother to allow the child to be born, if at all possible. The community must accept responsibility for the assault because it has failed to maintain a community standard or moral atmosphere to dissuade the assailant. 

In order to motivate the woman to continue the pregnancy, the community must offer encouragement and compensation.20 Compensation would not only take the form of providing medical care, but, more importantly, compensation would be provided for the continued care of the child and mother. The community must undertake affirmative programs to eliminate the blemish associated with involuntary pregnancies, whether resulting from assault or from the actions of unwed parents.

We find it difficult to sustain a general conclusion that pregnancies precipitated upon an incestuous relationship merit such a compelling state interest, sufficiently enough to warrant abortions. But, if a compelling interest is to be sustained, it must be based upon an assumption that the female person was of tender age and incapable of mature deliberation. The act would, in effect amount to a violation of the person in much the same manner as is manifested in cases of forcible rape.

When such situations do occur, an incestuous pregnancy may involve an initial traumatic experience coupled with possible psychological impairment. The unity of the family may also suffer serious disruption if the unborn child is permitted to live. Permitting absortions under these circumstances would appear to be within the interest of the legislative community. Nevertheless, in the event of a pregnancy resulting from an incestuous relationship, we again emphasize the communal responsibility to provide the necessary resources, and appropriate environment to encourage the birth of the child, if the mother so desires. Nor are we unconcerned about the role of the putative father in this situation; the community must adopt an approach of sympathetic understanding and concern for all parties concerned. The community atmosphere must be conducive to the acceptance of the mother and child.

While we experience thoughtful concern for parents of children who are born with serious mental or physical defects, we cannot immediately conclude that the interest of the state in parents having children free from defects is sufficiently compelling to warrant induced abortions. The interest of the legislative community can be found in sparing its citizens from the burden of raising a seriously deformed child, as well as in avoiding the expense incurred in establishing and maintaining child care facilities. We concede a legislative interest; however, we are unable to conclude that the interest of the legislative community is sufficiently compelling so as to have a priority over the right to life. While this is our general conclusion, we feel we must retain an open mind with respect to cases wherein medical evidence establishes an overwhelming case of severe mental or physical deformity and the likelihood that the status of human being has not been attained.

We wish to stress the importance of a community effort to create an environment whereby children born with mental and physical impediments will be accepted as full members. Regardless of the dimensions of the burdens imposed by nature, we must accept these children as human persons. Necessarily, therefore, the community must provide the resources to insure that these persons become contributing members of our society. We must recognize, however, that actual knowledge of a deformed child may have a detrimental effect upon the physical or mental health of the mother. In this instance, it would seem appropriate that an abortion be permitted, but only under circumstances where it 

19 Supra, note 6 at 1010. 

20 G. Zahn, A Religious Pacifist Looks at Abortion, Commonweal, 28 May 1971, at 282.

is shown that the continued pregnancy would gravely and permanently impair the physical or mental health of the mother. 

We have attempted in this paper to advance the inquiry and to expand dialogue upon the crucially important subject of induced abortions. Only those persons whom the issue actually touches can fully understand the anguish of mature conscientious deliberations. We, in NAL, urge our brothers and sisters, when confronted with this problem, to seek counsel with your own instinct-with your own sense of what is good. But, beyond all, this should not be a solitary process. The entire community must somehow become involved, even if the only contribution of some may be their charity and understanding. While we are hopeful that community action and progress will one day eliminate the need for abortions, it seems certain that the legislative community will act under the prevailing pressures. We, in NAL, offer our proposal as a reasonable alternative until such time as our ultimate hopes are attained.
