SUMMARY ON HUMAN LIFE-1973 

For nearly three years, NAL has been attempting to develop consensus among its members on the crucially important subject of abortion. Throughout the country, polaric positions have developed between those who proffer that all induced abortions are murder and those who insist upon an inherent right to an abortion upon demand.

We in NAL have accepted the responsibility of attempting to formulate common ground; to offer a position which will be of assistance to those men and women who are attempting to make mature, conscientious decisions whether or not to seek an abortion. Moreover, we are hopeful that the principles set out in our paper will form the basis for a model legislative response. 

NAL supports the position that induced abortions are a matter of moral concern; that the decision to seek an abortion must be made only following mature deliberation. Nevertheless, any decision concerning the continuation of life must be made only after careful consideration of all of the interests affected: the unborn child, woman, father, and the entire community. 

Based upon all of the available evidence, we have been unable to conclude that an unborn person is not a human life. We accept the principle that the moment of concetpion or some stage very close thereto, is the point at which human life begins.

We are agreed that an unborn child is a person entitled to basic human rights including: (1) the right to attain the end of prenatal development; (2) the right to become a responsible member of the community; and (3) the constitutional right to due process of law. 

We recognize the fundamental rights of a woman to possession and control over her own person, as well as to all those elements contained in the recently recognized right of privacy.

The right of a responsible father must receive substantial recognition. No abortion should be performed without, at least, attempting to obtain the acquiescence of the father.

The community must recognize its obligation to protect the health and welfare of its members, including the mother and the unborn child. The community must recognize that the fundamental rights of the mother of the unborn child may, at times, compete with each other. Therefore, it is the responsibility of the community-particularly the legislative community-to evaluate the rights of the parties and to determine which rights must be subordinated to those of another's. Finally, the community must utilize its resources to develop an environment in which the necessity for induced abortions will not occur. 

We have agreed that the legislative community, in weighing individual priorities, including the absolute right of due process, may conclude that the rights of the woman are superior to the unborn child's right to survive under these circumstances: (1) Where there is substantial risk that continuation of pregnancy would endanger the woman's life; (2) Where the continued pregnancy would gravely and permanently impair the physical or mental health of the mother; (3) Where the pregnancy was accomplished through illicit means. 

We have concluded that the legislative community does not possess such an inherent interest in preventing the birth of defective children, so as to overcome the unborn child's right to survive. While our conclusion is as stated above, we must remain open to reconsider these cases where medical evidence establishes an overwhelming case of mental or physical deformity, concluding that the status of human being is absent. 

STATEMENT BY C. STANLEY LOWELL, ASSOCIATE DIRECTOR, AMERICANS UNITED FOR SEPARATION OF CHURCH AND STATE 

My name is C. Stanley Lowell. I am associate director of Americans United for

Separation of Church and State, a group of 130,000 American citizens devoted to the principle of religious liberty for all persons and all churches. We are here today because we see in the matters under consideration-S.J. Res. 130 and S.J. 

Res. 119-threats to the civil and religious liberty of citizens of the United States. 

The former, the Helms Resolution, would flatly prohibit any abortion for any woman in the United States under any circumstances whatever. It would doom to death every mother who could not survive a childbirth. In any pregnancy situation it would let the mother die rather than remove the fetus in order that the mother might live.

The latter, the Buckley proposal, would ban all abortions in the United States save for a single exception. All abortions would be forbidden save only when medical opinion indicated that continuation of the pregnancy would cause the death of the mother. This is a trifle more humane of the two proposals, but not much. We believe abortion to be a matter where no constitutional amendment, and, indeed, no legal enactment is needed. The decision by the United States Supreme Court in 1973 carefully stipulated that abortion during the early stage of pregnancy should be permissible at the decision of the woman involved. We believe that this covers the matter adequately, that this is a situation where the civil and religious rights of the woman should take precedence over other considerations.

What is set forth in support of these proposals represents the vestigal survival of a cruel, obscurantist philosophy that should have been interred long since. 

Let us examine some of the implications. Certainly the proposals would destroy a fundamental civil and religious liberty of women. Let us offer examples. Suppose a woman is pregnant as a result of forcible rape or incest, or suppose that there is evidence of fetal damage, or the likelihood of damage to the physical and emotional health of the woman. The law would crack down ruthlessly, bar-

ring all relief, with no regard for any of these considerations. It is all very well to talk about the right of the fetus, but what about the rights of the woman? 

Has she no rights, no freedom? Which is worse-to allow an abortion or to force a woman to have a child she does not want?

Under these proposals the state, in the finest totalitarian tradition, would tell the weeping rape victim that the fetus has just as much right to live as she does and that nothing can be done about it. This is worse than cruelty; it is sadism. 

And to behold members of the clergy coming here clad in their holy robes to advocate this sort of thing staggers belief. 

The Supreme Court in an excellent 1973 opinion has charted a careful course and rendered an opinion on this matter whose logic is impeccable. What the 

Court recognized was the right of the woman to control her own body and to have such children as she chooses to have. At this point, the rights of the mature, human personality should take precedence over alleged fetal rights. To be sure, the Court carefully delineated the woman's right in this situation. Her right to an abortion under certain conditions is recognized, but the conditions themselves are carefully spelled out. To deprive the woman of this authority over her own body is to deprive her of basic civil and religious liberty. It is to degrade woman to the level of a common chattel. Why should government step into such a situation and force a woman to bear a child she does not want, may deeply resent, and have no intention of caring for? This is an area of experience where political authority should hold its interference to a minimum. 

The rights of the fetus are only a part of a number of rights and values that are involved in each pregnancy situation. Another right is that of the child to proper care and a fair opportunity to make something of himself. It is a low form of cruelty to insist ruthlessly on bringing into the world a child for whom there is no welcome, no proper care and nurture, and no chance for a decent life. It is all very well to argue about the rights of a fetus. But what about the rights 

H of the child? There is no virtue in a legal insistence on bringing into the world unwanted children doomed to poverty, disease and delinquency.

The entire effort of government to ban abortions is futile, in any case. Abortions cannot be banned, no matter what kind of restrictive or prohibitive laws may be passed. What you can do, and what you now propose to do in this legislation, is to transfer the place of abortions from the hospital room or the physician's office with its carefully sterilized equipment to the filthy backroom with its hooks and hangers. It is a proposal to exchange a perfectly safe procedure for a very risky procedure with a high fatality rate. The proposal before you is not humane; it is barbarous and wicked. 

We do not need to speculate as to the merit of keeping the abortion reform that has been achieved today. The facts speak for themselves. It is significant to note that dramatic improvement in certain categories has been recorded since abortion reform came to New York State where women who want abortions can now have them safely and economically. In New York City there has been a dramatic drop in out-of-wedlock births. Such births dropped in 1971 to 12% of all births from the previous year's all-time high of 26.4% of all births. In one 

New York City hospital, nearly 15 infants per thousand deliveries were put up for adoption or abandoned by their mothers. The year following abortion reform this figure fell to 6.6 per thousand births. Perhaps, even more importantly, maternal deaths per 10,000 births in New York City dropped from 5.3 in 1969 to 2.6 in 1972, the lowest figure ever recorded.

What is needed in this whole situation is a proper balance. Human beings should be left with the freedom to judge each situation in the light of its total context and in accordance with their own conscience. Emotional clergymen, who themselves have never had any direct experience with parenthood, come here pleading the cause of just one value that is involved-that of the fetus. A properlyoriented legislative purpose should consider the full composite of values. These values would certainly include the desires of the woman herself, the welfare of the prospective child, and the good of society. 

STATEMENT ON BEHALF OF THE AMERICAN JEWISH CONGRESS TO THE SUBCOMMITTEE ON CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENTS OF THE U.S. SENATE COMMITTEE ON THE JUDICIARY ON PROPOSED CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENTS DEALING WITH ABORTION 

The American Jewish Congress welcomes the opportunity to submit this statement on the subject of proposed amendments to the United States Constitution dealing with abortion.

The American Jewish Congress is a membership organization which includes in its program defense of the constitutional rights of all American citizens. One of the resolutions of its 1972 National Biennial Convention dealt with the subject of abortion. It reads as follows: 

"American Jewish Congress affirms its position that all laws prohibiting or restricting abortion be repealed. Restrictive or prohibitive abortion laws violate the right of a woman to choose whether to bear a child, her right of privacy and her liberty in matters pertaining to marriage, family and sex. "Abortions are performed; that fact cannot be denied. Meanwhile, prohibitive and restrictive abortion laws have perpetuated inequality between those who can afford an abortion and those who cannot, leading to grave risks to the emotional and physical health of the woman, her family and the community and aggravating already grave social problems. "Those who find abortion unacceptable as a matter of religious conviction or conscience are free to hold and live by their beliefs, but should not seek to impose such beliefs, by government action, on others. "It is, therefore, the position of American Jewish Congress that all laws prohibiting or restricting abortion be repealed and that the matter be left to the woman concerned."

The current effort to amend the Constitution so as to bar abortions is generally regarded as having been prompted by the decisions of the United States Supreme 

Court in January 1973 in Roe v. Wade, 93 S. Ct. 705, and Doe v. Bolton, 93 S. Ct. 

739, in which the Court invalidated a broad anti-abortion statute in Texas and most of a more limited statute in Georgia It is important to note, however, that the specific proposals for constitutional amendments pending before this Committee, S.J. Res. 119 and S.J. Res. 130, would do much more than merely nullify the effects of those decisions. 

On the main issues in the Wade and Bolton cases, the Court was divided 7 to 2. The principal opinion, which was written by Justice Blackmun, was handed down in the Wade case, which arose in Texas. 

After an extensive inquiry into the history of the law relating to abortion (93 S. Ct. at 715-721), the Court found three historic reasons for criminal abortion laws: (1) to discourage illicit sexual conduct. This argument was not made by Texas and, as the Court noted, the Texas abortion statutes did not distinguish between married and unmarried mothers (at 724). (2) To guard against the medical dangers of abortion procedures. The Court declared, however, that mortality rates for women undergoing early abortions, where the procedure was legal, appeared to be as low as, or lower than, the rates for normal childbirth (at 725). (3) To protect pre-natal life. The Court held that, "as long as at least potential life is involved, the State may assert interests beyond the protection of the pregnant woman alone" (ibid).

The Court found that there was a "right of personal privacy" guaranteed by the "Fourteenth Amendment's concept of personal liberty and restrictions upon state action" (at 727). But that right of privacy, the Court said, was not absolute and must be considered against important state interests in regulation. It added, however, that, "where certain 'fundamental rights' are involved. regulation limiting these rights may be justified only by a 'compelling state interest' " and "legislative enactments must be narrowly drawn to express only the legitimate state interests at stake" (at 728). Without resolving the question of when life begins, the Court found the protection of the fetus was not such a compelling interest, that the fetus was not a "person" within the meaning of the Fourteenth Amendment and that the term "person" did not include the unborn (at 729). 

The Court then divided pregnancy into three phases or trimesters and laid down the following rules to govern each (at 731-2): (1) For the first third of pregnancy (about 12-13 weeks), "the abortion decision and its effectuation must be left to the medical judgment of the pregnant woman's attending physician," without state interference. (2) For the second trimester, and until the fetus is viable, "the State in promoting its interest in the health of the mother, may, if it chooses, regulate the abortion procedure in ways that are reasonably related to maternal health." (3) For the stage subsequent to viability, "the State, in promoting its interest in the potentiality of human life," may regulate or even forbid abortion entirely, except where necessary to preserve the life or health of the mother.

The effect of this decision was to greatly limit the power of a state to enact legislation prohibiting abortions. It must be remembered, however, that, before the Court spoke, nothing in the Constitution or any aspect of our legal system required a state to treat abortions as illegal. In fact. as the Court pointed out in

its decision (93 S. Ct. at 715), the then existing state laws against abortion were "not of ancient or even of common law origin. Instead, they derive from statutory changes effected, for the most part, in the latter half of the 19th century." 

The constitutional amendments proposed in S.J. Res. 119 and S.J. Res. 

130 would of themselves make a prohibition of abortions part of the legal system of this country, leaving no discretion to the states. S.J. Res. 119, introduced by 

Senator Buckley for himself and Senators Hatfield, Hughes, Bennett, Bartlett, Young and Curtis, reads as follows:

Section 1. With respect to the right to life, the word 'person', as used in this Article and in the Fifth and Fourteenth Articles of Amendment to the Constitution of the United States, applies to all human beings, including their unborn offspring at every stage of their biological development, irrespective of age, health, function or condition of dependency. "Sec. 2. This Article shall not apply in any emergency when a reasonable medical certainty exists that continuation of the pregnancy will cause the death of the mother. "Sec. 3. Congress and the several States shall have power to enforce this 

Article by appropriate legislation within their respective jurisdictions." 

S.J. Res. 130, introduced by Senator Helms, reads as follows: "1. Neither the United States nor any State shall deprive any human being, from the moment of conception, of its life without due process of law; nor deny to any human being, from the moment of conception, within its jurisdiction, the equal protection of the laws. "2. Neither the United States nor any State shall deprive any human being of life on account of illness, age, or incapacity. 

3. Congress and the Several States shall have power to enforce this article by appropriate legislation."

The scope of these proposed amendents is breathtaking. The would end all distinctions between persons after birth and fetuses before birth.' Presumably, all jurisdictions would be required to treat abortion at any stage as murder on the part of both the mother and any attending physicians or nurses. Civil suits for damages could be brought against the mother, physicians and nurses by the next of kin of the fetus.

If this seems too speculative, then it must be concluded that it is impossible to assess the effect of these proposed amendments because, far from merely restoring the status quo as it existed before the Supreme Court decisions, they would put into effect a concept with which our legal system has no experience. 

Instead of dealing specifically with the matter of abortion, they attempt to create new constitutional principles whose implications can only be guessed. 

Restoration of the status quo ante could of course be achieved by a simple amendment empowering the various states to prohibit abortion. (Such a proposal is embodied in H.J. Res. 427, sponsored by Rep. Whitehurst.) Senator

Helms has made it plain that he opposes any such limited change. In his statement accompanying introduction of S.J. Res. 130, appearing in the Congressional 

Record of June 29, 1973 (119 Cong. Rec. 12481), he specifically rejected this approach, insisting that the fetus's right to life must be protected in all states. 

Even if the proposed amendments did no more than restore the situation that existed before the Supreme Court decisions, we would oppose them for the reasons stated in the resolution set forth above. By the time the Supreme Court spoke, experience with anti-abortion laws had made it clear to many Americans that they constituted a dangerous and unwarranted invasion of privacy and denied women the right to determine what happens to their own bodies. Moreover, they bred a wide disrespect for law because they failed in fact to prevent abortions. Prior to the Supreme Court's decisions, it was estimated that from one to 12 million abortions were performed outside hospitals or other proper medical settings each year within the United States and 5,000 to 10,000 deaths resulted from these procedures. Backstreet abortions accounted for one-fifth of all maternal deaths in the United States and the number was increasing. Kummer & Leavey, Journal of American Medical Association, January, 1966. Kummer,

Jesse & Spencer, Abortion, The Hidden Epidemic, 95 Virginia Medical Monthly, 447 (1968). 

1 S.J. Res. 119 (but not S.J. Res. 130) would make an exception to this broad principle where the mother's death was a reasonable certainty. However, if the supporters of the amendment are right in their belief that fertilized ovum constitutes a human being from the moment of fertilization, it is difficult to see how this exception can be justified. The fact that the exception is deemed necessary points up the unsoundness of the basic principle.

Anti-abortion laws also had the effect of discriminating against the poor. 

Those with means were in a position to pay for abortions performed by doctorslegally or illegally. Those who did not have the means frequently died or were permanently injured as the result of attempts at self-induced abortion or as a result of the ministrations of charlatans. 

By 1972, these facts were receiving increasing recognition in both the courts and the legislatures. Many lower court decisions unfavorable to abortion laws preceded the 1973 decisions of the U.S. Supreme Court. Furthermore, a number of states, independent of court action, substantially reduced the scope of their anti-abortion laws. The proposed amendments, as we have noted, would not only nullify the effect of the Court's decision but would also prevent state legislatures from legalizing abortion. 

We recognize that abortion is condemned by the tenets of more than one religious group in this country. Indeed, there are many in the Jewish community who believe that abortion is prohibited by religious principles in at least some cases. It is plain, however, that nothing in the Wade and Bolton decisions impairs the right and power of religious groups to urge their followers to comply with their anti-abortion principles and to use whatever sanctions their procedures embody to enforce them. It is equally plain that the fact that some 

Americans adhere to religious principles condemning abortion is not a reason for entrenching in our Constitution a prohibition applicable to all persons regardless of their religious views. 

For the reasons stated above the American Jewish Congress urges this Subcommittee to disapprove S.J. Res. 119 and S.J. Res. 130 and any other proposals that may be made to amend the Constitution so as to prohibit abortion or otherwise impair the validity of the Supreme Court's rulings in the Wade and Bolton cases. 

Respectfully submitted,

THEODORE R. MANN, Chairman, National Commission on Law, Social Action and Urban Affairs, 

American Jewish Congress.

ABORTION: ANOTHER VIEW 

(By Kenneth E. Grant, Pastor, Westminster Church, Temple City, Calif.)

I feel impelled to respond to the article by Norman Riedesel in the July issue of Monday Morning dealing with legalized abortion. I am wearied and saddened by his words, echoing as they do the theology of the Roman rather than our own tradition and reflecting an emotional rather than a rational approach to this admittedly sensitive subject. But let me take his points in order. 

Mr. Riedesel says that it is not a question of a woman's right to control her own body. (How can it be otherwise?) He suggests instead that it is her right and duty to protect her body from "sexual irregularities." Since a very large proportion of legal abortions performed are for married women I am not sure the term is entirely applicable. Granted that precautions should be taken against unwanted pregnancies, the problem at hand is what to do when such measures have failed, when pregnancy is a fact to be dealt with. Saying, "You shouldn't have" doesn't solve the problem.

Mr. Riedesel says the real question is whether or not a woman has a right to kill an "unborn child." With this phrase his entire position comes to focus. Those who view an embyro or fetus as a "person" in the fullest sense, who project it as a "child" in the same sense as the neighbor's little boy out in the yard, albeit yet unborn, will never accept the concept of abortion. That is clear. Those of us who find abortion acceptable (in certain circumstances) do not share this view of course, but see the development of a child in organic and progressive terms. 

The mere fact that a fetus bears human form does not mean it possesses human personality or consciousness at that stage. A snail possesses a nervous system. 

A monkey can suck its thumb. Medical science teaches that the "person" develons as the requisite structure of human life (body), enters the experience of human life and becomes both aware and responsive. To project personhood to the developing fetus steps beyond known reality and substitutes sentiment for reason in an area where it is crucial for reason to join hands with compassion to deal responsibly with life as it is. 

Mr. Riedesel's use of the Bible scarcely does justice to his theological edu cation. Were the movements of Rebekah's twin children in her womb the strug gles of combatting nations? In poetic imagery or prophetic symbolism perhaps,

but avid. Would we expect the ancients to have a word for "fetus"? The in no literal sense. So Bathsheba was "with child" after her affair with

Bible assumes God appoints certain men and women to their tasks before they are born. Does this lead us to assume they somehow exist as persons before birth? In God's mind and purpose, perhaps, but certainly not otherwise. And as for the babe leaping in Elizabeth's womb when Mary came to visit, we are surely permitted to see this too as poetic symbolism. Or does Mr. Riedesel suggest that fetus (John) somehow supernaturally recognized the fetus (Jesus) while both were still in their separate wombs? 

I am in full accord with Mr. Riedesel on one point at least: Human life is precious, both to God and hopefully to us as well. For this reason we must struggle to understand it, in each of its many stages of development, in its growth and decay, and to deal compassionately and responsibly with it clear through. For this very reason, I stand with the majority who have placed our denomination in favor of the responsible use of abortion where it may serve these ends. But I must conclude that Mr. Riedesel and many other sincere people are sincerely wrong: A woman is, in the early stages of pregnancy at least, "partly with child." She is "with a growing potential-child within her." Making decisions for that child-to-be before it becomes a conscious and aware person is a touchy but necessary task which we, as Christians, must face. 

OHIO CONFERENCE SOCIAL ACTION MORAL ISSUES COMMITTEE FREE METHODIST CHURCH, 

Westlake, Ohio, July 24, 1973.

Hon. JAMES EASTLAND, 

Senate Office Building, Washington, D.C. 

DEAR SIR: By action taken on July 14, 1973, the Ohio Conference of the Free

Methodist Church of North America instructed the Social and Moral Actions Committee to communicate to you the stand of our Bishops and this Conference on Abortion. Here is the position of the Free Methodist Church. 

Induced abortion is the intentional destruction of human prenatal life by surgical or other means.

The decision to terminate a pregnancy involves religious and moral values as well as medical and legal realities. Therefore, Christians may not determine their rights and privileges only by the extent of the permissiveness of the law of the state or the possibilities of safe medical procedures. 

Christian morality demands that we consider both the Biblical commandment and the human situation in which the law must be applied. Human life, whether nascent, mature, or senile, is sacred to the Christian because of his faith that life exists in relation to God. 

The intentional destruction of human life is murder when any degree of malice or selfishness accompanies the decision and act. Therefore, induced abortion may be morally justifiable only when the act has been decided upon by responsible and competent persons for the purpose of saving the life or sanity of a pregnant woman. Abortion, when it serves the ends of population or birth control, personal preference or convenience, and social or economic security, must be considered as selfish and malicious. Therefore, the intentional abortion of nascent life from conception on, except in the instance of extreme necessity, must be judged to be a violation of God's command: "You shall not commit murder."

We advise both physicians and parents that the moral commandment and law of love are transgressed unjustifiably when human life is destroyed for selfish or malicious ends.

It is our desire that any legislation coming before you, be voted upon with the above principles in mind. The action of the Conference by vote was unanimous, not one dissenting vote being received. Will you see that the proper committees receive this expression of the Free Methodist Church? 

May God guide you in these matters. 

Sincerely yours, W. R. WILLIAMS, Chairman.

To: Members of the Senate Judiciary Committee. 

From: Kansas Clergy Consultation Service on Abortion. 

APRIL 23, 1974. 

We are deeply concerned about the proposed Constitutional Amendments (Whitehurst, Hogan, Buckley, et al.) which are designed to overturn the Supreme Court decision on abortion rights.

We note that the issue is not, of course, one of being for or against abortion as such; just as it is true that one is not for or against heart surgery, or for or against kidney transplants. The issue is whether or not the individual person has the right to make the decision for himself/herself, in the light of his/ her best judgment and conscience.

The abortion rights issue is, therefore, fundamentally a religious question: 

Whether the woman (in consultation with her physician) has the right to determine what is God's will for her, as she understands it and as she is guided by her best religious insight and religious knowledge. 

The proposed Constitutional Amendments would violate the basic rights of persons to freedom of religion, guaranteed by the First Amendment.

We should like to take note here of the fact that there is a sizeable proportion of the Catholic religious community who are in basic agreement with our position. Fifty-six percent of the Catholics in a 1973 Gallup Poll agreed with the statement: "The decision to terminate a pregnancy should be made by the woman in consultation with her physician."

Also significantly, we note the position of Father Robert Drinan (U.S. 

Congressman and former dean of the Boston College Law School). Drinan himself is strongly anti-abortion, but holds that in a religiously pluralistic and democratic society such as ours, the only viable solution is to make the matter a question of personal moral decision. He also has openly called upon his fellow 

Catholics to use moral persuasion rather than legislative coercion, regarding those in our society who do not agree with them. 

We also note this testimony of a noted Catholic theologian and author, Father 

Gregory Baum, O.S.A. in regard to the abortion question: "If in moral matters there are many (Protestant) Christians who do not always understand the gospel in the same way as Catholics, and do not adınit the same solutions for the more difficult problems of modern society, nevertheless they share our desire to cling to Christ's words as the source of Christian virtue. 

When Catholics disagree with the teaching on abortion adopted by some Protestant churches and many Christian thinkers, they should respect this Protestant position as an attempt to deal in a Christian way with a difficult moral problem . . . Since no one claims that the traditional position is revealed by God, Catholics should not adopt a tone of voice as if their position is beyond challenge. Catholics may hold that, from their point of view, a liberal position on abortion is immoral . . . but they have no right whatsoever to suggest that the thinkers who differ from them are immoral. ." (Commonweal, Nov. 30, 1973)

We reiterate our opposition to the proposed Constitutional Amendments, as invasions of the right to practice our religion, and an unconstitutional intrusion upon the right of religious conscience. 

We respectfully request that this communication be entered into the record and into the testimony concerning the aforementioned proposals now under consideration by your Judiciary Committee. 

Respectfully submitted,

REV. WARREN REMPEL, Chairman, Kansas Clergy Consultation Service. 

Hon. BIRCH BAYH,

Senate Office Building, Washington, D.C. 

4559 KAHALA AVENUE, HONOLULU, HAWAII, April 26, 1974. 

DEAR SENATOR BAYH: I have received a telegram from Ms. Gloria Steinem, who represents a group of women desiring to be heard on the Right-to-Life Amendment on which your Committee is holding bi-weekly meetings. The telegram asks me to join them in a request to testify. It also asserts that only a few women have been permitted to testify. 

Although I do not associate myself with the Right-to-Abortion views of Ms. 

Steinem's group of Women Liberationists, I strongly support their request. The right of qualified and articulate women to be heard on a question which in-

volves the legal control of female biological functions and the legal deposition of the female anatomy can hardly be questioned. 

I also respectfully request that this letter-and my views on the Right-to-Life Amendment-be made part of the record of your hearings. 

The relation of religion to public morality, and of public morality to the making of secular laws, is recognized by all historians. 

The religion of a people forms their consciences and dictates their moral attitudes. Whenever, and wherever a religion dominates the culture and informs the consciences of a society, it creates a moral consensus. Law is the codification of what the community believes to be the right or wrong way for people to behave. 

All sound law is made on the basis of a moral consensus. It is not only difficult to make law, it is all but impossible to secure its observance in the absence of a consensus on its morality. A "crime" is what the law says it is, but if enough people dispute the judgment of the law, virtue rather than vice will be attributed to those who break it.

St. Thomas Aquinas himself warned rulers against passing any law, even for the good of the people, until the people themselves had begun to clamor loudly for it. To do so, he warned, would bring the law into disrepute, since more people would break it than would keep it. The American experience with Prohibition was a notable proof of the wisdom of St. Thomas' advice. Prohibition, a good and moral law, simply could not be enforced in the absence of a consensus on the moral obliquity of imbibing alcoholic spirits. Prohibition probably marked the beginning of the present-day contempt for the law, and fastened the Mafiaso and the crime syndicates upon us.

Today, our democratic, pluralistic American society is not only religiously fragmented, but is becoming increasingly anti-religious, or, if you prefer, unreligious. The old Protestant moral consensus, which dominated American thought, and consequently, American Law, for a century and a half, seems to have collapsed, and has been replaced by no other religiously-rooted morality which informs the general conscience of society. America, once a "Protestant country", despite its millions of Catholic citizens, has not become a "Catholic country". 

Consequently, there is no public consensus on a great many moral questions, especially those which have to do with marriage and divorce, marital and extramarital relations, and sexual behaviour. Abortion is just one of the many sexrelated questions which have come to be viewed as a matter of "situational ethics", and utilitarian, or relativistic morality. Many statistics on the subject of abortion indicate that not only several million American women resort to the illegal practice of it yearly, but that millions more Americans, of both sexes, no longer believe that abortion is even morally 'wrong', no less a legal crime ‘tantamount to murder'.

Nevertheless, at the heart of the controversy over abortion lies the question of murder. The criminality of 'the Crime of Cain' can be deduced from natural Law. 

But the religious basis, which has provided the moral foundation of all Law in the West against murder, was the Commandment of God, handed down to Moses, a Jew, thousands of years before Christianity came into existence. And throughout the millenia, depending on the moral consensus in any given age, the Law of Man has defined, redefined, and refined the 'Law of God' against killing, and what punishments were to be meted out to those who broke it. The law has designated many forms of killing to be murder-fratricide, matricide, patricide, infanticide, regicide and, in modern times, genocide. 

The law, however, does not consider all killing to be murder. Killing in battle, killing in self-defense, are not, for example, deemed murder. They are deemed to be morally and, consequently, legally justified forms of killing. And even in respect of those acts which the law deems to be murder, it recognizes degrees of murder-first-degree murder, second-degree murder, murder while insane, manslaughter, etc. And it tailors the punishment for them accordingly.

For centuries, Christians of all sects, and Jews, considered abortion, or the willful taking of a human life in the womb, as the crime of murder, although mutatis mutandi, in modern times the punishment for a woman who aborted her child was generally to "leave her to God", and to the moral condemnation of the community. The full force of laws against foeticide was-and still is-directed against the person, or persons, who illegally performs the abortion on the woman. 

Whatever arguments there may be for legal abortion, no amount of moral or legal sophistry can alter the fact-the scientifically unassailable fact that a human foetus, at any stage of its development, is human life, and that induced abortion is the killing of it. Both the moral and the legal question now turns on

whether induced abortion is (a) 'murder' in some degree, or (b) is some other act of killing, for which there is moral and legal justification Today few Americans think that killing a foetus in order to save the mother's life is an act of murder. They think of it as a killing in self-defense. Many also view the abortion of a foetus which has been medically determined to be malformed, deformed or 'sub-human', as a 'mercy killing-merciful both to child and parent. And many also think that when a woman conceives as the result of rape she should not be required by law to suffer the life-long consequences of the criminal violation of her person, and bring to term the child of a violent and criminal union.

There would seem to be a moral consensus in favor of legal abortion in the above-mentioned cases. And today, the laws of many states reflect it. 

But what are the moral and legal justifications for Abortion-on-Demand, or the right of every woman to kill her foetus for whatever reason she desires to do so?

A child in the cradle, in respect of its life, has all the rights of an adult, and killing it in the cradle is clearly the act of murder called infanticide. But does a child in the cradle of the womb have no rights? Is a child in the flesh the exclusive property, the chattel property of the female? Does the male, who also conceived or fathered it, have no rights? Is the killing of an unborn child to be left to the private judgment of the woman who bears it? Does society have no rights or obligations in respect of its unborn children?

In many ancient and pre-Christian societies, the Law considered the women and children of a man's household to be his chattel property, and it permitted him to kill them for whatever reason, if he chose to do so. But the Law of the 

West, rooted in Judeo-Christian morality, had arrived by the beginning of this century at the proposition that all human life is sacred, that no human life can be considered the property of any other person, and that no human life-including the life of a human foetus-could be willfully taken with impunity. 

If the right-to-abortion-the right of a woman to consider the life she bears as her personal property, which she is free to destroy whenever she chooses, is granted, it will require the Law either to give a new definition of human life, or a new rationale for why women, as a sex, are to have the privilege of taking it, at their pleasure, with immunity.

In conclusion, I believe that the old moral consensus against the illegality of all abortions has collapsed, and cannot be restored, either by strengthening the old laws or passing new ones. But I also believe that there is, as yet, no consensus for abortion-on-demand. I believe that a national debate on the subject is the best way to discover if any consensus exists, and if it does not, to clarify public opinion on the subject.

Consequently, I advocate a debate and a vote in the Congress on the Right-to- Life Amendment. This will provide an initial test on whether or not the old moral consensus against abortion has collapsed among the male half of our population. I say 'the male half', since the female half is only fractionally represented in the Congress. I hope that the Amendment will pass the Congress and be submitted to the States, which will give the women voters of America a chance to express themselves. (In passing, my own State of Hawaii, the first state to pass an abortion-ondemand law, passed it with the overwhelming approval of women voters. The 

State of Hawaii would certainly not ratify the Right-to-Life Amendment. What the voters of my State are bent on now is free abortions.) 

Permit me, in closing, to address myself, as a Catholic, to the charge that Catholics who are against abortion-on-demand are trying to "impose their religion" on others. This charge is unfair, and undemocratic. First, the Catholic religion is a great deal more than its teaching on abortion. Secondly, this particular teaching was once embraced by all Jews and Christians. The legislation now on our books against abortion, was placed there by Protestants. Thirdly, no person or group in America can be Constitutionally denied the right of free speech in respect to any question because of sex, race, or religion. Catholics and 

Catholic leaders have the same right to speak out and work against legal abortion as any other persons or leaders of any other group have to speak out and work for it. This includes Ms. Steinem's Women Liberationists, whose request to be heard I have supported in this letter, despite my disagreement with their Abortion-on-Demand views. Sincerely,

CLARE BOOTHE LUCE, side 

Former Member of Congress, and former U.S. Ambassador to Italy.

A RESOLUTION CONCERNING ABORTION REFORM LEGISLATION 

(A detailed statement which elaborates upon the rationale behind this proposed resolution has been prepared by a task force of the Department of Ministry to the World for advanced study by the Annual Meeting delegates.) 

Whereas our biblical-theological tradition speaks of human life created in the image of God, which is to say that men and women are free and responsible; and 

Whereas an ecological fact of the inter-dependence of all life confronts us with both the need for a reverence for life and the constant necessity to choose one life over another; and

Whereas human life is enhanced by increasing the range of responsible choices possible in a society; and

Whereas we have already filled the earth and subdued it to the extent to which the limiting of family size has recently become a positive social value; and 

Whereas birth control as a means of family planning is not entirely reliable, and

Whereas the removal of the fear of an unwanted pregnancy grants greater sexual freedom to a man and women; and 

Whereas the present legal requirements which force a woman to bear a child against her free choice is unnecessarily discriminatory against women and is a violation of her rights as a human being; and 

Whereas the biblical tradition always emphasizes quality of life over quantity of life (that is, the main question is not when life begins or ends, but what makes life human); and

Whereas the law should protect rather than invade private life; and 

Whereas the final authority for deciding whether or not a pregnancy should be terminated is the one who is pregnant, with the consent of a physician since performance of an abortion is a medical procedure; therefore be it resolved, That the Washington North Idaho Conference of the United Church of

Christ assembled in the 1970 Annual Meeting gives general support to abortion reform legislation which takes the matter of abortion out of criminal law and 43-245-75- -39

places it in the doctor-patient relationship; and specifically gives its support to Referendum #20 which will be presented to the people of the State of 

Washington on November 3, 1970. 

Be it further resolved, That this Annual Meeting urge its congregations and individual members to reflect upon this ethical issue in the light of the biblicaltheological tradition and take appropriate public action, both corporately and individually, regarding the issue of abortion in general and Referendum #20 in particular. 

BROAD THEOLOGICAL CONTEXT OF THE ISSUE OF ABORTION 

The first chapter of the Book of Genesis provides the Church with a compact summary of all the major theological concepts most pertinent to a responsible discussion of the ethical issue of abortion. This chapter is, of course, about 

Creation. Of most concern to us in this chapter is the paragraph about the creation of human life which speaks of the "Imago Dei," meaning "image of God."

Then God said, "Let us make man in Our image, after Our likeness; and let them have dominion over the fish of the sea, and over the birds of the air, and over the cattle, and over all the earth, and over every creeping thing that creeps upon the earth." So God created man in His own image, in the image of God He created him; male and female He created them. 

And God blessed them, and God said to them, "Be fruitful and multiply, and fill the earth and subdue it, and have dominion over the fish of the sea and over the birds of the air and over every living thing that moves upon the earth. . . And God saw everything that He had made, and behold, it was very good." (Genesis 1: 26 ff.)

This paragraph describes human life as being free and responsible, sexual, and procreative. The issue of abortion should be viewed within this theological context of Creation. "Imago" in the ancient near-East was a technical term referring to the symbol which a representative of a ruler carried with him, or which preceded him as the emblem carried by his standard-bearer. This "image" entitled him to speak on behalf of his ruler, even including the freedom to make decisions with full authority of his ruler. To say that human life is created in the image of 

God is to affirm that man is God's representative on this planet Earth. 

Man has been gived dominion (lordship) over the whole Creation. This means he is free to decide in any given situation. He is not a programmed automaton which has built in correct, absolutist responses to various issues. He is rather a free agent who daily lives with the terrifying risk of having to assume responsibility for his own life. God does not take that freedom and responsibility away from an individual; nothing in all Creation has the right to violate that freedom or deny that personal responsibility. 

Human life is sexual. To say that we are human is to affirm immediately that we are sexual. There are only male human beings and female human beings. 

In human life sexual differentiation goes bar beyond the biological function of reproduction alone. There is a prior spiritual function in that it becomes the means by which persons discover and celebrate their full humanity. Whatever age one is or commitments one has, self-discovery and self-fulfillment depend upon free and responsible use of our sexuality. Sexual freedom and responsiveness are integral to a religious understanding of humanity. 

Human life is also given the capacity to propagate. Men and women are called by God to be co-partners with him in the act of Creation. "Be fruitful and multiply, and fill the earth and subdue it." The account in Genesis describes this procreative function in terms of a blessing which is received from the hand of God. The author of this passage has very carefully separated the sentence about sexuality from a later sentence about child-bearing. As important as this blessing is, Genesis suggests that it is secondary in importance to the prior fact of sexual differentiation and expression. Within their freedom and discretion, human beings are given the opportunity to use their sexual powers to bring children into the world as they so choose. And by reverse implication, each individual is given the freedom to refuse to bring new life into the world if in any given situation one should so choose. 

Finally, there is the conviction expressed throughout the first chapter of Genesis that everything in the Creation is good. It's all right to be free and

make one's own decisions. It's all right to be male or female and to express this sexuality as one freely chooses. It's all right to have children. By implication it is also all right to limit the size of one's family according to the parent's free choice. This is a good place to be. 

THEOLOGICAL REFLECTIONS SPECIFICALLY RELATED TO THE ISSUE OF ABORTION 

Abortion is the expulsion of the fetus prematurely, thus arresting the development of life. This raises a number of moral questions, all of them centering on the exercise of freedom and the taking of human life. What specific guidelines for approaching this issue can be derived from the Doctrine of Creation? 

When speaking of abortion, the matter of taking life should be faced squarely. 

In our pluralistic society there are conflicting perceptions regarding the status of the fetus, arising in part out of our sophisticated understanding today of embryonic development. This leads some to speak in terms of the human rights of the unborn. But it must be recognized that there is no final answer to the complicated arguments about when life begins, about the difference between potential human life and actual human life. In fact, it can be destructive, for it may be an effort to play God by determining who is and who is not made in his image. (Are mentally retarded persons and coma-ridden stroke patients human? 

Is a four-month old fetus less human than a five-month old fetus? And so on.)

At whatever point in fetal development from conception to birth, abortion is the willful taking of life.

Are there any circumstances in which this taking of life can be justified? 

The question itself implies an intensely painful process which must of necessity enter into any such decision. It is no casual matter to choose to end a life. This is not so much a physical as it is an emotional reality. The unseen fetus necessarily remains an abstraction. But with an awareness of pregnancy, the husband and wife experience with a wide range of feelings something radically new in their lives. This new life becomes emotionally real as someone who is pictured in the family, as a boy or a girl, as a brother or sister to present children, as a child in relation to parents, as a person who hopefully would grow into an adult. To decide to take away this life is done only with deep anguish. 

A modern ecological perspective helps bridge the Creation narrative with the abortion issue. All life is precious. We are realizing in a new way that all life is interdependent, and furthermore there is an inter-dependence between living organisms and natural resources. We have been causal for too long about the environment and the various kinds of life. The theological concept of dominion has even been mis-used to rationalize gross abuses of the environment. Now the degree of ecological imbalance threatens the very existence of the human race. 

In this age of the moon-shot we have a new vision of the planet earth as a lonely space-ship with limited resources traveling at high speeds through the galaxy. The slogan "reverence for life" has assumed a special urgency. 

From this ecological perspective it must also be asserted that life comes in conflict with life. We must constantly choose one life over another in a myriad of complex situations. One person's continued existence becomes the occasion for another's death. The tons of noxious gasses released through the automobile exhaust by a family on a cross-country vacation are bound to kill other life, even human life whether directly through respiratory illness or indirectly through killing essential vegetation. Soldiers on the front lines in Viet Nam directly chose their lives over the lives of the enemy, and indirectly each citizen of this country chooses his life over that of the Viet Cong merely by living in and receiving his livelihood from this society. As world population increases and natural resources remain limited, the choice of one life over another which occurs now will of necessity become even more obvious to all. The image of the planet Earth as a space-ship with the human family as its passengers makes it clear that hard day-to-day decision of what shall live is a real fact of life.

It is a denial of human freedom and responsibility to take the absolutist statement, "Thou shalt not kill" and attempt to apply it literally in every situation. The fact of the matter is that we constantly choose who and what shall live. The problem is that too often this is done entirely unconsciously with no individual awareness of how life is inter-dependent and in conflict. Or such a decision is made with a callosued attitude which is only too obviously a denial

of the awful pain which any alive person surely must feel. The concept of dominion implies that we must exercise responsibility for our own lives, that daily we must choose one life over another, and that such a free choice should be as conscious and informed as possible in order to be most responsible. 

Within this context, abortion in certain circumstances is not only a necessary evil; abortion can be a positive good as a means of responsibly fulfilling human life. The possibility of abortion expands the range of alternatives which individual persons may use according to the dictates of their own sense of responsibility. By increasing these possibilities to exercise freedom of choice, human life created in the image of God is actually enhanced. 

We have already filled the earth and subdued it. No longer is it imperative for social survival that every fetus fully develop into a child. To the contrary, the population explosion is endangering the future of human society to the point of its possible extinction. The limitation of family size has recently become a positive social value. In certain circumstances it is possible that abortion as a means of family planning would be the most responsible course of action and not to have an abortion would be an irresponsible act. 

Birth control before conception is vastly improved but still is not by any means a certainty. The possibility of abortion extends the ability of husband and wife to make responsible decisions about the size of their family according to their age, income, emotional limits, moving plans, larger social needs, etc. (It should also be noted that birth control and abortion are medically moving so close as to be indistinguishable with developments in the so-called "morning-after pill." 

The possibility of abortion encourages greater sexual freedom. Just as the development of advanced birth control methods have helped to remove the fear of an unwanted pregnancy from the sex act, so too abortion could grant greater freedom to a man and a woman in their sexual expression. 

Abortion as a moral possibility also removes a burden which unnecessarily discriminates against women. As the one who carries the fetus, the woman has an obvious right to remove the threat of an unwanted pregnancy from her expression as a sexual creature. Every woman has the God-given right to enter fully into sexual expression as she chooses, but no one has the right to require a woman to complete a full nine-month pregnancy against her will. 

While moral censure against the unmarried mother has probably relaxed, it still is a vicious social inequity. Having to carry the fetus full-term and giving the child up for adoption is a horendous emotional crisis and at least temporarily drives a woman into seclusion. No woman should be required to be in either of these positions against her will. The punishment-motive is only thinly disguised in the often-repeated retort that no woman is required to enter into sexual relations either, implying that if she's immoral enough to have sex she deserves having to carry a full-term pregnancy. The possibility of abortion removes this insidious, although frequently inadvertent, opportunity for society to inflict punishment.

Finally, the biblical injunction from Genesis always emphasizes quality of life over quantity of life. We are called to be free and responsible. To speak of the human spirit is to speak of a quality of relationship with the Creator. The decision to bring new life into the world must consider the question of the quality of life are there adequate resources available to provide for this new life, is there a social unit present which wants the child and can give it the love so essential for human survival? Abortion is a means to prevent a child from entering the world when in the best judgment of the mother there is not a world big enough and loving enough to provide for this life. 

A CRITIQUE OF REFERENDUM NO. 20 

In the light of the general statement about abortion, how does the particular piece of proposed legislation entitled Referendum #20 look?

In summary, this referendum which will go before the voters of the State of 

Washington on November 3, 1970, includes the following basic provisions: "Abortion would be legally possible before 'quickening' (perception of fetal movement, around fourth or even fifth month) by the decision of the mother with the following conditions: residence in this state for at least ninety days, performed by a physician in a hospital or clinic, with the permission of the husband if they are living together, with the permission of parents or guardian if under age 18; also, no hospital physician, nurse, hospital employee or any other person shall be required to participate in a termination of pregnancy."

This referendum is a constructive step toward abortion reform. The wording of the referendum is couched in double-negatives. (i.e., it will no longer be illegal to have an abortion under certain conditions.) Strictly speaking, it is not so much a move to legalize abortion as it is a move to remove the historical legal prohibitions against abortion.

All political decisions are less than ideal. This referendum is no exception. It obviously is a compromise proposal including both good and bad points. While this referendum is not as good as the legislation in some states, it certainly is better than none and is a step in the right direction. 

On the plus side, it is a move toward removing the absolute prohibitions against abortion' It is certainly not "abortion on demand" as many are claiming. There are certain restrictions (some of them less than helpful as described later), mainly that the decision is up to the mother with the consent of a physician. 

Moral factors which enter the mother's decision and professional judgments which enter the physician's decision result in it being far more complicated and thoughful than what is suggested in the phrase "abortion on demand." 

By eliminating some of the social and moral stigma presently attached to abortion, it becomes possible for a woman to receive the best medical help possible for this critical aspect of her life. If a woman should decide that she wishes an abortion and it is not legally sanctioned, then she is left with the dilemma both of having to violate the law and quite likely being forced to receive help from an abortionist which is frequently less than safe. For one carrying a fetus less than five months old, this referendum would take the health needs of the woman much more seriously than is presently the case. 

It is also a step towards greater civil liberties, removing the degree to which the state dictates personal life. Any decision regarding an actual abortion is essentially a private concern of the mother which she shares with her husband. 

Any intrusion by the state into this private family matter is a violation of individual political freedom. Legislation prohibiting abortion also is an intrusion into the physician-client relationship, making it impossible for the physician to give professional help to a client in this important matter. The referendum is an at- 

T tempt to correct this historical abuse of state-authority by placing the decision with the individuals directly involved, viz., the mother, and because it is a medical issue, also the physician. The referendum also recognizes that within our state there are individuals in the medical field who would find it impossible to participate in an abortion due to their own religious convictions in the matter. 

The referendum protects the civil liberties of physicians, nurses, hospital employees and anyone else by not requiring anyone to participate against his wishes, and furthermore the referendum goes on to guarantee that no one may be discriminated against for refusing to participate in an abortion. 

On the negative side, Referendum #20 includes several conditions which are unnecessarily restricting and have a detrimental effect. The ninety-day residency requirement is a special handicap to the highly mobile lower class and discriminates against the poor. This makes it virtually impossible for a woman to receive an abortion in this state if conception takes place before moving here. Those who are relatively affluent can resolve this problem by flying to another state or country with more relaxed abortion laws. It furthermore leaves the impression that there still is something necessarily immoral about abortion, and the good image of the State of Washington might be tarnished if residients from neighboring states with prohibitive laws would come here to receive an abortion. 

The ninety-day residency requirement is both discriminatory and prejudicial. 

The requirement that the husband give consent to an abortion if living with his wife is grossly chauvanistic. In any normal husband-wife relationship there is mutual trust in which decisions regarding the family life are reached together. 

But the law is concerned with pin-pointing final responsibility for acts which effect the social sphere. Biologically and theologically, the male entrusts the life of the fetus to the female. To establish a legal right for the husband in this matter contributes to a confusion as to who is pregnant. If for any reason there should be irreconcilable disagreement between the husband and wife regarding the advisability of an abortion, the woman should have the authority to make the final decision. Under no circumstances should anyone, including a husband, be able to require that a woman bear a child against her will. 

The requirement for parental consent in the case of a pregnant woman under age 18 should be seen in the larger context of legal liability. Medical services of any kind cannot legally take on a counselling case with someone under age 18

against the refusal of the parents. These general legal restrictions might very likely change as society is becoming more sensitive to the question of the rights and civil liberties of the young. But that is another issue. The point is that the same principle of locating final responsibility with the pregnant woman should apply with a woman of any age. Since the issue here is the larger context of liability for all matters with persons under age 18, the specific inclusion of this requirement in the referendum is unnecessary and mistakenly suggests that parents should have the authority to require a young woman to bear a child against her will.

Finally, the requirement that the abortion take place only before "quickening" is confusing to say the least. It is an archaic, non-medical phrase which means the time that a mother becomes aware of fetal movement, usually around the fourth or fifth month. What is the reason for including this time limit? Perhaps because of the implied assumption here that human life begins with fetal movement. It could just as well be argued that human life begins with conception or birth. The law exceeds its limits when it enters into the essentially religious question of when human life begins, about which persons of various persuasions strongly disagree. Or is there the assumption here that medically abortion becomes vastly more complicated later in pregnancy? That is, of course, an accurate statement. But again, if this is the real reason for the requirement, this decision should be left to the physician who is in the best position to make a medical judgment given the particular circumstances involved. At any rate, the stipulation placing rigid time-limits on abortion should be removed from the law. 

CONCLUSION 

It is the responsibility of each person to weight all the considerations and reach his own opinions about Referendum # 20. As with any piece of legislation, it is possible to go either way according to one's own conscience after reflecting upon the issue. As Christians one of the resources we bring to bear upon a concrete ethical issue is the biblical-theological tradition. Finally, however, it is possible to exercise responsible Christian judgment and still take opposing views on a political issue such as Referendum #20.

The Church as a corporate body must also speak to this issue in some clear way. Because Referendum #20 raises such fundamental moral concerns such as the taking of life, the general public and political leaders are looking for some response from the religious community. The Washington North Idaho 

Conference of the United Church of Christ should communicate to the general public its corporate stand regarding Referendum #20. 

It is impossible for Christians, either individually or corporately, to avoid a yes-or-no decision regarding Referendum #20. As the theologian Harvey Cox reminds us: "Not to decide is to decide." 

The following persons were appointed by the Department of Ministry to the World as a special task force to draft a statement on the issue of abortion in general and Referendum #20 in particular. Individual members of the task force received packets of information in advance of the first meeting from the two groups taking opposing stands regarding the coming referendum: Washington 

Citizens for Abortion Reform (2005 Fifth Avenue, Seattle, Wn.) and Voice for the Unborn (201 Boren Avenue N., Seattle, Wn., or Box 1451, Spokane, Wn.).

Following advanced individual reflection, the task force met on August 13 and reached consensus about the detailed rationale behind the whole issue. The 

Chairman then prepared a draft of both a theological statement and a proposed resolution. The task force met again on August 25 and approved this draft with certain minor corrections included in the attached copy. Each of the persons mentioned below have expressly given permission to have their names attached to this statement.
