STATEMENT BY JOHN J. KEPPLER, EXECUTIVE VICE PRESIDENT, FEDERATION of Pro- TESTANT WELFARE AGENCIES, SUBMITTED TO U.S. SENATE JUDICIARY COM- MITTEE'S SUBCOMMITTEE ON CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENTS FOR HEARING HELD ON MARCH 7, 1974, ON CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENTS RELATING TO ABORTION 

The Federation of Protestant Welfare Agencies is deeply concerned about current efforts to amend the constitution to subvert the recent United States 

Supreme Court decision on abortion.

Federation believes that every woman should have the right to decide for herself whether or not to secure the early termination of an unwanted pregnancy. 

Our experience in New York State of the results of the 1970 Abortion Law indicates that out-of-wedlock births declined and that there was a marked decrease in the numbers of low weight infants-those with the least chance of survivalattributable to a major role played by access to legal abortion. This evidence alone must support the validity of the Supreme Court decision. 

We believe that there should be no special abortion law, and that abortion should be governed only by the laws regulating medical practice generally. Therefore, the Federation supports the repeal of all laws treating abortion as a crime, leaving the matter of abortion to be decided by the women affected and in the domain of sound medical practice. In New York State, before the enactment of the 

New York State Law, more than 2,000 women died each year as a result of illegal abortions. We feel that even one death is too many. We have come to believe that attempts to create and define grounds for abortion and set-up procedures and safeguards against violation will do little to ameliorate the problem in most cases where a woman wants to terminate a pregnancy. Such an approach will not solve the problem of the woman who seeks an abortion but cannot qualify under the law and it will not reduce the hazards and humiliation for the woman who will still feel compelled to resort to illegal and dangerous surgical procedures.

We, therefore, firmly stand in support of the United States Supreme Court decision and just as firmly in opposition to constitutional amendments which will change the desired effects of the decision. 

Sen. BIRCH Bayh,

ASSOCIATION OF UNIVERSITY WOMEN, 

5000 GIRARD AVENUE SOUTH, Minneapolis, Minn., February 22, 1974. 

Chairman, Senate Subcommittee on Constitutional Amendments. 

This is written testimony on S.J. Res. 119.

As a women's religious organization, concerned about the quality of life and, in particular, that of women and children, we urge that no legislation be enacted that would infringe upon the Supreme Court's decision on abortion. As an association we have supported the repeal of abortion laws not because we are of one mind on the issue, but because we feel that the decision must be left as the court ruled, between a woman and her physician. 

We, too, would welcome the day when there would be no incidences of abortion; yet, in reflecting upon our country's 200 year history concerning abortion, we believe that women will seek abortions regardless of stated law. Passage of Sen. 

James Buckley's Constitutional Amendment (S.J. Res. 119) would reinstate the medical chaos which preceded the January 22nd, 1973 decision, but would not eliminate abortion. Data now being compiled indicates that in areas where abortion has been legal for a statistically measurable length of time, there is a drastic decline in maternal death rates since in some areas dangerous illegal abortions were the main single cause of maternal death. It is our hope that you will solicit professional testimony from physicians, lawyers, social workers and statisticians on maternal health care changes since the January 22nd decision.

Although we are concerned about the misery which will be forced upon thousands of women, particularly the poor and medically uninformed, if the Buckley amendment becomes law, our primary concern focuses upon Constitutional guarantees. Many of us have experienced pregnancies which we naturally did not carry to full term. We cannot possibly understand how these misfortunes could be considered in terms of full legal personhood. Under the Constitutional guarantee of freedom of religion, each religious group has the right to define the beginning of life within its private philosophy. Therefore, making this parochial religious view law diminishes the meaning of these Constitutional freedoms and contradicts the very foundation of American Democracy-the right to one's personal religious beliefs.

It is our plea that our Constitutional guarantees are not undermined by the passage of the Buckley Amendment which would again eliminate equal access to medically safe abortion for ALL women, but would certainly not eliminate abortion. Sincerely, Hon. BIRCH BAYH,

SHARON BISHOP, President, the Association of Universalist Women. 

U.S. Senate, Washington, D.C. 

PRESBYTERY OF LONG ISLAND, 

Commack, N.Y., March 6, 1974.

DEAR SENATOR BAYH: It has been brought to my attention that you are currently holding hearings regarding proposed Federal legislation on Abortion. The 

Presbytery of Long Island has given considerable attention to this issue. It held a workshop to deal with the issue some time ago and it has had a special Task 

Force to make recommendations to the Presbytery. On June 13, 1972, the

Presbytery, which is composed of ministers and elders representing churches, approved the following resolution: "The Presbytery of Long Island declares that women should have full freedom of personal choice concerning the completion or termination of their pregnancies and that the artificial or induced termination of pregnancy therefore should not be restricted by law, except that it be performed under the direction and control of a properly licensed physician; supports the establishment of medically sound, easily available and low cost abortion services. "In order to fully implement these general statements in New York State and Long Island in particular, the Presbytery of Long Island declares support for the Blumenthal/Cook Bill (A9715) which would mandate Medicaid payments for all abortions; declares that we stand squarely behind the establishment, development, support and expansion of clinics in Nassau and Suffolk Counties where medically sound, easily available and low cost abortion services will be available to all, regardless of ability to pay; intends to communicate these actions to the Press and all appropriate iocal, county and state officials at appropriate times."

I believe that it is in keeping with the above that I should bring our position to your attention. 

Respectfully yours,

WILLIAM T. P. RAMBO. 

E. M. SKINNER, MINNESOTA COORDINATOR, 

St. Paul, Minn., March 1, 1974. 

Re S.J. Res. 119, to be heard March 6 and 7, 1974.

From: Religious Coalition for Abortion Rights. 

To: Senate Subcommitte on constitutional amendments.

These comments are being made by me as a representative of the Religious Coalition for Abortion Rights of Minnesota. The twenty groups from the three major American religious branches, which have joined together to support the Supreme Court decision, come from many different understandings of life and its creation. But they have a common commitment to the freedom of the individual to make decisions in good conscience. 

Churches and temples currently consist of more women than men. These women make their decisions with the help of prayer. Most of them also make the assumption that government is something afar which should stay out of the individual's personal life. Over the years these women have elected the delegates to the governing conventions at which humane abortion policies were voted. Once the Supreme Court ruled along the lines of most of those religious statements, these lay women assumed the law of the land was again to serve them. This past year has of course proved them wrong, and many do not know what to do. They represent the percentages in the national polls favoring the option of abortion, but they are not to be herded by directives from on high into mass letter-writing campaigns. Many are puzzled by much of the past year's activity in this Capitol, and they feel that their one small voice won't be heard. Thus I speak as their advocate, knowing that it is their prayers which have shorn me up, and guided me in the selection of these words. But note, I speak for the majority on this issue. 

Women are realistic. Their daily existence does not permit them to base decisions on things as they might become; they must live in the here and now. The

here and now consists of innumerable unplanned pregnancies each year, and the stark awareness that some families cannot absorb another child. These women might have a vision of the day with sure contraception, but they live without such assurance today. They live with a theology of realism, not with dreams. 

Theology which is based on sheer idealism is a slippery base upon which to build systems of either law or ethics, because it fails to take into account the existential realities of actual situations. 

We find it noteworthy that Senator Buckley's amendment does have a thread of realism in it, for in section two he sees that society would not gain by the death of a mother (whom we have seen) so as to give life to a fetus (whom we have not seen). If only he could go on to see that there is more than one kind of death! 

The situation of unwanted pregnancy is often characterized by suffering, anxiety and violence: in poor families because of hunger and squalor: in retardation and deformity where mothers undergo damaging illness during the critical, early weeks of pregnancy; in any family where a child is not wanted, and must grow with the agony of parental ambivalence, or even hostility and physical battering. 

When men seek to write restrictive laws for women, we have reason to be suspicious. Only when we no longer feel we are being punished for pregnancy, and that we are patients in need of medical assistance, can this issue be treated with sanity rather than emotion.

E. SKINNER. 

A MINNESOTA THEOLOGIAN SPEAKS ON ETHICAL PERSPECTIVES ON ABORTION 

The question of abortion is a serious and moral issue which has no single universally-accepted answer. The fact that many Christians sincerely disagree with each other on this matter is of considerable importance in determining public policy.

The "right wing" on the issue believes that from the moment of conception the fetus is fully human life. As such, it is sacred and must never be willfully destroyed. This view commonly assumes that fetal rights interpreted as fully human rights should be fully protected by law. 

The "left wing" or "abortion on demand" group rests its case heavily upon the absolute right of a woman to control her own body, including its reproductive functions.

A third position attempts to take into account the basic concerns of both the right and the left, but rejects the absolutism of either. This position argues that 

God values the fetus as genetically human life which is also potentially personal life. It also recognizes that God values other persons and relationships caught in the agonized and particular circumstances in which an abortion is contemplated. 

This view maintains that every abortion is fraught with moral ambiguity, competing human rights and claims. It recognizes that while some abortions may be unjustifiably chosen for short-sighted and selfish reasons, other abortions may well be morally justified as respecting the more compelling human values in those particular circumstances.

Many moral issues receive a broad consensus in the religious community. However, abortion is not one of these. Hence, what some persons consider a sin (any abortion, regardless of the circumstances) ought not through public policy be made a crime. "What is at stake is not the rights of anti-abortion groups to espouse their theological and moral convictions, educate their members and seek to influnce others. These rights are constitutionally guaranteed. . Rather what is at stake is the freedom of sizable numbers of citizens from the religious views of others with whom they sincerely disagree."

DR. JAMES B. NELSON, Professor of Christian Ethics at United Theological Seminary. 

[Sermon preached by the Reverend Alfred B. Starratt, Ph.D., in Emmanuel 

Church, Baltimore, on the First Sunday after Epiphany, January 13, 1974.]

THE CASE FOR LEGAL ABORTION 

On January 20th, the anti-abortion forces of this country are planning a big demonstration in Washington as part of their continuing attempt to overthrow the decision of the Supreme Court which states that abortion during the first three months of pregnancy is a private decision to be made by a woman in consultation with her doctor.

This minority group, not content to have freedom to follow whatever rules they wish to make for themselves in such matters, will use all methods available to

them to force their moral and theological views on all Americans. They plan to gather am impressive mass of demonstrators that will look important on the media even if the polls show that they are in reality a minority of Americans There will be emotional speeches about the "murder" of babies; slogans, placards, and horror-show photographs. They will do their utmost to persuade our law makers, by persuasion if possible, but also threats of election reprisals. We would be foolish to underestimate their power for they have the zeal of fanatics who believe that they have both God and absolute truth on their side. 

The foundation of their argument is that a fetus is a human being and, therefore, abortion is murder. Such dogmatic belief is not based upon scientific research, careful consideration of facts, or studies of the social consequences of the birth of an unwanted child. Their position amounts to saying, "It is so because I say so," or, for many of them, "It is so because the Pope says so." There is no rational ground for arguing with such dogmatism. Hence it matters not at all to these people that many of the large Protestant churches in this country have gone on record in favor of the Supreme Court decision. Those who favor compulsory child-birth are absolutely certain that they alone have the truth in this matter.

Let me remind you again of what the Supreme Court said. The Court affirmed the privacy of the abortion decision. Freedom to reject the service, for those who personal or religious views do not harmonize with abortion, received no less protection from the Court than did freedom to accept the service for those who wish to terminate an unwanted pregnancy. The decision coerced no one, but it opened freedom of choice for all. It is that freedom of choice, in a pluralistic society where there are many differing opinions, that many of us are now fighting to preserve.

Given that freedom of choice, why would some women choose to terminate a pregnancy?

In order to answer that question responsibly we must be aware that in our society the mother of a child is held to be primarily responsible for giving to that child seventeen to twenty years of personal commitment of time, energy, and emotional involvement. Instead of the social order lending every possible assistance to that project, many women face a strong set of obstacles as they contemplate raising a child. These are well summarized in a Study Paper put out by the National Council of Churches in 1973. I will quote from that paper as follows: "1. Quality medical care is often not available to women and children. When it is available, that cost makes it inaccessible or financially devastating for many. 

Supportive services, both before and after birth, are insufficient to meet nutritional, psychological and other needs. For women with low income, medical services most often violate human dignity by lack of privacy, long waiting periods and similar dehumanizing actions. "2. Throughout the country, adequate child-care services are not provided for women who need them in order to hold a job, to continue their education, to lessen the burden of a large family, or of overcrowded living conditions. "3. Job and pay discrimination may mean that a woman cannot afford to care for a child because of her economic position. "4. Only the most minimal care is available for malformed children or children with special needs. What is avaialable is in most instances too costly for poor or middle income parents. There is hardly any discernible intent on the part of society to provide a decent quality of life for battered children, for those malformed, severely retarded or physically handicapped, or for those who can not be cared for by their parents. "5. Society generally is still quick to place the stigma illegitimate on children born to unwed parents. It is women who must bear the negative judgementseldom are men described as unwed fathers. Some women may be rejected by their families. Others may find no place of acceptance in society where they can support a child. "6. Problems of adoption and foster care are unresolved. Those who recommend adoption of children born of unacceptable pregnancies may not realize the life-long emotional cost of bearing a child and then giving it away. Furthermore, adoption may not be a real possibility for children of minority background or for those who are in some way handicapped. "7. Welfare rules are punitive both in denying services on the basis of family size and in forcing fathers from the home. In a low income situation a family that is too large often forces older children to assume more responsibility than they should. Poor living conditions, where separation of children and adults is impossible, create the potential for sexual practices that are damaging to young persons.

"8. Contraceptives are not available to many women, especially the young and unmarried. Among the poor and the young, many do not even know they exist. 

Men do not assume equal responsibility for contraception either in personal use or in urging research on male contraception. "9. Potent forces of advertising, entertainment and business encourage sexual activity from an early age. Yet adequate sex education is not available, and many very young girls and boys do not understand sexual processes well enough to know what the consequences may be. Even the most informed and fully mature women find themselves victims of the sex pressures of society. Attitudes in the churches which accept these aspects of society, fail to deal realistically with sex and find the relationship between men and women more a matter for humor than serious consideration, do nothing to help solve this problem. "10. Women are consciously or unconsciously thought of as temptresses who seduce men into sexual relationships which may eventuate in pregnancy, and who are, therefore, deserving of punishment. The fact is more often the contrary that women are the victims who deserve support and help." 

It seems to me that these conditions in our present society have a great deal to do with the reason why many women in our country choose to terminate a pregnancy. The ten conditions mentioned in the Study Paper do not cover all cases, and I am aware that there are other individual reasons for not wishing to give birth to a child. But it can certainly be said that those who wish to diminish the number of abortions would do well to work to change these obstacles to happy child-bearing so that fewer mothers would choose abortion. For so long as these conditions exist in any great degree women will choose to terminate pregnancy, either legally in proper medical surroundings, or illegally at the hands of back-alley butchers.

At this stage in history most of of us should be aware that it is impossible for any one group in our society to impose its version of morality on all the rest. 

If abortion is again made illegal, the practice will not stop. It will mean only that those who can afford it will continue in one way or another to have safe abortions while vast numbers of the young, the ignorant and the poor will pay money they can not afford for abortions done by the unskilled in unsanitary conditions. May I remind you that the best estimates are that there were about one million illegal abortions each year before the Supreme Court decision, and as a result of conditions under which many of them were done it is estimated that 8,000 women died every year.

I think it a fair judgement to say that the anti-abortion zealots in this country would hold that no male and female should indulge in sexual activity unless they are fully prepared to give a good home to children. This is a beautiful ideal, but it will not become a reality by making compulsory child-bearing the law of the land. People will go on behaving as they have since the dawn of history, and forcing birth upon every pregnant woman is after-the-fact punishment that is proven beyond reasonable doubt to be ineffective. One may be genuinely concerned that our human sexuality shall be handled in a responsible way so that it will be a blessing rather than a curse in human relationships, and at the same time recognize that compulsory child-bearing is not an effective or proper means to arrive at that goal. 

I think we should also keep in mind the many positive results of the Supreme Court decision. Obviously we have put the procedure back into the hands of legitimate trained doctors in properly equipped hospitals and clinics. Obviously, too, we have been able to prevent life-long tragedies for hundreds of thousands of girls under the age of sixteen. We have also increased the chances that each child that is born is one that has been planned for and wanted by the parents. 

Those who are aware of the psychological and physical traumas suffered by unwanted children, and of the damage that many of these do to society when they become adults, must be thankful that there have been fewer of such tragedies. 

In addition, we can be thankful that as more and more awareness of the availability and small cost of the procedure spreads through the population, the women who choose to terminate come to the hospital or clinic at a very early stage of their pregnancy. A fetus is not a human being, but it is a potential person and the sooner the process of development is terminated the better. Furthermore, since abortion has become legal, we have been able to provide trained counselors to talk over the decision with the pregnant woman so that her choice is made with real consideration of all that is involved instead of running in panic-stricken fright to some illegal abortionist who cares only for her money.

As an alternative to abortion all of us would be pleased if a universal, safe, and foolproof contraceptive were available so that the only babies born were

those who were planned for and looked forward to with love by parents who could care properly for them. Some day such a contraceptive may be available. 

But until that day arrives we have a responsibility to use the intelligence that God gave us to care for persons and for society as a whole. And a fetus is not a person any more than an acorn is an oak tree. 

In the exercise of that responsibility, I ask each one of you who agrees with what I have said to write to your senators and congressmen this week so that they will know that the emotional demonstrations planned by the avocates of compulsory child-bearing do not represent the opinion of vast numbers of other Americans who have an equal claim to moral and religious concern. 

Let us pray: Defend, O Lord, the freedom of individual mind and conscience that has been the guiding light of this democracy, and grant that we may so use the intelligence you have given us that our freedom shall result in choices that demonstrate our responsible concern for the well-being of all people in this land. We ask it in the name of him who loved children, even our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen.

ALFRED B. STARRATT, 

Rector, Emmanuel Church, Baltimore.

TESTIMONY ON THE PROPOSED CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENTS TO PROHIBIT ABORTIONS 

The 1972 Annual Conference of the Church of the Brethren, meeting in Cincinnati, Ohio (June, 1972) adopted a Statement on Abortion. The full statement is attached.

In that statement, while upholding the sacredness of human life and opposing abortion because it destroys fetal life, we recognized that abortion is a valid option when other alternatives would lead to greater destruction of human life and spirit. In that statement, we also expressed support to those persons believing abortion the least destructive alternative. The official statement says, "We support persons, who after prayer and counseling believe abortion is the least destructive alternative available to them, that they may make decisions openly. honestly, and without the suffering imposed by an uncompromising community." 

The statement goes on to say. "Laws regarding abortion should embody protec tion of human life, protection of freedom of moral choice, and availability of good medical care. Brethren should work for laws that uphold these principles, eventhough there is differing opinion as to how such principles may be achieved. 

Brethren are asked not to try to enforce their highest ideal of morality by strict civil law."

It is our opinion that the Church of the Brethren statement supports the rights of individuals to make moral decisions according to conscience regarding abortion. 

We feel any laws regarding abortion must take this into account. 

WAYNE F. GEISERT. 

Moderator, Church of the Brethren Annual Conference.

DONALD E. ROWE. 

Moderator-Elect, Church of the Brethren Annual Conference. 

DEAN M. MILLER,

Immediate Past Moderator, Church of the Brethren Annual Conference.

ABORTION STATEMENT, CHURCH OF THE BRETHREN, JUNE 1972 BIBLICAL TEACHING 

A Christian ethic regarding abortion begins with the biblical teaching about the sacredness of life and about love for persons, two of the central themes of scripture. Abortion as used hereafter refers to any intentional interference with embryonic or fetal human life that results in the termination of that life prior to birth. When considering the biblical teaching about abortion one should remember that there are few scriptural passages directly related to the question and that the direction of scripture is not so clear that anyone can be dogmatic in his interpretation. No biblical passage condemns or approves of abortion as such. 

Nevertheless the Bible teaches that God is the creator of human life in its biological form as well as its distinctly personal qualities. Therefore we turn first of all to passages about life and then to passages about love and compassion. 

The Bible teaches that human life is a sacred gift from God. This does not mean that human beings have no part in the creation of new life, for God has clearly entrusted the cultivation and propagation of human life into the hands of persons (Gensis 1-2). Nevertheless, it remains a sacred gift from God and is at center a mystery beyond definition. Science can describe the development of the fetus, but if cannot penetrate the mystery and uniqueness of the person who is brought into being by the hand of God.

The mystery of the creation is heightened by the fact that it is difficult to prove from the scriptures just when personal existence begins. Many passages seem to suggest that personal existence begins long before the time at which a fetus may be born and live. Heart, blood, mind, and breath are all signs of personal life. Biblically the "heart" refers to the center of personal being. "You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your might" (Deuteronomy 12:23). The mind and the strength, thinking and moving, are evidence of personal life. Soul and breathing are closely associated, suggesting that full personhood comes with breathing. Body and personhood are so joined that the latter does not exist without the former. Thus the Bible seems to suggest multiple signs of personal human life, many of which are present long before viability.

At the same time it is difficult to prove from the scriptures that conception is clearly the beginning of personal human life. While in Psalm 51:5 the psalmist speaks personally about his own conception ("In sin did my mother conceive me") Jeremiah 1:5 speaks of being called of God before conception ("Before I formed you in the womb I knew you"). Reference to "conception" in scripture is nearly always accompanied by reference to "bringing forth" as in the phrase "conceive and bear." Although the growing fetus may occasion personal reference, the beginning of personal existence remains shrouded in the mystery of God's call. 

In the Bible the creative act of a loving God and the response of a caring community is decisive in calling forth personal human life. The announcement of a child to be born is normally a time of joy and thankfulness. Signs of quickening and movement within the womb heighten expectancy for the coming child (Luke 

1:44). Sensitive persons are moved with reverence in the presence of a growing fetus (Psalm 139: 13-16). Thus many passages suggest that the growing fetus is precious in God's sight and that the bodily signs of personhood are distributed throughout fetal development.

A comparison of the value of fetal life and the life of the mother seems to be implied in Exodus 21:22–25. There one who accidently hits a pregnant woman and causes a miscarriage may have a fine imposed upon him by the husband. Should the expectant mother die, the guilty party may be required to compensate by giving up his own life. Interpretations of the passage vary, but it would seem to suggest that while the life of the fetus is precious, it is not so precious as the life of the mother; and therefore an accidentally caused miscarriage is not necessarily treated as manslaughter. We must remember however that the passage is not considering voluntary abortion. We must also remember that Jesus tremendously heightened the commandment not to kill, even including an admonition against anger (Matthew 5:21-23).

Everything we know of Jesus from the scripture indicates his love and compassion for persons. He did not consider that the law was to be applied without regard for the persons involved. For this reason Scribes, Pharisees, and Saducees considered Jesus to be a lawbreaker. An important example is that of the woman taken in adultery (John 8:1-11). Her sin was so serious that she was on the point

of being stoned to death. Jesus did not abolish the high requirements of the moral law, but suggested that those without sin carry out the punishment. He then forgave her, asking her not to sin again. From Jesus we learn that when we espouse high moral principles with harsh consequences for many, we must be ready to forgive such persons and to offer them every opportunity to make their own responsible decisions. Jesus did not weaken the moral law against adultery; he rather set it within a context of compassion for persons. 

Over the years Brethren sought to follow the example and teaching of Jesus that religion and morality are ultimately voluntarily decided before God. Believing that the heart and soul of morality is the free choice of persons who love other persons, Brethren generally have been unwilling to rely upon military force, police force, capital punishment, religious inquisition, or punitive legislation. 

Brethren have sought rather to develop helping institutions and service for those who suffer, to introduce a note of compassion. 

SOCIAL CONSIDERATIONS 

The biblical affirmation that human life is sacred does not easily resolve the ethical dilemmas concerning the quality as well as the fact of human life. Such a dilemma is obvious when the life of a mother is threatened by her pregnancy. 

Most Brethren have been willing to allow that a fetus may be aborted to save the life of the pregnant woman. This seems to be within the direction of biblical teaching, although we marvel at the love of a mother who voluntarily risks her life in order that her child might be born. Surely no one should be required to do so. 

The dilemma is posed in another form when the threat of world overpopulation is considered. Various population estimates indicate that the world will be intolerably overpopulated within two or three generations if present population trends continue. The human reproductive potential is increasingly coming into conflict with the lives and quality of life of those already born. Is the threat of overpopulation with attendant starvation and death sufficient reason to resort to abortion? Reverence for human life should lead Christians to use medically safe and effective contraceptive methods rather than resort to abortion.

The moral dilemma of abortion is complicated by the fact that abortion is not so available to the poor as it is to those who are not poor. It is hardly just to retain strict abortion laws that are only enforceable against those who cannot afford to do anything but comply. The dilemma is also complicated by the fact that abortion is so prevalent, even in the face of great danger and degradation. 

Thousands of women each year willingly risk their lives and many die because of self-induced or illegally obtained abortions. Their decisions to abort could hardly have been made for the sake of mere convenience or whim, but must rather have been accompanied by severe mental anguish and despair. Even though abortion is not an acceptable means of solving problems, there are many situations in which a woman finds no alternative that she feels she can bear. In such cases, condemnation is destructive and does nothing to relieve misery; it only makes a woman less capable of coming to a rational decision. 

Merely condemning abortion is self-defeating. In our concern for the wellbeing of the fetus, we may add to the despair that has already driven the mother to seek a "way out" of her problems rather than find a constructive solution. On the other hand, merely condoning abortion is equally self-defeating. In our concern for the mother, we run the risk of encouraging her too easily to make a decision that is callous of all human life in its destruction of the unborn. 

We must not allow ourselves simply to voice a position and then be satisfied that we have met our responsibility. Rather, as Christians we must actively and compassionately share in the burdens that lead women to seek abortions. 

In seeking to preserve the life of a woman and the fetus she carries, we need to understand the life-destroying situations that drive her to abortion. Her family may already be so large and so poor that they are starving. The fetus may be defective and require expense and care, both emotional and physical, that she and her husband are unable to give. Faced with these and other difficulties, a couple must sometimes make an extremely difficult decision. When they prayerfully and maturely wrestle with all available alternatives and choose personal sacrifice for the sake of their unborn child, we celebrate God's compassionate spirit,

MEDICAL AND COUNSELING CONSIDERATIONS 

The range of individual choice regarding pregnancy and family planning is much broader than it used to be and modern medical developments promise to make it even more so. Modern contraception has made pregnancy a relatively deliberate and free option for many persons in our society. The risk to life and physical health of the mother as a consequence of pregnancy and delivery is now small; the physical risk accompanying medically ethical abortion procedures in the first trimester of pregnancy is much smaller. This risk increases, however, as pregnancy progresses. By way of contrast, the risk to health and life due to clandestine, unhygienic, often desperate abortion procedures at the present time is exceedingly high, and there are many hundreds of needless deaths yearly. Further technological advances in the utilization of intrauterine devices (IUD's), the "morning-after" pill, and the seemingly imminent appearance of effective oral medication that will abort by chemical means in the earliest stages of pregnancy promise to make it increasingly difficult to delineate contraception from abortion. 

Existing public laws with respect to abortion therefore, may well become increasingly irrelevant and unenforceable.

Technical discoveries about the genetic and congenital abnormalities of human development have increased the possibility of detecting carrier states of defective genes and chromosomal defects and of predicting such disease in potential offspring. Such conditions may occasionally be diagnosed as early as midpregnancy. 

Genetic counseling considers the degree of risk involved, the seriousness of the possible defect, the parents' willingness to care for a defective child, the possibility that a defective child might be helped by medical or surgical procedures to achieve a more nearly normal life, the possible result of the defect on the life of the child, on other members of the family, and on society. 

Psychological studies of women who undergo abortion by acceptable medical procedures have not supported generally held beliefs regarding the emotional stress of such an experience. In the majority of cases, general relief or a brief and mild depressive reaction is reported. Rarely do more severe disturbances appear. The emotionally disturbed woman who undergoes abortion seems to experience no loss of stability and, sometimes, even improves. Frequently expressed beliefs regarding the occurrence of involuntary infertility, difficulty in sexual functioning, as well as depression, are not substantiated by the presently available evidence. There is, however, continued expression of concern by psychiatrists and psychologists about adverse effects, short-term or long-term, individually or collectively, of repeated resort to abortion. 

Effective research has yet to be done to clarify the real psychological and social efforts of changing social codes regarding abortion and the response that large numbers of persons are making to these changes. Clinical experience with persons who have sought illegal abortion, usually in a context fraught with tension, secrecy, fear, and real risk to life and health, reveal frequent important emotional trauma and suffering from the experience. It appears that condemnatory attitudes, compassionlessness, profound insensitivity, and lack of understanding in ourselves and those around us lie at the heart of this distress. Even when no longer expressed in legal prohibitions, these attitudes tend to be preserved in the larger community, and often in the church as well, by keeping distant from the problem and by isolating responsibility within the hands of the medical profession. Professional people, as well as their patients, have need for persons of compassion and insight who will undertake to share the burden of moral decision and thereby bring a fuller humanity into the lives of all. The meeting of minds, whenever possible, of caring persons most involved and most to be affected by any decision brings dignity, moral sensitivity, and support to persons in crisis. 

Psychological studies of children and of family life have brought a new and increasing concern of behavioral scientists for the problems of the "unwanted child." Nearly everyone agrees that being unwanted in early childhood is devastating to the development of personality and is the cause of many behavioral and emotional problems.

The physician is committed to the preservation of life. When faced with a request for abortion, he is placed in a position of felt conflict that is often keen. 

Along with his commitment to life he and other counselors are also called upon to care about and relate to individual persons in their choices, conflicts and needs. 

He is asked to care enough that instead of controlling, dominating, or manipulating he seeks rather to set persons free to grow and to discover their own highest purposes.

A POSITION STATEMENT 

Brethren oppose abortion because it destroys fetal life. Let it be clear that the 

Brethren ideal upholds the sacredness of human life and that abortion should be accepted as an option only where all other possible alternatives will lead to greater destructon of human life and spirit. 

However, we confess that we are part of a society that contributes to abortion by denying parents the support and assistance they need. We further confess our lack of compassion, our condemnation of those who differ with our view of morality, and our need to coerce and compel others to our way of thinking. 

Thus, our position is not a condemnation of those persons who reject this position or of women who seek and undergo abortions. Rather, it is a call for Christlike compassion in seeking creative alternatives to abortion. 

We support persons who, after prayer and counseling, believe abortion is the least destructive alternative available to them, that they may make their decision openly, honestly, without the suffering imposed by an uncompromising community.

We oppose any action, direct or indirect, by parents, physicians, the state, or anyone that would compel a woman to undergo an abortion against her will. 

All who seek abortions should be granted sympathetic counsel about alterna tives available as well as the health and safety of publicly available physicians and hospital care.

IMPLICATIONS AND RECOMMENDATIONS 

It is vital to the spiritual and social well-being of the Brotherhood that it educate its members about the sacred spiritual quality of human life and human sexuality, family planning, and the meaning and practice of responsible parenthood. This effort should be both an individual and collective responsibility. The 

Brotherhood should also support organizations such as Planned Parenthood and Clergy Consultation Service in their educational efforts. 

Christian parents must seriously consider limiting family size, since overpopulation poses a very real threat to the whole of human life. However, this should be achieved by contraception and voluntary preventive measures, such as male or female sterilization, rather than by abortion. 

The Brotherhood should do everything it can to assist and encourage mothers and fathers to want and care for all their children. For example, Brethren can show their concern and compassion by providing homes for unwanted children or by giving of their time and resources to families who cannot afford the care of another child or cannot bear the physical strain of an additional infant. 

For many Brethren, situations such as threat to the life and health of the mother, rape, incest, or possible fetal deformity are considered sufficient to warrant abortion. However, such situations need not necessarily lead to abortion unless they threaten serious destruction of the life or spirit of the family. The precise definition of circumstances must be left to the mother, father, physician, pastor, and other significant persons who are well informed and in whom the mother and father have confidence.

Counseling should encourage the mother and father to work through the decision in view of the value of human life, the options available, including adoption and foster care, the consequences of options, and the well-being of those most directly affected.

Physicians are urged not only to consult with their medical colleagues, but also to seek other ways to share the burden of moral responsibility so frequently thrust upon them. They are encouraged to resist the inclination to shoulder the weight of decision in isolation from others who are involved and concerned. Any physician or attendant who, because of personal moral conviction, chooses not to perform or participate in the abortion, however legal, should be free to do so in good conscience, and should receive the full support of the church. We urge a physician with such convictions to refer patients who may desire an abortion to another competent certified doctor.

Laws regarding abortion should embody protection of human life, protection of freedom of moral choice, and availability of good medical care. Brethren should work for laws that uphold these principles, even though there is differing opinion as to how such principles may be achieved. Brethren are asked not to try to enforce their highest ideal of morality by strict civil law. Recommendations 1. That the Brotherhood make available a course of study on human sexuality and responsible parenthood. Such a course should be designed to assist congregations and families in their teaching and individuals in personal growth.

2. That a "fellowship of families" be organized in a network throughout the 

Brotherhood for the purpose of helping those families who need support and assistance in wanting and caring for their children. Examples of such assistance include taking in an unwanted child, sharing in the care of a handicapped child, sitting with children so that parents can renew their own relationship, or giving material and financial aid. The strength of such a fellowship should be in its ability to respond creatively to any situation in which families need help in wanting and caring for children. 

3. That, at the joint initiative of the Brotherhood and of interested physicians, a group of physicians, informed pastors, and knowledgeable laymen be called together to consider ways to promote sharing the burden of responsibility for moral choice, so often left to the physician alone. 

HUMAN RIGHTS AMENDMENT 

(United Church of Christ/Rev. Albert W. Kovacs)

FALSE CLAIMS 

Unauthorized and illegal claims of the Board of Homeland Ministries or the Council for Christian Social Action of the United Church of Christ, or those of a paper Religious Coalition for Abortion Rights with these two agencies cooperating, in support of abortion are being made as if they were the position of the churches and the members of the United Chruch of Christ. By the rules of the 

United Church of Christ itself, no segment of the Church, even the General Synod, can claim to speak for the membership or churches. 

STATEMENT ON PRONOUNCEMENTS 

Because of unauthorized statements by persons or agencies purporting or seeming to represent the Church, it was deemed essential "that they themselves are clear as to the nature and limits of the authority their utterances possess." This action was taken by the Second General Synod on 8 July 1969 (Minutes page 128) in a "Statement on Pronouncements" passed then and never rescinded. It spells out further: "A Church agency speaks only for itself, not for the whole fellowship, except as members of that fellowship concur on their assent is won by the weight of what is spoken." "An utterance of the General Synod or any of its agencies binds no member of the United Church of Christ except as he is convinced and his commitment secured by what he accepts as the rightness of the utterance itself. This is axiomatic for the freedom of the Christian man.' "Every agency is urged, in published announcements of its views, to make clear the authority on which its statement is based in a way to avoid any misunderstanding of other bodies in the matter."

UCC BOARD BREAKS CHURCH RULE 

In a typically improper and unauthorized action, the UCC Board of Homeland 

Ministries addressed a statement, "TO ALL MEMBERS OF THE CONGRESS" 

to be found in the Congressional Record of 23 January 1974, E 96. Nowhere in that paper is a statement to clarify to you legislators that it does not carry any authorization or weight except that of the Board's members themselves. 

It has broken in spirit the sense of responsibility, in purporting to speak for the churches and members by use of their title as an agency of them, and committing a flagrant sin of omission. It is shameful when churchmen and churchwomen in high places display such a lack of integrity, in a day when some of those same men and women are foremost in the movement to purge politicians. 

Speak about those in glass houses!

AUTHORIZED TO SPEAK CHURCHES AND MEMBERS ONLY 

Authority was specifically given UCC groups to speak to pastors, members, churches and other UCC bodies in the Resolution passed on "Freedom of Choice Concerning Abortion" by the Eighth General Synod, and concurred in by the Ninth. But there is no authorization to any board, instrumentality or agency to influence the governments of the United States, individual states, or even other denominations or interdenominational bodies. 43-245 0-75-40

It falsely claims in its letter to Congress that the Ninth General Synod urged "the constituency of the church and the Congress" to "resist attempts to erode or negate the recent Supreme Court decision (on abortion)". The resolution can be found, copied from the Minutes, in the Congressional Record, p. E 99, 23 January 

1974. No authority is given to address any but UCC people. The word "Congress" or any other name of a governmental body is not even mentioned ! 

REPETITION OF PRACTICE 

Despite the necessity under church law to spell out specifically one's limitation of authority to speak for others, UCC leadership has failed on this count time after time before federal bodies alone, not to count the others. Yet that pronouncement was voted so that persons of other religious persuasions and polities may be clear as to the individual's or agency's place and voice. 

When the president of the church himself does this, purporting to act on behalf of the members and all the churches, it set no good example for the bodies after him. Before this Senate's own Appropriations Committee, he said: "My name is 

Robert V. Moss. I am president of the United Church of Christ, a Protestant denomination of two million members. I come before you as a churchman, a citizen, and especially as the chief executive officer of the General Synod, the United Church's central policy-making and representative body." After that, since many 

UCC people aren't even up on their own church polity, it would be difficult for a Senator unaquainted with UCC ways to understand anything but that he was authorized to speak for all two million of us. 

No one regrets having to make this statement about Dr. Moss and my UCC brethren than I. He was without doubt one of the finest professors I studied under at seminary, and I spent an occasional evening in his home while a seminarian. The others are friends, or at least colleagues of mine. I am willing to agree to disagree on an issue in a friendly spirit. But when they flout or ignore the rules by which we must all play the game, I will disagree as openly and honestly as I can for truth's sake.

UCC STIFLES OPPOSITION 

The United Church of Christ falsely claims its love for truth, certainly at the leadership level, and stifles news that presents another perspective. After striving through the FCC to "liberate" television and radio from tightly held controls, it does the same thing itself when its own interests are at stake. 

CASE IN POINT 

At present I am the president of the Board of Directors of Pennsylvanians for Human Life, and have dedicated considerable energy to the passage of a Human Rights Amendment to protect unborn lives from abortion, except to save the life of the mother. I notified of my election to the board several UCC publications, including A.D. (church monthly magazine), Keeping You Posted (bi-weekly leadership bulletin) and our area Conference News. Being contrary to official stands, it simply was not reported in any one of them. 

Upon my election to the president's chair last October, I notified all of them again. The only response that I had was a return of the notice from the editor of the Conference News, that it was too late for inclusion. Another issue of the 

News has been printed, but without any report of it, despite a special reminder. 

Not even an acknowledgement came from the other sources. 

Unfortunately, the UCC has company in restraint of truth, including a selfstyled defender of liberty, Americans United for Separation of Church and State. 

I sent them news of this, and they failed to publish it too. In fact, while they publish reports of even miniscule Protestant agencies that support abortion, they have yet to print the pro-life statements of anyone but Roman Catholics. 

The Archbishop of Canterbury and the Reformed theologian Karl Barth and the Lutheran Church-Missouri Synod have voiced opposition to abortion at various times, but not a jot of this has been reported by them, no less the UCC. 

UCC CONFERENCE BLOCKS OPPOSITION 

The abortion issue came late to the Penn Northeast Conference of the United

Church of Christ. Just a short time before our Spring meeting the denomination released two tardy proposals by the Executive Committee on "The Status of

Women in Church and Society" and "Toward Freedom of Choice in the Area of Abortion." Although sent in the mail to pastors and delegates, they were so late as to preclude serious dialogue or arrange study programs in the churches, to ascertain the mind of the members themselves. There was no theological background offered by experts to the laity, no less to pastors, and no concern for consulation of theological resources. 

Recognizing that our limited knowledge could not make an acceptance vote responsibly, even in May, the Christian Witness Commission reported: "In regards to the proposal for action we recommend that the Penn Northeast Conference support this action and that the Penn Northeast Conference provide opportunities to study the abortion issue by providing educational forms for both clergy and laity in order to understand the abortion issue more fully and the implications thereof." The total ignorance of the theological implications was appalling for a church body, and no one can deny that any support for abortion among the delegates was based on practical grounds related to the inconvenience to the mother-to-be or society. The churchmen were weighing the value of life in dollars and cents! or in opposition to Catholics!

The item was not even voted upon separately, but simply with the whole of the commission's report: "We call attention to the recommendations of the Christian Witness Commission as presented in their report regarding the pronouncement, proposals and resolution to be brought up at General Synod. And we urge members and local churches to study the issues and express their views to the appropriate persons and comittee." (Minutes, p. 51)

Despite the directive to provide educational forums, nothing was done prior to the next annual Conference meeting a year away. The leadership had made up its mind, why listen to the pew?

A brief comment on the subject of abortion arose during the Health and Welfare Commission report in 1972, after the year's inaction. I took issue with the failure of the Conference to follow the directive of the last meeting. When I asked why the directive had been ignored, I was told that a discussion on the issue was planned for the Fall of 1972, some 15 months after the motion to move. The Minutes: "Rev. Meiss yielded the floor to Rev. Albert Kovacs who has asked time to speak to the issue of abortion which was raised in the report. He noted that a seminar on abortion is planned for next fall. Perhaps, he suggested, that the seminar be held, not in September, but in June and that it be held for more than one day because of the complexity of the issues involved." (Minutes p. 48) 

Theologically apathetic, the delegates and pastors simply put up with the time it took to shuffle this request for seriousness aside. It didn't matter. 

When the seminar was held in the Fall, it was poorly announced at a late date and lost amid other announcements. That day only about 15 ministers and 15 laymen shared in the program of study and discussion. The panel consisted of the expected imbalance. The pro-life side was represented by a Roman Catholic mother, a former teacher. The anti-life side by a minister's wife (I think), an old physican who admitted to having performed abortions on two girls pregnant by black men (and you all know how bad that is!), and a college professor. The pro-abortion moderator saw to it that everything was fair, at three voices and opinions to one.

NO RIGHT TO CLAIM 

How can the PennNortheast Conference dare to claim its views represent the 40,000 church members it serves? It cannot-and it does not! That is better than the UCC denominational leadership that also cannot-but does! 

CONCLUSION 

The United Church of Christ, officers or boards or agencies, cannot affront the United States Senate with a claim to speak for the members of that church on the issue of abortion. Foremost, they have not provided the opportunities for the members to study the subject in a Christian frame of reference and then listen to what the people are saying. The unwillingness of the leadership to hear can be reflected by the decline in denominational support in 1972 (1973 figures may show a pitifully small increase in an inflationary year), the continued drop in membership, and other indicators.

The claims of representation, which may be considered real in view of the mandated disclaimers required by church law, are false. They are unauthorized, by the zealously guarded free polity of the churches. 

The freedom to dissent is unalterable, but news of dissent is squelched throughout. So-called news media are merely house organs extolling the views of the new hierarchy. Numbers of churches refuse to give any support to the UCC, but that is not reported. Actions against abortion by other Protestants or in the UCC is ignored. 

In a time when Dr. Moss and other officers are demanding accountability in government, it is time they were held accountable in the Church. How dare they? 

Who can believe their witness, when it reflects only their thinking? When I spoke against abortion in my Conference, an awfully boorish minister said, "Aw, shuddup, Kovacs!" The Moderator said nothing! I did. The unborn are also silenced, in God's name.

1971 ANNUAL, SOUTHERN BAPTIST CONVENTION RESOLUTION NO. 4-ON ABORTION 

Whereas, Christians in the American society today are faced with difficult decisions about abortion; and 

Whereas, Some advocate that there be no abortion legislation, thus making the decision a purely private matter between a woman and her doctor; and

Whereas, Others advocate no legal abortion, or would permit abortion only if the life of the mother is threatened: Therefore, be it 

Resolved, That this Convention express the belief that society has a responsibility to affirm through the laws of the state a high view of the sanctity of human life, including fetal life, in order to protect those who cannot protect themselves; and be it further Resolved, That we call upon Southern Baptists to work for legislation that will allow the possibility of abortion under such conditions as rape, incest, clear evidence of severe fetal deformity, and carefully ascertained evidence of the likelihood of damage to the emotional, mental and physical health of the mother. 

1969 ANNUAL, BAPTIST GENERAL CONVENTION OF TEXAS 

ABORTION Meaningful and necessary changes in abortion laws have been delayed in Texas. 

This delay ignores: 

1. The expressed need for change from a majority of lay and medical groups, including a special Texas Medical Association committee to study abortion laws in Texas; 

2. Infringement of personal liberty by prohibiting best medical judgment and practice in certain instances; 

3. The need or protection for victims of rape or incest ; 

4. The misfortune of continued unwanted pregnancy in instances of fetal deformity; and 

5. The high instance of illegal abortion with its 8,000 to 10,000 maternal deaths yearly in our country.

This delay in needed legislative changes is the result of a strong and well organized lobby effort, and can be combatted if Texas Baptists will: 

1. Inform themselves of the real issues and opinions of knowledgeable and fair minded people; 

2. Express themselves as individuals to their respective legislators of our State; and 3. Recognize that Christian love at times dictates an affirmative action against an attitude of "doing nothing." In this instance people are regularly denied the benefit of best medical judgment and practice by a statute based primarily on a 

19th Century dogma.

THE ECUMENICAL MINISTRY TO THE UNIVERSITY OF NEW HAMPSHIRE, 

Durham, N.H., February 28, 1974. 

Hon. BIRCH BAYH,

Chairman, Senate Judiciary Subcommittee on Constitutional Amendments, Senate Office Building, Washington, D.C. 

DEAR SENATOR BAYH: I am writing to you regarding the forthcoming hearings which your Sub-Committee will be holding on the various Constitutional Amendments to reverse the Supreme Court decision of January 22, 1973, on abortion. 

I am taking the liberty to enclose the statement that I made before the House and Senate Committees on Health and Welfare here in New Hampshire. The testimony that I made is based on my experience as a campus minister who has done extensive problem pregnancy counseling with women both in the University and in the Seacoast area of southeastern New Hampshire. Although the testimony is eleven months old, the concern is essentially the same except for the fact that I have seen a good many more women over the past eleven months, even though the accessibility to information and to hospitals and clinics is much easier. 

I believe that the Supreme Court decision is, in fact, the just and moral decision as well as the decision that preserves the fundamental tradition of English and American jurisprudence, which has recognized the rights of a potential human life around the time of viability and later. To extend the same rights to a potential life any earlier is to adopt a limiting view as to when human life begins. 

It is limiting in that those who disagree that human life begins at conception are denied their right to disagree. Biblically speaking, the Hebraic position is that human life begins at birth when an infant takes its first breath with the intimation of freedom and self-determination. The function of law then seems to be to allow for the maximum choice in the moral-religious belief about the

beginning of life and in the options available to the woman and/or couple facing a problem pregnancy.

Thank you for looking at this extensive letter and testimony. I hope that the hearings will lead to an upholding of the Supreme Court and to the defeat of the Constitutional Amendments which would limit the free choice of women. 

Sincerely yours, Enclosure.

LAWRENCE H. ROUILLARD. 

TESTIMONY, MARCH 27, 1973 Madame Chairman and members of the Committees on Health and Welfare: 

I am the Reverend Lawrence H. Rouillard, the Ecumenical Minister to the University of New Hampshire, Durham, and an ordained Episcopal priest. I wish to speak in favor of House Bill 606, an Act relative to Abortion. 

I speak also as a member of the Clergy Consultation Service, a nationwide organization of clergy-women and men-with 24 members in the New Hampshire-Vermont group. We have "covenanted" together "to provide counsel to women and other persons involved with 'problem pregnancies' . . . because of a common concern for persons facing serious personal problems arising from unwanted pregnancies and because of our awareness of the lack of widespread opportunity for humane and compassionate counseling related to such problems." 

This statement puts an emphasis on the care of "persons"-women and menas the primary focus for our work. “Person" for me involves the Hebraic understanding of the human being as a psychosomatic unity, including what we normally label as the physical, psychological, emotional, and spiritual dimensions of our humanness, and the person in relation to society. Thus, to be a person one needs to have the power of self-determination or to seize one's freedom, and yet to stand responsibly in relation to other persons. A human act, a moral act, involves a knowledge of one's circumstances as well as one's self, the freedom to choose and to accept both the responsibility and accountability for one's decisions by understanding one's options and the consequences of each. 

The concern of the Clergy Consultation Service is with the woman as a person, who stands in relation to the man involved in her problem pregnancy, to the potential life inside her, and to society. We seek to be available in a confidential counseling situation to the woman-and the man if possible—both before a decision is made and after the decision in a way that affords her (and him) an opportunity to reflect on the event, where she is in her sense of selfworth, where they are, and what the future holds for each of them. That briefly gives you an orientation to the Clergy Consultation Service from my perspective, at least.

I began counseling women with problem pregnancies in January, 1971 and ha vẹ seen 258 women since then, including 48 during the first three months of 1973 The women have represented a cross-section of our state, ranging in age from 13 to the late 40's, coming from all over New Hampshire but especially from the seacoast area and the university, with diverse economic and social backgrounds, and reflecting the pluralism of living arrangements that our transitional society has. In a majority of instances, the man has been present. Both the woman and the man have been encouraged to present their respective views on the situation confronting them and the choices available-i.e. marriage, having the child and either keeping the child or putting the child up for adoption, or abortion. The decision is ultimately the woman's. Roughly 90% of the women I have seen have chosen to have an abortion either at the clinic we refer to in New York City for first trimester abortions using suction curretage or at the hospital we use for second trimester abortions involving late D & Cs (dilation and curretage) or saline solution abortions. At both facilities, there is a concern for the whole woman in that counselors work with each woman or are available to her and all abortions are performed by licensed physicians and surgeons. 

What has been my experience and reflections that lead me to endorse this bill?

First, I believe that a woman has the right to decide which option to take. 

She should have available to her not only good medical consultation and care but other counselors as she needs or desires. With the exception of a few who were either immature or callous, women do not choose to have an abortion easily, frivolously, or without careful thought and pain. The decision usually involves consultation with the man if the relationship is at all significant to them both. Again, in the majority of situations, there is a real commitment to each other, an acceptance of a shared responsibility for the pregnancy and the decision. No woman looks forward to undergoing an abortion at any stage of pregnancy. However, for those who go to the clinic, there is a sense of surprise that "medical care could be sc caring,' as one married woman described her experience there.

Second, there is a low-rate of women coming for a second abortion which is similarly borne out in the data from New York, I have seen only two women-both married and with children-who have had a second abortion In New York, the percentage of women repeating is 1.3%. Both of these run counter to the oftenexpressed concern about abortion becoming a commonly-used form of contraception. I always talk with the woman and the man about effective contraceptives and their use and urge them to discuss contraception with her physician when she goes for a post-abortion checkup. I do not subscribe to abortion as being a contraceptive method but recognize it as a needed choice for women when contraceptives fail or are not used. 

Third, abortions are being performed in the first trimester with increasing safety both physically and psychologically for the women. This data from New 

York and the other states with similar statutes unquestionably affected the Supreme Court's decision. In counseling women who are in the second trimester, I make it clear that to choose to have an abortion involves much greater risk to the whole woman. The decision remains hers and my counseling with her is one of shared anguish.

Fourth, the medical data from New York continues to support both the Supreme Court decision and this act which follows its guidelines so closely. 

Again, this is crucial to the moral issue regarding both the woman and society as a whole. Fewer women die in pregnancy and childbirth; hospitals admit fewer women with medical problems from illegal or self-attempted abortions; fewer infants die in the first month or year of life; out-of-wedlock births declined for the first time in 19 years of record-keeping in New York City; and the safety of abortions is improving due to the growing trend toward abortions in the first trimester and the competency and experience of the physicians doing them then and later. I know of no doctor or hospital which do abortions beyond the 20th week from the last menstrual period when "viability" becomes a critical factor for them and for me both in the moral sense and in the risk to the woman. 

Fifth, I know from experience the importance of an open, non-judgmental pastoral relationship with the woman and the man if he is present that leads to other opportunities for ministry. Several women have returned for additional counseling. Some couples have asked me to officiate at their marriages some time later or to do pre-marital and post-marital counseling with them. Gccasionally, I have worked through a problem pregnancy with a high school student, with her parents, and with the assistance of other counselors or supportive people. There have been increasing opportunities to meet and talk with doctors and nurses, teachers and students about the changing dimensions of human sexuality and sexual relations and to make common cause for the development of the personhood of women and men. 

There remain, however, many concrete and substantial issues in this area that the law cannot touch and rightly so: the meaning of life and death; the conflict of rights and their resolution; a deeper understanding of freedom; the kind and quality of supportive services for women, rich and poor alike; the need for "human life education", what we have called sex education or education on human sexuality, in schools and churches and for all ages and stages of life. 

This act does begin to maximize the choices and the freedom of women in New Hampshire to become more fully human and thereby, to help us who are men to attain to our maturity and personhood as well.

ROMAN CATHOLICS FOR THE RIGHT TO CHOOSE, 

Pittsburgh, Pa., March 1, 1974.

MEMBERS, SENATE SUBCOMMITTEE ON CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENTS, 

Senate Office Building, Washington, D.C.

HONORABLE GENTLEMEN: "Roman Catholics for the Right to Choose" is a group of Pennsylvania citizens who hereby petition this subcommittee to reject all proposals before it which seek to reinstate restrictive abortion laws. 

We are all Catholics, and many of us are totally opposed to abortion for ourselves. But we feel very strongly that we have no moral right to make this decision for others. As the late Cardinal Cushing of Boston said (speaking of birth control): "Catholics do not need the support of civil law to be faithful to their own religious convictions, and they do not seek to impose by law their moral views on members of society". 

This Subcommittee will hear much testimony from representatives of our church. They will speak with deep conviction about the sanctity of the previable fetus. But we believe they will neglect some of the equally important consequences of using our particular scale of values as the basis for secular law. 

What do we, particularly we who are Catholics, lose when we advocate a constitutional amendment such as those proposed?

First, we threaten our own religious freedom. We give government the power to pick one philosophy and use it as the basis for law. If others can be forced to live by our beliefs, could we, too, not be forced at some future time to live in a manner which violates our consciences? We strongly oppose establishment of any precedent for government to enter into what is essentially a deeply personal decision. We do not want a society in which childbearing is in any way a governmental decision.

And even if such a constitutional amendment were enacted, would the protection of fetal life be insured? The previous restrictions on abortion did not protect the fetus, and we believe a constitutional amendment would be no more effective. 

Would we be willing to enforce such a law, by putting women who have abortions on trial for murder, as well as the physicians who perform the procedures and the individuals who finance them (fathers, husbands, mothers, and so on)? 

Clearly, few people are willing to do so!

One sometimes wonders if the church does not seek such a constitutional amendment to keep those of our faith "in line", since Catholic women find themselves seeking abortion with at least equal frequency as do non-Catholic women. 

We talk about religion as the "conscience of society". But we don't seem to act as though our position had any moral force unless backed up by law. 

We think this issue is hampered by the confusion of a life-and-death ethic with a sexual ethic. We who are Catholic come from a church which is able to deal with "killing" under all sorts of circumstances. We have complex teachings on capital punishment, self-defense, "just" war, and so on. Only in the area of abortion do we have an absolute prohibition in which circumstances are irrelevant. Could, perhaps, this relate to the old idea that pregnancy and childbearing are a woman's punishment for sexual intercourse? We really haven't worked our way out of this, and we think it confuses our thinking and our ability to deal with unwanted pregnancy in a more realistic manner.

The Catholics represented by RC/RC support the Supreme Court's decision regarding abortion. Thus, we urge this Subcommittee to reject the proposals before it.

When our church recognizes that its special-interest legislation cannot be achieved, perhaps then we can devote our full resources towards genuine "prolife" progress: maintenance of our parochial school system for the Catholic education of our children in our doctrines; support for those with problem pregnancies, whether stemming from reasons of health, finances, or other crisis situations; and succor for the ill, the aged, and the incapicitated. 

Very truly yours,

MARY ELLEN TUNNEY.
