A CONSIDERATION OF ABORTION AS A MEANS OF AVOIDING UNWANTED PREGNANCIES 

One Pastor's Ministry to Those who Experience Unwanted Pregnancies 

THE LOCAL SITUATION 

I work in a small town in Mississippi (Population about 14,000). The largest industry in Starkville is Mississippi State University which has about 10,000 students. When I arrived, the New York abortion law had recently been passed. 

As a result New York had become the center for legal abortion activity. Before that time I had not personally had any contact with abortion referrals. 

I work as a member of a team ministry involving a college chaplaincy and responsible for three missions. The College Chaplaincy is performed in the context of an inter-denominational group known as the University Common Ministry. 

MY ENTRY INTO PROBLEM PREGNANCY COUNSELING 

Shortly after my arrival the counseling center at Mississippi State University obtained a new director who promptly opened a crisis center telephone operation known as project HELP. The clergy in the University Common Ministry were asked, along with other members of the helping professions, to provide training for the individuals who would answer the telephones. In addition the trainers, like myself, were used to provide back-up support to the individuals who answered the telephone. Soon after the Center opened in January of 1972, it became clear that a substantial number of telephone calls involved women, usually single, who were pregnant and did not wish to be. At this time several of the clergy involved in the ministry to the University began to undertake problem pregnancy counseling.

In August 1972 a Family Planning Clinic opened and soon, as part of its activities, began offering pregnancy tests. Many coeds who suspected they were pregnant went to the Family Planning Clinic for tests. As the reputation of the Clinic grew, women from many distant localities also went there for pregnancy tests, contraceptives and other sex-related medical needs. A substantial number of women who were diagnosed pregnant sought help other than carrying the pregnancy to full term. The rules of the Family Planning Clinic wisely did not permit direct abortion referrals since personnel did not possess counseling talents and the physicians did not have time to discuss the question fully with the patient. Three of the clergy volunteered to undertake problem prgenancy counseling for the clients who desired it. During the period of August 1972 through 

July 1973, 69 women were referred for counseling, of whom 63 obtained abortions. For six the outcome is not known. Not all referrals came from project 

HELP or the Family Planning. Some came from physicians; others (after a positive pregnancy test at some other location) were referred by friends. Thus 

I saw individuals who came from many areas of the State of Mississippi, married and single, black and white. The one common denominator was youth. All were under 30 years of age.

INVOLVEMENT WITH THE CCS 

During 1972 and 1973, clergy here were contacted by a representative of the 

Clergy Consultation Service on Therapeutic Abortion (CCS). The representative, who was in Meridian, was receiving a number of referrals from this area of the State. Since his work load was too great he sought help from clergy in this area. 

As a result the clergy here received information and accrediation with the CCS. 

Once this was established most abortion referrals were made to the Women's Services Clinic in New York. This clinic had been established by the CCS in 1970 after the passing of liberalized abortion legislation in that State. Shortly after the 

1973 Supreme Court decision concerning abortions we received information that the University of Alabama Medical Center in Birmingham would perform abortions. Since the spring of 1973 our abortion referrals have been made to that facility.

THE PEOPLE WHO SEEK THERAPEUTIC ABORTION 

Generally, society recognizes people as being either married or unmarried. In the problem pregnancy counseling that I have encountered, I have dealt with both married couples and single women; however, there is a third group for which there is no legal or ecclesiastical position . the married but unwed. 

This third category of people might be considered betrothed or enjoying a kind of "trial marriage." They are living together, sometimes openly, often during only a portion of the time like on weekends, and are making concurrent decisions much as any married couple might, but their union has not been licensed by the state or blessed by the church. a. The married couple who desires to terminate pregnancy and who has been referred to me usually does not want a child, at least at that time. The pregnancy is unwanted, unplanned and frequently would pose financial hardship if carried to term. The choice usually is to have the child or to undergo an abortion. 

Such couples are not willing to consider carrying the pregnancy to term and then placing the child for adoption. In only one case have I received a referral of a married couple for the health of the mother. Usually birth control methods have been tried but have been misused or have simply failed. In some cases ignorance is the major factor. b. The unmarried and unaccompanied single girl who is pregnant and seeks an abortion usually falls into one of three classes, the sociopath/psychopath, the cry for help, and the sexually active woman who just got caught or whose birth control methods failed. (1) The sociopath/psychopath is usually pregnant and simply wants to end the pregnancy as rapidly as possible. This kind of person will find an abortion one way or the other. (2) The cry for help is the girl who, in some other circumstances, might well attempt suicide. There have been some studies which suggest that some unwanted pregnancies are a suicidal gesture. (3) The sexually active woman who is single but not maladjusted will usually engage in birth control practices, though in some cases these may fail and she may then resort to abortion as an extension of birth control. (4) Rarely do I encounter a young woman who became pregnant to hold onto a relationship in the process of breaking up. This last category finds abortion attractive only as a way out of the predicament; but since the pregnancy is purposeful they are most prone to decide to carry the pregnancy to term. Either they reaffirm the relationship and marry or they have the baby and put it up for adoption. None that I have counseled have remained single and kept the baby. (5) Equally rare is the woman who becomes pregnant and decides not to do anything about it. I have encountered situations when the birth of the baby occurred unwanted and unplanned in the girl's home in full view of her shocked and angered parents. These women tend to keep the baby as part of their act of definance. While this is not abortion counseling per se, we tend to receive referrals from these people since they are likely to again turn to pregnancy as a way of dealing with frustration. One single woman with whom I counseled sought an abortion for her second pregnancy after deciding that the father of the first was not desirable. c. The unwed but married couple often is contemplating marriage but for reasons of economics, education, and fear of affecting the sensibilities of families and friends would prefer quietly to terminate the pregnancy. The couple considers the decision together and the male partner, as if married, gives considerable emotional and usually, financial support to the female. The couple may or may not have been engaging in frequent sex. Often the sexual encounters have been in

the heat of passion rather than as couples living together constantly. Those actually living together full time who come for abortion counseling are few. Once they have decided to live together in common law, they usually obtain birth control methods. d. One paragraph needs to be included concerning the special problems of black women who are considering abortions. Several with whom I have counseled came very much desiring an abortion. Typically they were unwed, already had one child, were poor, and had passed the 15th week of pregnancy. For reasons involving expenses and the fact that in most cases they were beyond the 20th week of pregnancy, abortions were not done. In each case the individual was pregnant with a very much unwanted child but had not known of the possibility for abortion until the pregnancy was diagnosed. All desired abortions in spite of pressure from family and friends in the black community which generally does not approve of abortion. Among the black radicals it is considered genocide. Generally, the black community is considerably more accepting of the illegitimate child than the white community; but this does not necessarily make the child wanted by the mother. Counseling with blacks requires special concerns since a proabortion decision may not have the kind of social support that it has in the whitemiddle-class-college-age community. Indeed, sometimes the opposite is true for 

I have known some whose peer group identification rested upon a complete pregnancy and raising of a child, preferably during the high school years. e. The choices: (1) For the married couple there are three choices (listed under section 4. a. of this paper) when there is a pregnancy that is unwanted. (a) To have the child in spite of attendant difficulties. (b) To have the child and place it for adoption. (c) To have a therapeutic abortion. (2) For the unmarried females there are five choices: (a) To get married and have the child. (b) To have an abortion and then get married. This may not seem to make much sense but I know of some who have done just that. (c) To have the child and keep it. This no longer runs as strongly against social dictum as it once did; there are so many divorcees around that a woman with a child may frequently be considered a divorcee. Bastardy, of course, does not pose the problems it once did now that we have a somewhat more egalitarian society. (d) To have the child and place it for adoption. There are many homes which desire a child as long as it is healthy and caucasian. (e) To have a therapeutic abortion. (3) For nearly all those who are pregnant and do not wish to be, suicide occurs as a passing thought. Without adequate support it may well be attempted but by and large pregnant women do not seek this course of action. 

THE DECISION MAKING PROCESS 

Young women who find themselves pregnant, but do not wish to be, normally move through several stages in their decision-making process. These stages, outlined in part by Scott and discussed fully in his article,¹ are easy to recognize. a. The Stage of Psychological Shock.-The initial reaction to the discovery of an unwanted pregnancy is shock. It may come gradually, for the woman suspects pregnancy prior to confirmation by medical tests; but when the medical verdict is announced some shock always occurs. Some women are hard hit at this point, especially if they are young and unmarried. Denial may take place and strong wishes that it would just go away are entertained. Sometimes there is the hope that if she waits long enough perhaps a miscarriage will occur, or that the monthly period is just late and will come. Much of this is usually worked through by the time the women presents herself to the physician for a pregnancy test since this very presentation is an admission of the pregnancy possibility. When the diagnosis is made a sympathetic physician can be very helpful. 

With the normal individual, guilt feelings run high. A physician who behaves in an offhand or cold manner can cause severe disturbance for his patient at this highly vulnerable time. I have personally observed the results of such misguided medicine and the unnecessary trauma it caused. The time of diagnosis is a particularly vulnerable psychological moment, aptly symbolized by the phys- 

1 Leonard Scott. "Possible Guidelines for Problem Pregnancy Counseling." Pastoral 

Psychology, Vol. 23, No. 224, May 1972. p. 44.

ical examination which can be frightening in itself, especially to the young, unmarried woman who has rarely, if ever, undergone physical examinations. 

As a counselor I frequently see women who have already passed through this first stage. When I do see women who have not yet had a pregnancy test, the first step on my part is to ask them to seek one. If they have not seen a physician, then that becomes the first order and they are referred either to a private physician or to the Family Planning Clinic. On occasion this diagnostic step is resisted. If the woman has had a pregnancy test, I ask for certification from the physician. The Family Planning Clinic provides this as a matter of course. I do not try to give the details for abortion referral, adoption, or marriage at this point since the individual is usually overwhelmed by her emotional uncertainty. I do try to provide a reassuring atmosphere by assuring the woman that I shall work with her until the crisis is completely resolved. I assure her that various options are open and that I shall not suggest any measures which are illegal or unsafe nor will I tell her what she must do. I also encourage her to express the emotions she feels. Frequently this is a time for tears, tears of guilt, tears of fear, tears of anger. It is also a time to surface suicidal thoughts which the woman may be considering. It is a mistake to assume that abortion information is looked for, so I do not present this unless it is sought. I do ask about the male corespondent and frequently a decision is made at this time to involve him in the process to follow. My main targets for this meeting are to establish a relaxed counseling atmosphere and to reassure the woman by guiding her to make the immediate decisions that must be made, namely to discover whether she is pregnant and to decide who must be told. b. The Stage of Uncertainty, but with Deliberation.-I frequently see women at the stage of uncertainty in the decision-making process. They come looking for help at the time the pregnancy is discovered or they are referred by the Family Planning Clinic after they have indicated that they desire an abortion. 

Women who intend to marry or place the baby for adoption are rarely referred to me by the Family Planning Clinic. This stage of uncertainty is a time used to integrate the knowledge of the pregnancy and the emotional factors. It is a time when the various factors bearing on the pregnancy are weighed and it is a time to look at the options available. When I counsel with women who have already passed through this stage of uncertainty it is necessary to backtrack and review the options. If they have passed through this stage, this kind of discussion renews the uncertainty and meets resistance and resentment. 

For this reason I prefer to see women at the time pregnancy is discovered rather than when they have already made a decision for abortion. c. The Stage of Being Decided but Manifesting Strong Anxiety with Reluctance to Discuss Anything.-Most referrals are women who have already made a proabortion decision. Single women who have opted for marriage usually know how to arrange their marriage. Black women who are single and wish to have the baby will simply do so, as will whites, though the whites may go to a home for unwed mothers or visit a distant relative. Of course, a married couple will not contact us unless they have a strong wish or reason to desire an abortion. Therefore, most of the women who are referred at this stage of the decision-making process have decided for an abortion; however, they manifest considerable anxiety about their decision and are frequently unwilling to discuss it. They interpret any questions about their decision as an attempt to have them change their minds and react with silence or hostility. 

Usually I begin a session with someone referred to me because she has made a decision to obtain an abortion by a short discussion of her problem. I negotiate a verbal agreement by stating what I see as my function in the counseling process. 

Briefly this means that we will review her situation, discuss the available options and review the woman's decision. I advise her that while I will discuss her situation. I shall not try to push her to a decision which I think right. The decision is hers. Once she has made her deicsion I will provide the necessary information and support; however, she will have to make the appointments and her own arrangements. Usually, I encounter resistance to reviewing the decision already made. The resistance varies directly with the amount of rationality that was used. If the decision was extremely emotional and panicky, resistance is higher. 

A second part of our agreement is that the woman will see me when she returns from her abortion. I explain that I have three reasons for this post-abortion meeting: (1) To obtain feed-back on her treatment at the medical facility; (2) to obtain feed-back about the adequacy and completeness of my counseling; (3) to give the woman an opportunity to talk about her experience.

Once the verbal agreement has been negotiated we begin the process outlined above. This may or may not be accomplished in one session. Usually two are required. We discuss such things as what led up to the pregnancy, the possibility or need to involve the male correspondent, the options available, the woman's religion and her ethical commitments, which may have some bearing on how she will feel about having an abortion, and her general feelings about her condition. 

We also consider whether or not the family of the woman must be, or should be, informed. 

While the young white single female sometimes resists involving the male correspondent, she usually agrees to do this, though she expresses doubt that he will participate or care. In some cases, particularly the married but unwed, the woman is eager and willing to involve the man and he is eager to come. In a high percentage of the cases the man is not only willing to discuss the matter, but is also highly concerned and supportive of the woman. In the days of sending people to New York, some of the men insisted on accompanying the women. Now that the referrals are made to Birmingham nearly every man who has come for counseling has accompanied the woman. In every case where the man has come to participate in the counseling process, he has not only given emotional support, but also provided financial support. This has occurred even when the couple had already decided to break up as soon as the crisis was solved. 

After a rather complete discussion I provide the woman with the necessary information so that she can make appointments and obtain the necessary laboratory work. Since she needs a referral letter from me that the letter provides a control and assurance that she will return to complete the counseling process. 

When we referred women through the CCS to New York a series of control numbers was issued to each clergyman, and the woman had to have the control number on the certificate from the physician.

In order to be referred to the University of Alabama Medical Center a woman must have the following: (1) A letter from a physician certifying to the pregnancy and length of gestation. (2) Urinalysis. (3) Blood hematocrit and blood type and group. (4) A letter from the clergyman making the referral. d. The Stage of Being Decided and Requiring Information, Support and Clarification to Carry Out the Decision.—In my experience a woman often enters this stage after or during the previous session. Once she has decided to make arrangements for the abortion, relatively little support is required. Normally, when the woman comes for the next session, perhaps accompanied at this time by the male correspondent, we go over the situation briefly. I then talk it over with the man involved and ask the couple to review their discussion and the decision-making process. At this time, if the decision for an abortion remains firm, I provide them with any further information they may want, a complete sheet of printed instructions and the referral letter. We normally make a post abortion appointment at this time. e. The Stage of Relief Following the Implementation of the Decision.--Not all women actually return for post abortion counseling. Those from out of town are least likely to return. Perhaps distance is a factor. Those who are of the sociopathic or psychopathic type are also very unlikely to be willing to actually show up for the termination sessions. Now that we are referring women to Birmingham rather than New York I no longer follow up on my own. One of my serious concerns in the New York trip was the risk of sending young unaccompanied women to New York. Many of them had never left Mississippi or flown in an airplane. 

At the time one common concern was, "Will I be hijacked, and have my friends or family wonder what I am doing in Cuba?" One woman whom I referred to New

York was propositioned by the cab driver and another was short-changed. The 

Birmingham referrals not only significantly reduce expenses but also are easier and safer because the travel arrangements are simpler. These facts have eased my anxiety considerably.

Women who do come for the post-abortion counseling universally express relief that it is over and a sense of well being. Whether this good feeling later gives way to depression or other symptoms is unknown since longer range follow-up has not been done. We share the experience and review the counseling process. 

If this is to be the terminal session, and usually it is, I advise the woman of my continuing availability should she wish to discuss the matter further or encounter any difficulties. We also take some time to discuss the woman's future sexual

activities. Some express a desire to cut out any sexual activity, others, a desire to obtain functional contraceptives. At this time I also urge the woman to return to her physician for a checkup if she has not already done this. This advice is also given by the physician who performs the abortion. When the male is present for this session (and he usually is if he accompanied the woman for the abortion), we discuss their relationship as well and provide the male a chance to talk out his feelings. A universal comment on the part of the male is that he appreciated his inclusion and found the wait in the ante-chamber of the surgery the most difficult part. The clinic does include the male in the detailed pre-abortion briefing so that he is a full participant for everything except the abortion itself. f. The Stage of Wanting to Forget.-This is the last stage that I have routinely observed. Usually a desire to forget is expressed in the last session. One woman who was counseled and whom I heard of through a third party carried this to the point of total denial and showed some morbid psychological symptoms. By this time the woman, or the couple, have acknowledged that a mistake was made. They have carefully reviewed and thought through their course of action so that they did not act out of sheer panic and guilt and they have made their choice and carried it out themselves. Since abortion is not the kind of thing you can talk about like an appendectomy, no matter how liberal our society has become, and since key friends and family members are often kept in the dark, the woman tries to put it aside and forget what is now a bad chapter which has been closed.

THE ROLE OF THE FATHER 

I have already said a considerable amount concerning the involvement of the male correspondent in a problem. pregnancy crisis. Obviously the husband must be involved if the couple is married. A woman who seriously desires an abortion against her husband's wishes would have to take a serious look at their marriage relationship. Of course, no husband could force his wife to undergo an abortion. 

To date I have not counseled with any married couple who were not in agreement concerning their decision.

When single women are accompanied by the male correspondent this provides a sense of support, financial and emotional, which is extremely helpful to the woman. But for the man, usually also entertains some sense of guilt, this is an opportunity to redeem himself and assume his responsibility. Often the woman finds herself reassuring the man that their action was not solely his fault and that she was a willing and responsible correspondent in the sex act. Since the couple may be entertaining the idea of marriage it remains to be seen what the abortion will do to their long-term relationship. Follow-up work is needed in this area, but is difficult because of the sensitivity of the subject. 

THE INVOLVEMENT OF THE WOMAN'S FAMILY 

One of the key questions for the young single woman, typically a college coed, is whether or not to tell her family. For the woman under 17 years of age the family must be told and part of the counseling process must deal with this. 

This can be a very valuable experience for the woman and the family, if the family is not vindictive or demeaning. Unfortunately, I have encountered instances where the family responded supportively yet used the event later in dealing with the woman manipulatively. This behavior built needless guilt and hostility.

For the young woman 17 years of age or over and relatively independent, the decision is a very different one. She does not have to abtain parental approval in order to obtain an abortion. Typically, she is living away from home, but is still financially and, in many ways, emotionally dependent on her family. Typically she comes from a white, middle class, protestant family which is relatively conservative. The young woman's desire is to extricate herself from her predicament without undue shame or reproof. Consequently, I point out that secrets may damage the woman's familial relationship and will very much damage it if her secret should come out inadvertently. If, after considering this, the woman still wants to act without parental knowledge. I do not push the issue further. 

The woman's desire is to preserve her image and status with her family. If she can do this she is much more likely to retain a high self esteem. The fact that she has acted stupidly is acknowledged. By her own action she is resolving her crisis in an adult fashion, using the medical and counseling resources she sought out. This can give her a new sense of independence and self confidence as she learns to face up to and attend to the consequences of her behavior.

701

EMOTIONAL PROBLEMS 

There are some other general areas that I look for in the counseling process. 

One area is that I try to ascertain something about the emotional state of the woman. Women who appear sociopathic in their orientation to life frequently have also used illicit drugs. This may or may not become part of the counseling process. One young woman came in still high and, of course, I insisted upon her return to discuss her pregnancy in a more sober condition. I also look for serious psychiatric problems which might be aggravated by the pregnancy and an abortion. I maintain a relationship with a clinical psychologist as a back-up in difficult cases.

ABORTION AFTER THE FIRST TRIMESTER 

One of the most agonizing problems in Problem Pregnancy Counseling is dealing with the woman who is beyond the first trimester of pregnancy. The medical factors are that abortion is relatively easy in the first trimester. If the woman has gone beyond the 11th or 12th week of pregnancy then she must wait for an abortion until sometime between the 16th and the 20th weeks. The method used for second trimester abortions requires the woman to deliver the fetus after saline solution has been injected into the uterus to destroy the fetus. 

The medical risks are higher as is the possibility of viability for the fetus. Thus for purely medical reasons this is not a very advisable solution. 

Another consideration, however, is the emotional state of the woman. Any intelligent woman, who has waited beyond the first trimester to seek an abortion in an otherwise normal pregnancy, has considerable ambivalence about the pregnancy. Among the women whom I have counseled concerning problem pregnancy, nearly all those who decided against having an abortion were in the second trimester of pregnancy. The ambivalence rests on the possibility that the woman may really want to bear the child or has strong reservations about abortion. The reasons for wanting the child or her reservations are varied. She is now seeking an abortion due to shame or possibly the failure of her plans for marriage. Supportive counseling and an exploration of her motivations and real desires are very helpful at this point. 

THE PASTOR'S DILEMMA 

The Pastoral Dilemma in problem pregnancy counseling is not significantly different from any other morally loaded and emotionally laden counseling issue. 

The pastor, in my opinion, must refrain from giving reign to a judgmental position or to "playing God" by thinking he knows what "is best." His task, then, is to allow the individual to reach her own decision, and to be able to assume responsibility for her action. The pastor must react as a sounding board, but more than that, he must also bring to the individual's attention the reprecussions and ramifications of her behavior. Of course this is a very subtle matter since the pastor's opinions and judgments may often be indicated non-verbally and so put off the individual with whom he is counseling as to block the relationship. This is especially true when dealing with cases involving sexual behavior and human reproduction which is shaded by such highly emotional overtones, and which may mean that the pastor will help someone to carry out something which he (the pastor) is not fully in favor of. For the highly sensitive pastor this can be agonizing. For the opinionated and self-righteous pastor the agony may not be a factor, but the potential damage to the client (who is talked into something not really wanted) may be severe. A pastor who cannot be open about the options available to the pregnant woman should not be doing problem pregnancy counseling.

ABORTION: THEOLOGICAL AND ETHICAL CONSIDERATIONS 

Abortion has long been a dirty word having all kinds of illegal and unethical connotations. Only recently have liberalized legislation and the recent United 

States Supreme Court decision opened the matter to real consideration in this country. Other countries such as Japan have had liberal abortion laws for some time; Great Britain passed liberalizing legislation in 1967; but in the United 

States it was not until 1970 that abortions more or less on demand became available. Only in 1973 has abortion been ruled to be a matter not legislatively deniable, particularly in the early weeks of pregnancy. Historically the Christian Church has taken a stand opposed to abortion and infanticide often to protect not only the child, but also the mother. By and large, abortions which were safe and simple were not available until the advent of modern day medicine. 43-245 O- 75 - 46

LIFE AND DEATH-FETAL EUTHANASIA 

When one deals with abortion certain related issues immediately crop up. 

Among them are the following questions: a. Does anyone have the right to take a life? b. If life may be taken purposely, what are the proper circumstances? c. When does life end? d. When does life begin? e. What is life?

These questions are related not only to the medical dimensions of ethics made possible by recent advances but also to any issue having to do with purposeful ending of human life. Among these issues are capital punishment, war and suicide. It is interesting to note that frequently the Church has taken an apparently contradictory stand. To take a position that any destruction of life is wrong would be to take a position not only against abortions but also against euthanasia in any form (passive or active), war, capital punishment, and suicide. 

For my purpose in this paper it is more advantageous to limit discussion to those aspects of life and death encountered in medicine. Along with raging debates over the ending of life at its conception or shortly after, we have also encountered lengthy debate over the issues of euthanasia. I define active euthanasia as action by the physician or someone else to cause death either by providing poison, or cutting off the life support machinery. Passive euthanasia is allowing someone to die because further treatment is refused. At the center of this argument lies the question of "When does life end?" Furthermore, there is the point that human suffering shou'd not be perpetuated simply to continue life when that life has no meaning, when that life is one of debilitating pain or irrevocable unconsciousness, and when that life results in immense expense and trauma to the family and the society.

Euthanasia for the critically ill or elderly is what most people have in mind when they use the word. Intimately related to the abortion issue, however, is the concept of fetal euthanasia. While this might be seen as always an active euthanasia, now medicine also allows passive fetal euthanasia. Euthanasia for the fetus has been proposed and performed when there was reason to believe that the baby would be born grossly deformed or injured. For example, Down's

Syndrome has been considered reason for fetal euthanasia as have other serious defects caused by drugs, diseases like rubella, or by known genetic factors. 

Another consideration, however, is that of passive fetal euthanasia. Modern medical techniques have made it possible not only to diagnose fetal problems but also, at least in some cases, to treat the fetus in utero. Thus passive euthanasia may now be accomplished by failing to treat a condition which could be remedied and which would cause death to the fetus if not remedied. An allied question here is that the fetus cannot be treated without cooperation from the mother and at least some maternal discomfort. To refuse to treat the fetus and cause death either on the part of the physician or on the part of the mother might be seen as a kind of passive euthanasia. On the other hand there is a real question that an unwilling mother could be forced to undergo treatment for the fetus if she did not choose to cooperate.

Allied to this question is another. Fetal care, like some medical procedures, might be considered ordinary. But other procedures reach toward the extraordinary. Such extraordinary and, perhaps, experimental methods might well extend fetal life but there is a serious question whether such extraordinary care must be provided in order not to contribute to the death. The question of passive fetal euthanasia is as complex as any dealing with abortion. If the baby is truly wanted then a parent may go to extraordinary length to safeguard fetal life when nature might have otherwise intervened to cause a natural abortion or miscarriage. This is an area of ethics for which there is no historical precedent. 

Just treating the fetus in utero is charting new medical territories; and so are the ethics of the preservation of fetal life.

REASONS FOR ABORTIONS 

There are really two main divisions which must be made when dealing with the issues of abortion. The first division is the medically undesirable pregnancy; the second, the unwanted pregnancy. Both these divisions fall under the general category of problem pregnancy. Abortion is one of several ways of dealing with a problem pregnancy. All problem pregnancies have one thing in common: there is no "good" solution. They always involve an agonizing decision and they can be solved only by choosing between evils of pain and personal disruption.

a. Medically undesirable pregnancies occur in two areas. There are those pregnancies which threaten the life and health of the mother. Historically, this is the area over which the Church has suffered the most agony. In the 10th century it was ruled that abortion could be performed early in the pregnancy in order to save the life of the mother. Early in the pregnancy meant prior to ensoulment when it was theorized that an actual human being first existed. 

Ensoulment, the medieval term used to say that life was present, was a concept derived from Aristotle who maintained that ensoulment occurred after 40 days for males and 80 days for females. Usually moral theologians used the 40 day time period. Abortion to save the life of the mother was considered proper under the additional doctrine that the fetus was really a dangerous invader. The fetus was innocent of wrong doing, of course, but was nevertheless a danger to the mother. The Church has always permitted killing in self-defense; therefore abortion of a dangerous fetus was seen as self-defense.

I mention the medieval discussions only to demonstrate that the Church has historically been uneasy about quick decisions concerning abortions. In reality, until modern times abortions early in the pregnancy were rather difficult and frequently resulted in considerable harm (if not death) to the mother. Poisons, physical abuse and irritants were used. The poison was as dangerous to the mother as to the fetus since it had to be administered to the mother in order to affect the fetus. Before the days of antiseptics the insertion of irritants involved a great risk of infection. Thus abortion to preserve the life of the mother was frequently something that occurred at the time of birth when a birth could have been successfully accomplished only by caesarian, a procedure usually fatal to the mother. On some occasions craniotomy was performed at birth to allow passage of the head. This was especially necessary if the child was hydrocephalic. 

A craniotomy is, of course, always fatal to the baby. 

In the 19th century the Catholic Church hardened its position on many doctrines besides Papal infallibility. Abortion was one of them. It was during this time that abortion to save the life of the mother was most clearly contravened by ecclesiastical dictum. This included the abortion of ectopic pregnancies which were sure to result in the death of both mother and child if unattended. In practice, however, abortions for the protection of the life of the mother have not really been an issue in the modern practice of medicine. Though difficult to obtain, they have been legally performed throughout this century. When modern day "Right to Life" people oppose this, they place themselves in a position of being more rigid than any of the laws or medical practices in the United States in this century. Even the Catholic Church has relented from condemning both mother and child to death.

It is my contention that to allow the mother to die for the fetus is wrong. To allow both mother and fetus to die is a double wrong. The possibility for the mother's life, her responsibility for her family, the fact that she has a place in life and that she fulfills a need, particularly if other children exist, all point to the fact that the fetus, certainly not yet a person, but at best only a possibility, has less right to live. I see no way that ethics can justify any position other than that of saving the life of the mother, for to allow her to die would clearly be the greater evil.

Medically undesirable pregnancies are also suggested and performed because the fetus promises not to be whole in body and mind. This is the practice of eugenics. For genetic reasons such as Down's Syndrome the fetus may be grossly deficient. Drugs and maternal illness such as rubella may also have affected the fetus negatively and caused mental retardation, gross deformities, or physical difficulties which will bring into the world a seriously handicapped individual. In many cases this individual may live only a relatively short time and at great expense. In other cases the life may be sufficiently long, but it will be completely dependent and unable to support its existence. In some cases fetal anomalies may be diagnosed early in fetal life; in other cases known genetic problems or medical problems may make medical authorities reasonably certain that the baby will be born defective. Of course many fetal deformities are not discovered until the time of birth and so it was the practice of at least some ancient civilizations to expose defective infants to certain death. A modern analogy to this is that at least some physicians are known to refuse assistance to a newly born baby which 

2 Gregory IX, Si Aliquis. "If anyone for the sake of fulfilling lust or in meditated hatred does something to a man or a woman or give them to drink, so that he cannot regenerate, fulfilling or she conceive, or offspring be born, let it be homicide." The key words are “. lust or meditated hatred

Abortion to save the life of the mother did not meet that prerequisite and was in fact allowed.

is seriously defective from some readily recognizable problem such as Mongolism. 

If the baby survives the birth trauma, it is cared for, but it is in no way assisted. 

The new laws concerning abortion do not permit abortions beyond the 24th week except where the choice is the fetus or the mother. Most physicians are reluctant to perform abortions beyond the 21st week. At least some states permit abortions earlier than the 24th week; therefore, deformed or damaged infants beyond the 24th week are not legally abortable. Prior to the 24th week the deformity must be diagnosed and a decision made. The basis on which one might make such a decision will be given later in this paper but, in the ethical dilemma it presents, this kind of abortion is not fundamentally different from one due to an unwanted pregnancy. b. Abortions of unwanted pregnancies fall into at least four categories. The first is an abortion due to rape. This has been regarded by some moral theologians in the same light as abortions to preserve the life and health of the mother. 

In this case the pregnancy is an unwanted, even if innocent, invader. The rape is clearly an invasion of the woman and the results of that rape are a compounding of that invasion. When the rape is incestuous, there is, of course, also the possibility of an abortion for genetic reasons. Whether this should include the category of statutory rape is a moot point since the young woman was probably a willing participant, even if the law does consider her as having been abused under the alleged grounds that she was too young to make a clear decision about the sexual act.

The unmarried person desiring an abortion as preferable to an illegitimate baby and the trauma of an unwanted pregnancy which will hamper the normal continuation of life plans is the person who is really the target of the most fire from anti-abortion forces. The Church has never stood for toleration of illegitimacy. The sanctions brought to bear against single pregnant women in the white community are severe. One of the redemptive factors of our times is that pregnancy among unmarried women is becoming more tolerable. I am convinced that many abortions have been performed on women who would have carried the child but feared the sanctions of society against herself and the child. The need for homes for unwed mothers and all their attendant secrecy is a testimony to our society's intolerance. White racists have frequently castigated the black community for its tolerance of illegitimacy, but in most cases black families have without prejudice adopted, in fact if not in law, the children that came their way. Unfortunately, the Church usually stood in the position of castigating the unwed mother for having an illegitimate baby at the same time it prevented her from preventing the production of that baby. 

The unmarried woman who finds herself pregnant has several choices. Among middle class whites this situation used to produce many shot-gun weddings that were ill founded and undoubtedly contributed to divorce rates, marital unhappiness and later-child abuse. Other women had the baby more or less in secret then placed it for adoption. A few women had the baby and kept it. Many guesses have been hazarded about the number of abortions which took place. They were illegal and frequently unsafe. More than one woman died due to complications from abortions performed by amateurs. Many women were also rendered severely ill and in some cases sterile as an aftermath of improper and unsterile abortion procedures. None of the solutions were very satisfactory. The only legal outcome produced social sanctions, severe guilt problems and severely disrupted lives. 

The woman, of course, bore the brunt of these difficulties. The abortion option also left severe guilt problems as well as risks due to the illegality. 

It now appears that most of the psychiatric problems following abortions were due to inadequate consideration of the decision and guilt caused by having knowingly performed an illegal and socially unacceptable act. Once abortion is legalized and societal support is felt, relatively little trauma is produced, certainly less than occurs in cases of forced marriage or forced pregnancy. There are some women, both married and single, who desire an abortion simply because they do not feel that they have the financial means to support another child. 

This occurs principally among black single women and white married women. 

Naturally the pregnancy is unplanned and may have occurred because of failure of contraceptive methods.

Still other families seek abortions because a child is inconvenient. These are the families who believe in family planning. Finances may be one consideration, but often are not the final consideration. The couple may be following an educational path or a vocation which, in their minds, precludes a child at that time.

A baby in this family may be truly unwanted and if born, neglected. Of course it would be unacceptable to place the baby for adoption since this would result in a public rejection of the child, something that society still does not sanction, even if the law does.

THE MORALITY OF ABORTION 

Nature already performs many abortions in spite of medicine's attempts to prevent them. Generally, they are called miscarriages. Usually these occur because something is wrong with the fetus or the mother. Nature, in its wisdom, knows this and acts to prevent the continuation of an unfortunate series of events. In many ways man can consider abortion as a way of aiding nature much as man aids nature by the prevention of death through use of medicine. a. Opposed to the pro-abortion stance are those who raise the question of the rights of the fetus. I shall leave for the moment any discussion of when life begins. In some cases the courts have ruled in favor of the rights of a child not yet born, in essence fetal recognition in court. Here is a crucial point, for a fetus is affected by the mother and vice versa even though they are separate entities. This school of thought takes the posiion that the fetus is a life to be protected from murder like any other life. An abortion is considered to be murder. b. In direct opposition to the rights of the fetus to live are the rights of a woman not to be forced into pregnancy. The strong legal sanctions against rapes are a part of this issue. The right of the woman not to bear a child which might cause her death, as in the presence of certain malignant neoplasms, or which might cause both the death of the mother and the fetus, such as in an ectopic pregnancy, is a matter that has been disputed in ecclesiastic circles. In some quarters it has been maintained that no abortion should ever be performed regardless of whether it would lead to maternal death or the death of fetus and mother. By and large, however, society and, during certain periods, the Church have regarded abortion as the lesser of two evils in regard to saving the mother of the child. In De Santo Matrimonii Sacramento (Venice, 1737), the Jesuit Tomas Sanchez also argued that contraception because of rape was permissible for the semen was not in possession and was considered as a thief who could be pursued and attacked; however, this had to be achieved quickly and really as a contraceptive technique rather than an abortifacient. 

The crux of ecclesiastical doctrine concerning sex and pregnancy has been that the natural reason for coitus is pro-creation. Therefore, interruption of the possibility for pregnancy (contraceptives) or of the pregnancy itself (abortion) is wrong. Until the 20th century, and really only the latter part of our 

20th century, contraceptive devices which were efficient, inexpensive and easy to use were not available. Availability of contraceptive devices has seriously disrupted the Church's anti-contraceptive position which is the only logically tenable position relative to a rigidly anti-abortion position. The fact is that even in such instances as when the Church allowed abortions, carnal lust and sexual pleasure were regarded as evil and wrong. In a sense maternity was deemed the fee of sexual pleasure. Sexural pleasure other than to promote human reproduction was, and by some still is, considered wrong. 

The position that the fee or price of sexual pleasure was maternity has always been a greater burden for the female than the male. Marriage as a social institution was especially important to protect and tend to the female and the fruits of sexuality, children. When the sire was unknown, as in rape, or unavailable, due to death or desertion, it has always been the female who bore the brunt of the pregnancy, the child rearing, and frequently, community ostracism. In our society the other innocent party was the child who suffered considerably in its illegitimacy. The Roman Catholic Church has maintained a steady opposition to contraceptives. Its position has been to leave to fate what man can control. The dilemma for the female in this is that she must bear children or forego sexual pleasure. In a sense she faces forced maternity or celibacy. 

With the advent of modern, convenient and inexpensive contraceptive techniques the woman now has developed the same right as the man: To enjoy sexual pleasure without the immediate possibility of pregnancy. In essence she has won the right not to be forced into maternity. This right may stand in direct conflict with the fetal right to life. The question we face is when does the balance swing? At what point does the fetus' right to live outweigh the mother's right not to continue a pregnancy? This question has nothing to do

with saving the mother's life or with the possibility of a severely damaged fetus. It has to do with the woman's right not to have to bear a child as the possible result of enjoying her sexual potential. c. In cases which involve the health and potentially the life of the mother the medieval Church developed a doctrine based in part on property rights. 

To the mother whose life was endangered by the continuance of a pregnancy the fetus was considered an innocent but dangerous aggressor. As such the rights of self-defense intervened when asserted prior to quickening or ensoulment. Quickening and ensoulment were taken to indicate that life was there. 

In practice this meant that abortion to defind the life of the mother was permissible during the first trimester; however, medical science did not really know how to accomplish abortions safely. Prior to the 20th century abortion was negatable purely on the grounds of the danger to the mother. But before antiseptics there was always a question whether the mother would survive the abortion. d. As a further development of the medieval doctrine of the fetus as an innocent but dangerous aggressor I would like to offer that in some cases the fetus is an innocent but unwanted intruder from which woman has a right to protect herself. Under this view pregnancy is not seen as the natural outcome of sexual union. Whether it comes from sexual union or from artificial insemination, unless it is wanted, pregnancy is an intrusion on the privacy of the mother. 

The fetal carrier or potential mother must act quickly to disavow the intrusion or the fetus establishes itself in its own right. For emotional and medical reasons as well as for ethical reasons, it would appear that if a pregnancy is allowed to continue into the second trimester the fetus has established certain rights to life. (1) If a women truly does not want a child and the pregnacy is unplanned she will seek assistance as rapidly as possible. After six weeks a pregnancy is usually within the physician's capbility to diagnose. When a woman waits longer than necessary (past the first trimester) to take action to terminate her pregnancy, she is usually very ambivalent about it. If she really wants the baby then it is not an unwanted intruder. An abortion, when a baby is truly wanted, is for psychological reasons contra-indicated. Furthermore the maternal attachment to the fetus normally grows as the period of gestation lengthens and she experiences physical changes. The chances of considerable grief trauma with its attendant guilt and anger are considerably greater as the length of gestation increases. (2) Medically an abortion during the first trimester is both simpler and safer. It can be accomplished in a matter of minutes by dialation and suction, perhaps with curettage. It can be performed on an outpatient basis with minimal trauma. Abortion in the second trimester becomes a much more complex affair. 

There is increased risk to the mother. Depending on the technique used and the length of gestation a live and possibly viable birth may occur. (3) From a point of view of ethics and medicine it is extremely difficult to consider when life begins and ends, but it would appear that viability for the fetus can be achieved sometimes during the latter part of the second trimester of pregnancy. Consequently it would appear that abortions performed after the first trimester of pregnancy should be discouraged except under the gravest of consequences. e. Eugenics, under which all abortions are performed in Japan, regardless of reason, is the most difficult area with which to deal in terms of ethics. Among the ancients malformed children were left to die, amounting in essence, to infanticide. 

Today some doctors do not give special aid to a defective child, allowing it to die unless nature wills that it live. Fetal deformities may not be visible as in the instance of heart defects, and some deformities are repairable. Of course many fetal defects prevent life so that the infant dies shortly after birth. With modern medicine and our current knowledge of genetics some fetal malformation may be predictable. The question to be faced is: Should an abortion be performed to terminate fetal life when we have good reason to believe the fetus will be malformed and defective? An ensuing question is: What grade of malformation justifies an abortion? Is abortion justifiable if the malformation is surgically correctible such as heart defects? I would suggest that the same criteria apply to deformed fetus and to an unwanted fetus. If a defective fetus is unwanted it becomes an invader of the privacy of the parent. Prior viability (the end of the second trimester) it should be abortable. Of course if fetal death occurs in utero it should also be abortable at a time when this is medically indicated.

At this juncture I might point out that the doctrine of the unwanted invader can be carried too far. Once viability occurs, that is the child can live from other care than that provided by the natural mother in utero, society must take up that care if the natural mother is unable or unwilling. The child is in essence orphaned and becomes a ward of the society and of the state. 

In a sense abortion of a defective fetus can be viewed as aiding nature. Miscarriages occur either because the fetus is defective or because the maternal womb is inhospitable. Now that man has the capability of assisting nature in this respect it should not be considered improper to do so, any more than it is improper to treat a disease and cure it, when allowing nature to take its course would result in death. f. A consideration in deciding whether or not an abortion should be performed is contained in the ethical dictum that what should be done is that which effects the greatest good for the greatest number. This must sometimes mean that few are sacrificed to protect the many. It is the principle under which an army sends out scouts, often to certain death. Not to do this may lead to mass societal suicide. 

It is under this doctrine that the need for population control is evident. The problem of overpopulation has been debated and stated in many other publications. 

It needs no airing here except to note that it occurs on at least two levels: (1) The first level of overpopulation is impersonal. It is the simple assessment that on a national and global scale we are gradually multiplying the human race to such a degree that its survival is at stake because there are insufficient resources. This level of overpopulation is best handled by birth control information and education; but the actual decision concerning birth control is a personal one. It must be done on the second level. (2) The second level is personal overpopulation. A family at poverty level and expecting its sixth child is overpopulated. Decisions concerning population control may be global in emphasis and design; but they must be accepted on a personal basis. Abortion is not a recommended method strictly for population control. It is expensive, troublesome and more risky than any contraceptives currently in use. 

The effect of widespread abortions will be to limit the population, but I do not think that the personal decision of an individual to have an abortion can be decided on that basis. g. One of the more virulent anti-abortion writers has noted that if abortions had been permitted Beethoven might well never have existed since there were both maternal and fetal reasons that might have prevented his birth by rationalizing an abortion. The implication is that an abortion limits the possible creation of a great contributor to society. No one can argue with this easily. It should be pointed out, however, that one might just as well create a Hitler as a Beethoven. 

Determination of the lifelong outcome of a particular birth is not yet within the scope of human capability. If one argues that abortion might deny life to a genius it would behoove men to reproduce as frequently as possible in order to increase the chance of producing genius. The whole argument is ethically ridiculous since we are asked to make decisions on the basis of possibility. An abortion should be performed or not performed only on the basis of reality. To speculate endlessly about the possibility of what might be fruitless. To base ethical judgment on that basis is silly.

WHEN DOES LIFE BEGIN? 

When does life begin? When does life end? Around these two questions hangs the most profound ethical dilemma. It is a dilemma that is not reconcilable for the questions seek to establish a point in time. For working purposes we can do this but for theoretical or ethical purposes it is no more possible to define a point in time than a point in space. Birth, life, death are all processes, very complicated processes. If we could determine the point at which life begins, the abortion issue would be immediately reconcilable. Some would take a position that whenever there is a possibility of life it has in fact begun and thus can all contraceptives under the argument that man should "be fruitful and multiply." While the 

Roman Catholic Church and some smaller sects adhere to this position, it is no longer socially tenable. All of the main line Protestant denominations allow the use of contraceptives and many Catholics use contraceptives, often with priestly approval, in spite of papal dicta. The issue of euthanasia squarely faces the same problem in the other direction. We do not allow putrefaction to occur before we agree that life is no longer present. Yet some would suggest that life no longer exists when no meaningful life is possible, such as an irreversible coma. They argue that comatose existence is not human living and should not be sustained.

The creation of life is a process of events, that, with increasing probability as the process moves, will produce a mature human being. There is a very low probability that an ovum will be fertilized by a sperm during or after coitus. Many conditions must be just right for fertilization to occur. There is a slightly higher probability that a fertilized ovum, a zygote, will find its way to the proper place and advance to the next developmental stage by attaching itself to the womb in order to obtain nurture. If one contends that life begins at conception then abortion of ectopic pregnancies must be disallowed. Similarly both the Morning 

After Pill and Intra Uterine Devices must be condemned since both are methods of contraception which permit the ovum to be fertilized but prevent it from cleaving to the wall of the uterus. Yet, Intra Uterine Devices are frequently and routinely used as contraceptive devices. For this reason some who argue for life at conception also argue that that it is not life until the zygote has nested and attached to the mother. Once it has attached itself to receive nurture it becomes a blastocyte. Judging from the number of miscarriages which occur it is still a matter of medium probability that the blastocyte will survive to maturation. 

The longer it survives, of course, the higher the probability that it will survive to birth. Brain and heart action do not commence until the end of the first trimester of pregnancy and under present medical knowledge viability ex utero is not possible until the end of the second trimester of pregnancy. Therefore, the agonizing dilemma is to decide at what point in the continuum of life we can say with some certainty that life is, and that life should be allowed to continue. 

Since viability occurs after the second trimester of pregnancy, laws are now framed to preclude abortion, except to save the life of the mother, beyond the second trimester. Actually, abortions beyond the first trimester are discouraged, even if not disallowed by most physicians.

For want of a better measure the medical profession now considers heart action and brain wave as the indications of life. When brain wave ceases death is said to occur even though some of the automatic responses can be sustained, particularly if respiration and heart stimulation are used. Certainly putrefaction can be averted by use of heart lung machines for at least some period of time after clinical death as has been demonstrated by perfusing organs for transplant. I would suggest a similar kind of judgment concerning the beginning of life. Thus life should not be considered present without heart and brain action, or prior to the completion of the first twelve weeks of development. 

In considering the presence of life we must also consider its quality. There is a difference between human life and human existence which I should like to delineate. Life without meaning and fulfilling potential is mere existence. It is living death left to the demand. The agony of the Flying Dutchman and other such mythical creatures as Prometheus is that they cannot die and their lives have no meaning. We should not consider human life to exist when that life is mere meaningless existence. Not only is it a burden to those around it, but it is a needless and pointless agony. While it may often be difficult to point to a life without meaning and argue for termination, certain occasions are easy to identify. Certainly life should not be encouraged if it cannot exist with meaning; nor should it be artificially promoted; nor should it be allowed if the birth can be prevented without endangering the mother needlessly and causing the fetus to survive possibly debilitated.

ABORTION ON DEMAND 

One fiction concerning abortions is the Women's Liberation point of view which argues for "abortion on demand." The adherents hold that any woman who desires an abortion should be able to obtain one from a physician. This is a fiction. Abortion should be obtainable, but not on demand. Nor for that matter should we provide appendectomies, tonsillectomies or medication on demand. 

Any medical process involves the patient and the physician. For this reason no one should ask a physician to perform an act which he opposes. Furthermore abortion also involves a third party, the father. It should never be performed without at least considering the father and allowing him an opportunity to participate in the decision.

Abortion is, like any portion of pregnancy, a difficult emotional experience. 

Counseling is needed to work through these emotions so that decisions are not made in panic to be regretted later through long nights of depression. Indeed no major surgical or medical procedure should be undertaken without proper counseling. One of the shortcomings of the medical profession is that its members do not use the counseling available to help their patients decide and live with their

decisions when they face difficult medical problems. Frequently these are normal problems not requiring psychiatrists or psychologists. Well trained social workers, clergy and other counselors can often help a person overcome the emotional trauma to be faced. 

Related to the issue of abortion on demand is the case involving a prospective mother still in her minority. Parents may intrude either to force an abortion or to prevent an abortion. For any woman sane and otherwise able to make decisions, the final decision must be hers. Abortions on demand by parents or by the government are clearly a violation of the woman's right to privacy. Equally, denial of abortion by parents or government when it is otherwise safe and indicated is also a violation of personal rights. The common element is that medical procedures are private and decisions concerning them should be left to the patient in conjunction with her physician and her counselor. 

THE ABORTIONIST 

Little research has yet been undertaken into effect of abortions on the abortionist. Yet stories about the trauma caused to the doctor and other medical attendants abound. Obviously, the effect differs from person to person, but clearly, performing abortions in the same context as providing maternity care presents a difficult emotional situation. This is particularly true with second trimester abortions which may result in the possibility of live birth. In one room a medical team may be fighting desperately to save the life of a 22 or 23 week fetus that has arrived early. In the next room they may be aborting at 21, or even in some cases, a 24 week old fetus.

Maternity care and delivery facilities should be separated from the facilities in which abortions are performed. There is no need to subject patients and medical staff to needless emotional difficulties. 

One word of caution needs to be added here. Just as no one should be forced to undergo an abortion, or for that matter any medical procedure, medical personnel should not be forced to perform procedures which they cannot, in good conscience, countenance. Abortion may be performed when desired by the patient and agreed to by the physician. The physician, in turn, must be certain that he is not requiring other medical personnel to act against their faith or their emotional and intellectual integrity.

THE HISTORY OF ABORTION 

Abortion is not a new issue. While medical knowledge and practice made abortion hazardous and unwise as a medical procedure prior to the 20th century, it was performed. Soranos of Ephesus (c A.D. 98-138) discussed abortion methods and listed the "following ways of achieving destruction of the embryo: purging the abdomen with clysters; walking about vigorously; carrying things beyond one's strength; bathing in sweet water which is not too hot; bathing in decoctions of linseed, mallow and wormwood; applying poultices of the same decoctions: injecting warm and sweet olive oil; being bled and then shaken after softening supositories.' ."3 Soranos continued by opposing the use of sharp instruments and by providing a list of contraceptive drugs.

Abortion was mentioned in the Hypocratic Oath which says in part, "I will not give a deadly drug to anyone if asked for it, nor to suggest it. Similarly I will not give a woman an abortifacient pessary." Abortion was suggested as a means of population control by Plato as well as by Aristotle. Aristotle insisted that it had to be performed before there is "sensation of life." 

The early Church opposed abortion. It was accused, as were the Jews, of child sacrifice. This was a very sensitive issue in those troubled times. Rome which practiced abortion was castigated for the pagan practice of abortion and child sacrifice via exposure. In the writings of the early Church fathers opposition to abortion was absolute.

During the Medieval period of our Church's history abortion was faced somewhat more realistically and arguments were put forth to justify abortion, at least in certain cases. These have already been discussed in this paper. Generally, they involved abortion to save the life of the mother or because of rape. In no case did the Church permit the risky procedure of abortion for the convenience 

John T. Noonan, "An Almost Absolute Value in History." The Morality of Abortion, taken from Soranos, "Gynecology," Corpus Medicorum Grecorum, p. 4.

or desire of the mother. Sexual intercourse was viewed as the method of procreation, a divine obligation, not to be tampered with or inhibited by man. 

Thus the Church until the 20th century generally prohibited any act which prevented conception and fruition as well as abortion. The suggestion that sexual intercourse might be beneficial for one's emotional life without the benefit of children was unthinkable prior to Freud. While birth control methods were available, they were at best untrustworthy. Sex without birth and birth without sex (parthogenesis not withstanding) are 20th century developments. While contraceptives were used, often without good results, for a long time, common use of contraceptives by married people did not begin until the 20th century. 

They were not generally accepted for use by unmarried people until the sexual revolution of the 1960's when large numbers of people, married and single, desired, and frequently were encouraged to use contraceptives. Abortion in the 

1970's is but a continuation of the mass acceptance of contraceptives. (For a complete review of the Church's historical position and rationale, one should read John Noonan's work already cited in this paper.) 

DENOMINATIONAL POSITIONS 

The position of modern day Christian Churches regarding the ethics of abortion is in a state of flux. Only recently, all ecclesiastic sources condemned it un equivocally. The Roman Catholic Church still does. What follows is a review of the position of some of the ecclesiastical judicatories concerning abortion. a. The Roman Catholic Church currently holds that a new life begins at conception and therefore forbids destruction of an embryo or fetus except in cases of indirect abortion when a remedy is used to effect a cure of a disease or condition of the mother likely to be fatal, which incidentally causes the death of the unborn child.

The Church's teaching is based on Canon 2350, on the action of Pope Benedict XV in 1917, and on the encyclical Casti Connubi, issued by Pope Pius XI in 1930. The encyclical states that "the life of each (mother and fetus) is equally sacred and no one has the power, not oven the public authority to destroy it." 

In his encyclical Humanae Vitae, issued in 1968, Pope Paul VI said: "We must once again declare that the direct interruption of the generative process already begun, and above all, directly willed and procured abortion, even if for therapeutic reasons, are to be absolutely excluded as licit means of regulating birth." 9 4 The Roman Catholic position remains unchanged as of 1973. Catholics have been among the leaders in opposing liberal abortion legislation and deploring the 

1973 United States Supreme Court Decision. b. The Jewish position concerning abortions varies among Orthodox, Conservative and Reform groups. The Orthodox take the most restrictive view and the 

Reformed the most liberal. In 1967 the Union of American Hebrew Congregations said: 

We commend those states which have enacted humane legislation in this area and we appeal to other states to do likewise and permit abortions under such circumstances as threatened disease or deformity of the embryo or fetus, threats to the physical or mental health of the mother, rape, and incest, and the social economic and psychological factors that might warrant therapeutic termination of pregnancy.

We urge our constituent congregations to join with other forward-looking citizens in securing needed revisions and liberalization of abortion laws.5 c. The American Baptist Convention (resolution adopted at meetings May 29June 1, 1968): "Recognizes that abortion should be a matter of responsible personal decision" and urges legislation that (1) the ending of a pregnancy before the twelfth week "be at the request of the individual(s) concerned and be regarded as an elective medical procedure governed by the laws regulating medical practice and licensure," and (2) after that period a pregnancy be terminated "only by a duly licensed physician at the request of the individual(s) concerned" for reasons suggested by the Model Penal Code of the American Law Institute (substantial risk to physical or mental health of the mother; risk that the child would be born with grave physical or mental defect; rape, incest, or other felonious acts as the cause of the pregnancy). 

4 Report for American Friends Committee, Who Shall Live?, p. 95. 

5 Quoted in Who Shall Live, op. cit., p. 98.

Further, we encourage our churches to provide sympathetic and realistic counseling on family planning and abortion.

We commend study, research, and development of understanding on the part of the populace led by the people of our churches toward an enlightened view of this provocative problem. d. The United Church of Christ at its 8th General Synod, June 25-29, 1971, published a four page opinion concerning abortion. In part it states: 

Inevitably ... a judgment will be made or assumed as to when personal human life begins and at what point society has an interest in it and affirms an obligation toward it. Although a form of life exists in the sperm and the unfertilized ovum, a new kind of life emerges at the moment of their union. Many regard conception (up to 72 hours after coitus), others implantation (seven days), as the beginning of an inviolable life. But while such life is human in origin and potentially human in character, the integration of bodily functions and the possibility of social interactions do not appear until later. Alternative candidates for the beginning of significantly human life are the final fixing of the genetic code (three weeks), the first central nervous system activity (eight weeks), brain development and cardiac activity (12 weeks). Some time after the twelfth week "quickening" occurs; that is, the mother can feel the arm and leg movements of the fetus. "Viability" in the present stage of technology begins between the 20th and the 28th week, and the fetus has a chance for survival outside the womb.

An ethical view does not require an undifferentiated concern for life. It places peculiar value upon personal life and upon the quality of life, both actual and potential. In that light it is understandable that today an increasing number of persons find it difficult, if not impossible, to attribute anything more than the potentiality of human personhood to the embryo in its early stages. The implication is that factors other than its existence may appropriately be given equal or greater weight at this time-the welfare of the whole family, its economic condition, the age of the parents, their view of the optimum number of children consonant with their resources and the pressures of population, their vocational and social objectives, for example.

On the other hand, many would agree that during the later months of a normal pregnancy life should not be interrupted except for the most serious reasons (such as the physical or mental health of the mother, abnormality or disease of the fetus, incest, or rape).

This distinction is of the greatest importance. Individuals contemplating an abortion should make a responsible decision early, certainly within the first two or three months.

LEGISLATIVE POLICY 

The theological and scientific views on when human life begins are so numerous and varied that one particular view should not be forced on society through its legal system.

Present laws prohibiting abortion are neither just nor enforceable. They compel women either to bear unwanted children or to seek illegal abortions regardless of the medical hazards and suffering involved. By severely limiting access to safe abortions, these laws have the effect of discriminating against the poor. 

For these reasons, the Eighth General Synod of the United Church of Christ calls for the repeal of all legal prohibitions of physician-performed abortions. 

This would take abortion out of the realm of penal law and make voluntary and medically safe abortions legally available to all women. Simultaneously we ask that adequate protection be given to "conscientious objectors" against abortion, including physicians, nurses and prospective mothers." e. The United Methodist Church has studied the abortion problem and issued the following position in 1972:

The beginning of life and the ending of life are the God-given boundaries of human existence. While individuals have always had some degree of control over when they would die, they now have some degree over when and even whether new individuals will be born. Our belief in the sanctity of unborn human life makes us reluctant to approve abortion. But we are equally bound to respect the sacredness of the life and well-being of the mother, for whom devastating damage may result from unacceptable pregnancy. In continuity with past
